d_transformation.contrast_type: Trajectory group vs no or very low social media use trajectory group (low increasing vs reference; high increasing vs reference), adjusted mean difference in year-2 NIH Toolbox score points
d_transformation.native_metric: B (adjusted mean difference vs reference trajectory group)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Dichotomous (group-contrast) IV on continuous DV: d = (M_group - M_reference) / SD_pooled, using the adjusted mean difference B as the numerator and SD_DV as the denominator; CI endpoints converted the same way (d_lo = B_lo / SD_DV, d_hi = B_hi / SD_DV).
d_transformation.notes: No whole-sample or pooled SD of the cognitive outcomes is reported. sd_dv is set to the unadjusted weighted SD of the reference group (no or very low use) from the Table top panel (p. 1949): Flanker 14.2, ORRT 16.9, PSMT 16.2, Pattern comparison 20.8, PVT 15.6, Total composite 10.6. Comparison-group SDs are similar (low increasing: 14.0, 15.9, 16.5, 20.7, 14.6, 10.4; high increasing: 14.6, 14.1, 16.1, 21.3, 14.4, 10.4), so a pooled SD would differ little; coders may instead compute a pooled SD from the two groups' SDs and their shares (57.6%, 36.6%, 5.8% of N = 6554, weighted), or use the normative NIH Toolbox SD of 15 that the authors cite in the Discussion. sd_iv is not applicable (categorical IV). The resulting d is a group contrast, not a per-1-SD or per-hour effect, so it is not directly comparable to continuous-IV d values from other papers. Outcome score type (uncorrected vs age-corrected) is not stated in the letter.

papers.extraction_flags:
This paper is a 2-page JAMA Research Letter.What was extracted: one model, M1. It is a weighted multiple linear regression with robust standard errors, comparing 2 social media trajectory groups (low increasing and high increasing) against the no-or-very-low-use reference group, across 6 NIH Toolbox outcomes at year 2. That gives 12 estimates, all copied from the Table on p. 1949. I checked every value against the PDF text layer and they all match.

Things a human should verify:
1. Supplement missing. Supplement 1 (eMethods: how the trajectory model was built, the social media item, exclusions, ABCD release, race breakdown) is not in the PDF. Those fields are marked "not reported in the letter."
2. sd_dv is my choice, not the paper's. The paper gives no whole-sample or pooled SD. I used the reference group's unadjusted weighted SD from the Table. Coders may prefer a pooled SD or the normed SD of 15 the authors cite. All group SDs are recorded in the notes.
3. IV and DV overlap in time. Trajectories cover baseline to year 2 (the Figure shows ages 9-13), and the outcome is measured at year 2. So the exposure is not strictly before the outcome.
4. Exact p-values missing for some cells. Cells printed as "<.001" have p set to null, with the printed label kept in p_label.
5. d is a group contrast. It compares groups rather than measuring per hour or per SD, so it is not directly comparable to estimates from continuous-IV papers.
6. Covariate details are thin. Site is entered as a covariate, not a random effect. "Other screen time" components and the score type (uncorrected vs age-corrected) are not specified.

excluded_models.model: Group-based trajectory model of social media time (baseline to year 2)
excluded_models.location: Methods p. 1948; Figure p. 1948; eMethods in Supplement 1 (not in this PDF)
excluded_models.why: Measurement step that derives the IV (trajectory classes); it pairs social media time only with age/time, not with an individual-trait outcome, and produces no phone/SM-trait estimate.

excluded_models.model: Unadjusted weighted means (SD) by trajectory group

excluded_models.model: Adjusted means (95% CI) by trajectory group
excluded_models.why: Model-predicted group means from the same regression as M1; the contrasts against the reference group are already captured by the Difference in mean estimates.

primary_models.dv: Year-2 NIH Toolbox Cognition Battery scores, run as six separate outcomes: Flanker test, Oral Reading Recognition Test (ORRT), Picture Sequence Memory Test (PSMT), Pattern Comparison Processing Speed, Picture Vocabulary Test (PVT), and total composite score. Score type (uncorrected vs age-corrected standard scores) is not stated; the Discussion refers to an NIH Toolbox standard deviation of 15. Unadjusted weighted means (SD) for the reference group (no or very low use): Flanker 97.6 (14.2), ORRT 103.5 (16.9), PSMT 108.2 (16.2), Pattern comparison 108.3 (20.8), PVT 106.3 (15.6), Total composite 104.8 (10.6). Low increasing group: 95.4 (14.0), 99.4 (15.9), 104.7 (16.5), 107.8 (20.7), 99.6 (14.6), 101.4 (10.4). High increasing group: 94.3 (14.6), 96.7 (14.1), 100.3 (16.1), 106.9 (21.3), 94.8 (14.4), 98.6 (10.4). No whole-sample SD is reported.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table, bottom panel 'Difference in mean (95% CI)' (p. 1949); results text p. 1948; interpreted in Discussion p. 1948. Trajectory derivation described in eMethods in Supplement 1 (not bundled in this PDF).
primary_models.estimation: Multiple linear regression with robust standard errors, one model per cognitive outcome (6 outcomes). Software not reported in the letter. Sampling weights based on the American Community Survey (US Census) applied. Site entered as a covariate; no random effects described. Trajectory groups estimated beforehand with group-based trajectory modeling (details in eMethods, Supplement 1). Alpha not stated (P < .05 treated as significant in text). No multiple-comparison correction reported. No interaction tests, stratified models or sensitivity analyses reported in the letter.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal design using three ABCD time points: baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10), year 1 (2017-2019) and year 2 (2018-2020). Social media time (hours per day) from baseline to year 2 was summarized into trajectory groups with group-based trajectory modeling; the Figure plots trajectories over ages 9 to 13 years. Trajectory group is the IV; cognitive performance at year 2 is the DV (one score per child, not repeated measures), with the respective baseline cognitive score entered as a covariate. Note that the IV window (baseline to year 2) overlaps the DV time point (year 2), so the exposure is not strictly prior to the outcome. No interaction or stratified analyses are reported.

iv_axis.label: Low increasing SM trajectory vs no/very low
High increasing SM trajectory vs no/very low

primary_models.sample: ABCD Study, release not stated in the letter. Analytic N = 6554 adolescents; 51.1% male and 48.9% female. Baseline ages 9-10 years. Exclusion criteria and race/ethnicity breakdown are not reported in the letter (possibly in Supplement 1, which is not in this PDF). Trajectory group sizes: no or very low social media use 57.6%, low increasing 36.6%, high increasing 5.8%.
primary_models.iv: Social media time trajectory group, a 3-level categorical variable derived by group-based trajectory modeling of youth-reported social media time (hours per day) from baseline to year 2. Groups: no or very low social media use (57.6%, +0.3 h/d by age 13 years; reference), low increasing social media use (36.6%, +1.3 h/d), high increasing social media use (5.8%, +3.0 h/d). Entered as two indicator variables against the reference group, so each estimate is an adjusted mean difference between a trajectory group and the no or very low use group. The underlying social media time item and GBTM specification are described only in eMethods (Supplement 1).

papers.title: Addictive Screen Use Trajectories and Suicidal Behaviors, Suicidal Ideation, and Mental Health in US Youths
papers.extraction_flags:
I checked them all against the Figure 3 adjusted column (p. 224) and against the text.

1. Where the numbers come from: all estimates are taken from Figure 3, which is a forest plot with printed values, not a table. No supplement is bundled in the PDF, so eFigures 1-3 (models also adjusted for screen time), eTable 5 and eAppendix 5 could not be checked.

2. p0 placement is non-standard: the reference group is the low trajectory, and its event rate differs by platform (social media low 3.0% / 14.2%; mobile phone low 2.7% / 13.3%). So I stored p0 on each estimate as an extra field. The dv_axis p0 holds only the whole-sample prevalence (5.1% / 17.9%) as a fallback, and that should not be used because up to 49% of the sample is exposed. Check whether the d pipeline reads p0 per estimate. If it doesn't, M1 may need to be split into a social media card and a phone card.

3. SD_DV for M2: I used the analytic-sample year 4 SDs (internalizing 10.8, externalizing 9.3, from the Table on p. 222) instead of 10 by construction. These SDs cover N = 4,285, but the CBCL models use N = 4,206.

4. P values and significance calls:
   - Only FDR-adjusted P values quoted in the text are recorded. Most are printed as "<.001", so p is null with p_label filled in.
   - For the phone increasing trajectory and suicidal ideation (RR 1.22, CI 1.01-1.48), the text prints FDR P < .001, which looks implausibly small for that CI. I copied it as printed.
   - For the phone high trajectory and internalizing (0.66, CI 0.00 to 1.33), no P is printed and the CI touches 0. The text does not report it as an association, so I coded it non-significant. Please verify.
   - For the other cells with no printed P value, significance was inferred from whether the CI excludes the null and from the text.

5. Design caveats:
   - The exposure is a hard class assignment from latent class mixed models, so classification uncertainty is not carried into the outcome models.
   - The last exposure wave (year 4) is the same wave as the outcomes, so the analysis is not strictly prospective.
   - No site or family clustering and no weights are described.

6. Exact covariate coding of income, education and marital status is not stated; the equations assume the categories shown in the Table.

7. Excluded as not phone/SM: the video game trajectory estimates (VGAQ) were excluded under FT-IC2 clarification 2. The baseline total screen time analysis (Figure 4) was excluded because it bundles TV, gaming and phone/SM with no breakout.

8. Possibly extractable: baseline clinical differences between trajectory classes (text p. 222) were left out as descriptive. A human coder may want to reconsider them.

primary_models.equation: log(E[Y_i]) = b0 + b1*HighTraj_i + b2*IncreasingTraj_i + b3*age_i + b4*sex_i + b5..b8*race_ethnicity_i + b9*income_i + b10*parent_education_i + b11..b12*marital_status_i + b13*baseline_suicidal_ideation_i + b14*baseline_suicidal_behaviors_i + b15*baseline_CBCL_internalizing_i + b16*baseline_CBCL_externalizing_i, where Y is year 4 suicidal behaviors or suicidal ideation (0/1) and HighTraj/IncreasingTraj are dummies for one platform's trajectory classes (low = reference). RR = exp(b1) or exp(b2). Exact dummy coding of income, education, and marital status is not stated.

primary_models.estimation: Poisson regression with robust standard errors to estimate risk ratios for binary outcomes. All analyses in R version 4.3.1. Trajectories were estimated first with latent class linear mixed models (lcmm package, ref 37), fit separately for each platform on age and quadratic age; the number of classes was chosen by lowest BIC, average posterior probability >70%, odds of correct classification >5.0, and minimum class size 5% (eTable 4, eAppendix 4; supplement not bundled). Class membership was then treated as a categorical exposure (hard assignment; classification uncertainty is not carried into the outcome model). Two-sided alpha = .05 with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction within each group of tests. No survey weights, site clustering, or family clustering are described. Sensitivity analyses: (1) adding baseline total screen time as a covariate (eFigures 1-3, supplement not bundled; text says associations were not altered and screen time was not independently associated); (2) COVID-19 timing (eAppendix 5, not bundled; described as consistent); (3) E-values for unmeasured confounding, range 1.10-4.21 (p. 223). No sex or race interaction tests or stratified estimates are reported.

primary_models.dv: Two binary year 4 outcomes from child- and parent-reported KSADS (past year). Suicidal ideation = any of passive ideation, nonspecific active ideation, specific active ideation, active ideation with intent, or active ideation with plan and intent endorsed by youth or caregiver: 760/4,240 (17.9%). Suicidal behaviors = any of preparatory actions for imminent suicidal behavior, interrupted attempt, aborted attempt, or suicide attempt endorsed by youth or caregiver: 218/4,240 (5.1%) (Table, p. 222).
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort. Exposure is membership in an addictive-use trajectory class estimated from SMAQ or MPIQ scores at the year 2, year 3, and year 4 follow-ups (ages about 11 to 15). Outcomes are suicidal behaviors and suicidal ideation over the prior year assessed at year 4, so the last exposure measurement is concurrent with the outcome assessment. Baseline (year 0) suicidal ideation, suicidal behaviors, and CBCL symptoms are adjusted for. One outcome observation per child; not repeated measures. Social media and mobile phone trajectories enter separate models (each with its own low-trajectory reference), and each outcome is modeled separately.

primary_models.sample: ABCD Study release 5.1, baseline (2016-2018) through year 4 follow-up (data through January 2022), 21 US sites. Of 11,868 baseline participants, 7,233 were excluded for not completing any of the year 2, 3, or 4 follow-up surveys (year 4 data limited to the available random subset, n = 4,754), and 350 more for missing age, sex, race and ethnicity, parental income, marital status, or parental education, giving an analytic sample of 4,285. CHAID analysis showed no selection bias versus participants without year 4 data (eAppendix 1, supplement not bundled). Outcome-specific N: 4,240 completed the KSADS suicidal behaviors and ideation items; 4,206 completed the CBCL. Baseline mean age 10.0 (SD 0.6) years; 2,051 (47.9%) female, 2,234 (52.1%) male; 96 (2.2%) Asian, 426 (9.9%) Black, 830 (19.4%) Hispanic, 2,515 (58.7%) White, 418 (9.8%) multiracial and/or other. Household income <$75,000: 1,722 (40.2%). Parents married 3,138 (73.2%); parental education below bachelor's 1,474 (34.4%). Binary-outcome models use N = 4,240. Year 4 prevalence: suicidal behaviors 218 (5.1%), suicidal ideation 760 (17.9%).

primary_models.iv: Trajectory class membership from latent class linear mixed models fit separately per platform to repeated addictive-use scores (years 2, 3, and 4 follow-up; ages about 11 to 15) on age and age squared. Social media addictive use was measured with the 6-item Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ; Likert 1 = never to 6 = very often), mobile phone addictive use with the 8-item Mobile Phone Involvement Questionnaire (MPIQ; 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). Scores are CFA-weighted (range: social media 4.5-26.8, mobile phone 5.6-39.5); Cronbach alpha = 0.88 per scale. Youths without social media accounts or mobile phones were assigned 1 (never / strongly disagree) on skipped items. Social media classes: high-peaking (n = 410, 9.6%), increasing (n = 1,342, 31.3%), low (n = 2,533, 59.1%). Mobile phone classes: high (n = 2,109, 49.2%), increasing (n = 1,052, 24.6%), low (n = 1,124, 26.2%). Classes were dummy coded with the low trajectory of that platform as reference, so each estimate is a class-vs-low contrast within one platform's model.

primary_models.iv: Trajectory class membership from latent class linear mixed models fit separately per platform to repeated addictive-use scores (years 2, 3, and 4 follow-up; ages about 11 to 15) on age and age squared. Social media addictive use was measured with the 6-item Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ; Likert 1 = never to 6 = very often), mobile phone addictive use with the 8-item Mobile Phone Involvement Questionnaire (MPIQ; 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). Scores are CFA-weighted (range: social media 4.5-26.8, mobile phone 5.6-39.5); Cronbach alpha = 0.88 per scale. Youths without social media accounts or mobile phones were assigned 1 (never / strongly disagree) on skipped items. Social media classes: high-peaking (n = 410, 9.6%), increasing (n = 1,342, 31.3%), low (n = 2,533, 59.1%). Mobile phone classes: high (n = 2,109, 49.2%), increasing (n = 1,052, 24.6%), low (n = 1,124, 26.2%). Classes were dummy coded with the low trajectory of that platform as reference, so each estimate is a class-vs-low contrast within one platform's model.

These are stored per estimate as 'p0' because the reference groups differ by platform; dv_axis p0 holds the whole-sample prevalence (5.1%, 17.9%) only as a fallback and should not be used because exposure prevalence is far above 10%. SD_DV for M2 is from the Table (p. 222): year 4 CBCL internalizing SD 10.8, externalizing SD 9.3 in the analytic sample (not SD 10 by construction, since the sample SD is reported). Using the marginal SD rather than a within-group pooled SD is an approximation. The year 4 CBCL SDs are for all 4,285 participants, while the CBCL models use N = 4,206.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: OR = RR*(1-p0)/(1-RR*p0); d = ln(OR)*sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), with p0 = observed event rate in that platform's low-trajectory reference group. M2: d = B / SD_DV (adjusted mean difference over the analytic-sample SD of the year 4 outcome as an approximation to the pooled SD).

primary_models.equation: Observed: SM[i,t] = mu_SM[t] + RI_SM[i] + w_SM[i,t] (+ fixed covariates); DEP[i,t] = mu_DEP[t] + RI_DEP[i] + w_DEP[i,t] (+ fixed covariates), t = 0,1,2,3. Within-person: w_SM[i,t] = a_t*w_SM[i,t-1] + c_t*w_DEP[i,t-1] + u_SM[i,t]; w_DEP[i,t] = b_t*w_DEP[i,t-1] + d_t*w_SM[i,t-1] + u_DEP[i,t], t = 1,2,3; cov(u_SM[i,t], u_DEP[i,t]) estimated each wave; cov(RI_SM, RI_DEP) estimated. Focal: d_t (SM -> later depression) and c_t (depression -> later SM), freely estimated per interval. Covariates: sex, race/ethnicity, income, parental education, ACEs, parental monitoring, family conflict, study site.
primary_models.iv: In the SM-to-depression direction, the IV is youth-reported time spent on social media, ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, administered each year. Hours and minutes per weekday and weekend day were combined as [(weekday mean x 5) + (weekend mean x 2)]/7 = mean daily hours. Descriptives (Table 2, untransformed hours/day, M (SD)): baseline 0.12 (0.42), year 1 0.22 (0.60), year 2 0.68 (1.54), year 3 1.21 (2.05). Table 2 footnote states the social media variables were transformed in the final analytic model because years 0-1 were reported in ordinal categories and years 2-3 in continuous hours (0-24); the exact transformation is described only in Supplement 1. In the reverse direction, social media time at the next wave is the DV. The focal predictor in each cross-lagged path is the within-person deviation from the person's own mean, not raw hours.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Results, Within-Person Associations and Between-Person Association (pp. 5-6); Figure 2 (p. 6); full parameter table is eTable 3 in Supplement 1 (not bundled in this PDF); model fit comparison in Results p. 4-5 and eTable 1; interpreted in Abstract, Key Points, Discussion pp. 6-7 and Conclusions p. 7.
primary_models.estimation: Structural equation model in lavaan, R version 4.4.2; maximum likelihood with robust SEs (MLR) and scaled test statistic; full information maximum likelihood for missing outcome data. No survey weights reported. Final unconstrained RI-CLPM fit: CFI 0.977, TLI 0.968, RMSEA 0.031 (90% CI 0.029-0.033), SRMR 0.022. Traditional CLPM: CFI 0.917, TLI 0.807, RMSEA 0.132; constrained RI-CLPM: CFI 0.966, TLI 0.957, RMSEA 0.036, SRMR 0.027. Two-sided P < .05; no multiple-comparison correction reported. Standardized cross-lagged effects interpreted against Orth et al benchmarks (small 0.03, medium 0.07, large 0.12). No sex or other interaction/stratified analyses reported in the main text.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal panel with 4 annual waves (baseline, year 1, year 2, year 3; ABCD 5.1, follow-up through 2022). Social media time and depressive symptoms are both measured at every wave and modeled reciprocally. Latent random intercepts separate stable between-person differences from within-person (state-like) deviations; autoregressive and cross-lagged paths are estimated among the within-person components, plus within-wave residual covariances. The final model is the unconstrained RI-CLPM, which lets cross-lagged paths differ across intervals, so each interval (baseline to year 1, year 1 to year 2, year 2 to year 3) gets its own estimate in both directions. The authors compared this against a traditional CLPM (poor fit) and a constrained RI-CLPM before retaining the unconstrained version as final.

Analytic sample N = 11,876 after excluding participants missing baseline age or sex assigned at birth; all available data retained at each wave via full information maximum likelihood, so wave-specific Ns vary (social media use: 11,832 baseline, 11,175 year 1, 10,370 year 2, 10,301 year 3; depressive symptoms: 11,859, 11,199, 10,895, 10,093; Table 2). d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines §4a, SEM standardized path). Applied to CI endpoints for d CI.
d_transformation.notes: Estimates are already standardized, so SD_IV / SD_DV are not needed; sd_iv/sd_dv left null. Table 2 (p. 5) gives untransformed SDs for reference, but the social media variables were transformed in the final model (method described only in Supplement 1), so those SDs do not correspond to the modeled metric. Standardization is of within-person latent deviations, so the derived d reflects within-person effects and is not directly comparable to between-person per-SD-of-hours d's from other papers. Year-2 residual covariance (0.08) is read off Figure 2 without CI. Random-intercept covariance sign differs between text (-0.01) and Figure 2 (r = 0.01).

papers.extraction_flags:
1. The PDF has only the 10-page article. Supplement 1 (eMethods, eTables 1-3) is not included, so the full parameter table (eTable 3), the covariate effects (eTable 2) and the transformation applied to the social media variable all come from the main text and Figure 2 only.
2. The paper does not say how social media time was transformed in the final model (years 0-1 were reported in ordinal categories, years 2-3 in continuous hours). The Table 2 SDs are untransformed, so sd_iv/sd_dv are left null. That is fine because the betas are already standardized.
3. The random-intercept covariance sign does not match: the text and Abstract print -0.01 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.02, P = .46), but Figure 2 labels it r = 0.01. I used the text value.
4. The year-2 within-wave residual covariance (r = 0.08) comes only from the Figure 2 label. It is drawn in black (significant), but no CI or p is printed.
5. Coders should decide whether the non-directional covariances (the random-intercept covariance and the year-2 and year-3 residual covariances) belong in the matrix or should be struck. The 6 cross-lagged paths are the core estimates.
6. The derived d from standardized within-person RI-CLPM paths is a within-person effect. It is not comparable to between-person d per SD of hours from other papers.
7. Table 1 prints parent education as college or more 17.2% and high school or less 82.8%. That looks inverted, but I copied it as printed.
8. p values printed as <.001 are stored as 0.001, with p_label "<.001".

This paper has no qualifying phone/SM estimate in the bundled PDF, so primary_models is []. The PDF is the 9-page article only; Supplement 1 is not included. Every printed model uses total daily screen time as the IV. That variable bundles TV, videos and videogames, so it fails FT-IC2 Step 2. The communication subcategory (texting + social media + video chat) qualifies under Step 2, and the Methods define it as an exploratory analysis. But the article body gives no number for it, only the narrative line in the Discussion on p. 1005 that "communication time effects did not involve sleep duration". Any communication-time coefficients are in Supplement 1 (eResults, eTables), which I could not read. A human should get Supplement 1 from JAMA Pediatrics and extract the communication-time models from there. If those models turn out to have no printed coefficients either, the Stage 2 INCLUDE decision should be revisited under FT-EC4. SD_IV is available from Table 1 (communication time M 0.4, SD 0.8 h/day, N = 976). SD_DV for the CBCL depressive score (raw score, not a T-score) is not in the article body. Spot-checked against the PDF: 0.12 (0.04-0.20, P = .008); -0.21 (-0.28 to -0.14); Fig 3 path -0.23 (-0.28 to -0.16); 36.4% (18.2%-63.6%); F = 19.05; Table 1 communication 0.4 (0.8).json

primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed-effects model (software not stated in main text). Significance defined by Bonferroni correction across tests (Figure 2 caption); only significant cells are colored and labeled with beta in Figure 2. SEs and p-values in Table S1. The coefficient is described as beta but, given magnitudes (e.g., -4.28 per daily hour), appears to be unstandardized. Associations significant at both waves were passed to one-sample Mendelian randomization (Figure 1, Figure 3). No sex or other interaction tests reported.
primary_models.design: Two separate cross-sectional analyses of ABCD data: one at baseline (ages ~9-10) and one at the 2-year follow-up (ages ~11-13). At each wave, screen use and the outcome are measured at the same wave. The authors treat associations significant at both waves as 'consistent' (Figure 2 right panel) and only carried those forward to Mendelian randomization. No pooled repeated-measures model and no wave-by-IV interaction is described in the main text. Each of the six screen activities and reading time is entered in a separate model per outcome (the figure reports one coefficient per activity x outcome); whether activities were entered jointly is not stated in the main text.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study (release not stated in main text). Baseline analytic n = 7107; 2-year follow-up n = 4505 (Table 1, p. 3). Household income <$11,999 0.28, $12,000-24,999 0.14, $25,000-49,999 0.23, $50,000-99,999 0.25, >$100,000 0.10 at baseline (follow-up proportions differ: 0.05/0.05/0.13/0.28/0.49). primary_models.name: Linear mixed-effects regression of NIH Toolbox cognition and CBCL syndrome scores on daily texting, social networking site, and video chat hours, fit separately at baseline and 2-year follow-up
primary_models.iv: Daily hours of three phone/SM activities from the ABCD youth screen time questionnaire, each analysed as its own IV: Text = texting on a cell phone, tablet, or computer; SNS = visiting social networking sites; VC = video chatting. Units are hours per day (Table 1 reports M +/- SD in hours). Baseline: Text 0.19 +/- 0.42 (41% any use), SNS 0.09 +/- 0.31 (17%), VC 0.16 +/- 0.38 (36%). 2-year follow-up: Text 0.53 +/- 0.96 (67%), SNS 0.51 +/- 1.10 (45%), VC 0.33 +/- 0.77 (43%). The weekday/weekend weighting used to form daily hours is not described in the main text. The same models were also run for TVM, Video, Game, and reading time (not phone/SM; not extracted).
primary_models.equation: Outcome[i] = b0 + b1*ScreenActivity_hours[i] + b2..bk*covariates (sex, household income, parental education, others unspecified in main text) + random effect(s) (unspecified in main text) + e[i]; fit separately at baseline and 2-year follow-up for each activity x outcome pair
primary_models.dv: Five NIH Toolbox cognition scores (picture vocabulary, flanker, pattern comparison processing speed, picture sequence memory, oral reading recognition) and eight CBCL syndrome scales (anxious/depressed, withdrawn/depressed, somatic complaints, social problems, thought problems, attention problems, rule-breaking behavior, aggressive behavior). Higher cognition = better ability; higher CBCL = more problems. Whether NIH Toolbox scores are uncorrected or age-corrected standard scores, and whether CBCL scales are raw or T-scores, is not stated in the main text. No descriptive statistics for the DVs are given in the main text.

covariates.detail: The Experimental Section (p. 9) defers model details to the Supporting Information. The Discussion (p. 8) says sex, household income, and parental education were taken as covariates 'in our analysis'; the full LME covariate set and random-effects structure (e.g., site, family) are not stated in the main text.

papers.extraction_flags:
1) The Supporting Information (Tables S1-S10) is not in the PDF. M1 has 78 cells, and only the 23 significant ones have values. I copied those values from the cell labels in the Figure 2 heatmap; the figure is an image, so I read them off zoomed renders of the page. The other 55 cells are blank in the figure (not significant after Bonferroni), so their B is null. SEs and exact p-values exist only in Table S1. Someone with the supplement should fill these in.

2) The Results text and Figure 2 disagree in several places:
- Text x picture vocabulary: the text says -0.93 and -1.56. The figure shows -2.20 at baseline and -0.93 at follow-up.
- VC x picture vocabulary: the text says -2.11 and -2.64. The figure shows -3.18 and -2.11.
- VC x picture sequence memory: the text says -1.46 and -1.90. The figure shows -2.43 at baseline and a blank (not significant) cell at follow-up. The -1.46 in the figure belongs to VC x oral reading recognition at follow-up.
I entered the figure values and explained each mismatch in the cell notes. Check these against Table S1.

3) The main text does not list the LME covariates, the random effects, the software, or whether the DV scores are raw, T-scores or age-corrected. The only covariates named are sex, income and parental education (Discussion, p. 8). Because of this, SD_DV is unknown for M1 and its cells cannot be converted to d. The coefficients are called beta but look unstandardized.

4) M1 is two separate cross-sectional LMEs: baseline (n=7107) and 2-year follow-up (n=4505). I coded the IVs by wave so each cell gets the SD for its own wave.

5) M2 is the one-sample MR of Text, SNS and VC on daily reading time (Table 2). I treated reading time as a qualifying behavioral outcome; please confirm that eligibility call. Only SEs are printed, so CI fields are null. SNS p is printed as "0.000". Text has p=0.045 but is not bolded, so I marked it non-significant under the authors' Bonferroni rule. Its d conversion uses the baseline reading-time SD of 0.67, on the assumption that the MR used baseline data.

6) M3 is a single reverse-MR estimate with phone/SM as the outcome: picture vocabulary -> VC hours, B=-0.001, corrected p<10^-8. It comes from the text only. The MR analytic n and confounders are not reported in the main text.

7) Several analyses were excluded because the main text gives only a range or unlabeled plot points: the forward MR for Text, SNS and VC (Figure 3a), the mediation and two-step MR indirect effects (Figure 6b/6d, Tables S7/S9), and the LME of screen use on reading time (Figure 6a/Table S6). A coder with the supplement could add them.

d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 hour/day of the screen activity (M1, M2); per 1 picture-vocabulary score point (M3); converted to per 1 SD of IV
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV for Text, SNS, and VC at each wave comes from Table 1 (p. 3): baseline Text 0.42, SNS 0.31, VC 0.38; follow-up Text 0.96, SNS 1.10, VC 0.77. M2 is convertible: SD_DV for daily reading time is 0.67 at baseline (Table 1); the MR wave is taken as baseline from Results p. 4. M1 is not convertible as extracted because no SDs for the NIH Toolbox or CBCL scores are reported in the main text and the score metric (raw vs. T-score; uncorrected vs. age-corrected) is not stated, so SD_DV cannot be assumed to be 10 or 15. M3 is not convertible because the SD of picture vocabulary is not reported. No CIs are printed anywhere in the main text (Table 2 gives SE only), so derived d CIs are unavailable. Non-significant M1 cells have no printed value (Table S1 only).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1)

d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 additional hour/day of the modality at baseline
d_transformation.notes: Chinn conversion of the aOR yields d for a 1 hour/day contrast, not a 1-SD contrast. Baseline SDs of the IVs are in Table 1 (p. 889): texting 0.56, video chat 0.52, social networking 0.45 h/day, so 1 hour/day is roughly 1.8-2.2 SD of these IVs; a per-SD rescaling would be ln(OR)*SD_IV before the Chinn step if needed for comparability. p0 = 0.011 is the weighted one-year follow-up BED prevalence in the full sample (Table 1), not an unexposed-group rate; it is not needed for the OR conversion. The outcome is rare (1.1%), so OR approximates RR.

d_transformation.notes: SD_IV from Table 2 (p. 398), baseline analytic sample: social media 0.38, social engagement 0.79. SD_DV taken as the 2-year follow-up SD of the raw task score from Table 2 (Flanker 7.49, Pattern Comparison 15.09, Picture Sequence Memory 12.14, Picture Vocabulary 8.31, Oral Reading 6.50), because the DV is the T2 score. B is conditional on the baseline score (residual change), so the derived d expresses the association with residualized change scaled by the raw T2 SD, not by the residual SD, which makes it smaller than a d on residualized change would be. No CIs are reported (only SE), so d CIs are not computed. Social media is highly right-skewed (M 0.10, SD 0.38 h), so per-SD contrasts reflect a small number of heavy users.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) I counted 'social engagement' (texting + video chat, summed weighted daily hours) as a qualifying IV. It is a composite built only from phone/SM items, so it passes FT-IC2 Step 2, and the texting item says 'cell phone, tablet, or computer'. Coders should confirm this. 2) Each lifestyle factor was fit in its own model, so the social media B is not adjusted for the other screen types. 3) For SD_DV I used the 2-year follow-up raw-score SDs from Table 2. B comes from a residual change model (it conditions on the baseline score), so d scaled by the raw T2 SD is a convention choice to check. 4) Only SE is reported, so CIs are null. Several p values are printed as '< 0.001', so p is left null and p_label is filled in. Significance follows the pFDR asterisks. 5) The social media x sex interactions and the semi-partial R2 values are only in the Supporting Information (Tables S2-S5), which is not bundled in the PDF. 6) Race/ethnicity of the sample is not reported. 7) Unrelated quirks in the paper: sleep duration on the Flanker is marked significant at pFDR 0.119*, and the text gives SE = -3.03 for the sex interaction. primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed-effects models fit with lmer in R version 2023.09.0. Random intercept for family ID; no site random effect or survey weights reported. Complete-case analysis, no imputation. FDR correction (pFDR < 0.05) applied separately for each outcome across the eight lifestyle-factor models; significance markers in Tables 3-4 refer to pFDR. Exploratory sex moderation tested for all associations; only passive watching (Flanker) and physical activity (Picture Sequence Memory) were significant and stratified in Table 5; text states sex did not significantly moderate any other associations, with nonsignificant interaction output in Supporting Information Tables S4-S5 (not in the PDF). No sensitivity analyses for the social media or social engagement estimates are reported.
primary_models.sample: ABCD release 5.1, baseline and 2-year follow-up. Complete-case analytic sample of N = 7043 adolescents (complete data on cognitive scores at both time points, all lifestyle factors, and covariates); 52.2% male, 47.8% female. Mean age 118.98 months (SD 7.50) at baseline and 144.32 months (SD 8.03) at follow-up. Mean income-to-needs ratio 3.46 (SD 2.28); average parent education 15.08 years (SD 2.63). Race/ethnicity breakdown not reported. Baseline visits 100% in person; at 2-year follow-up 92.3% in person, 0.3% remote, 7.4% hybrid (Table 2, p. 398).
primary_models.design: Longitudinal, two waves (ABCD baseline and 2-year follow-up). Each lifestyle factor is measured at baseline and each cognitive task score at the 2-year follow-up (T2) is the DV, with the same task score at baseline (T1) entered as a predictor (residual change score model). One observation per child; the outcome is a single follow-up score, not repeated measures. Each lifestyle factor was entered as the sole predictor in a separate model, giving eight models per outcome; social media and social engagement therefore each have their own model per outcome and are not mutually adjusted for other screen types. No time x IV interaction; a negative B means smaller increase in the task score from baseline to follow-up per additional hour of the IV.

papers.extraction_flags:
All 12 estimates were checked against the table images on pp. 351-352 and match.

Items to verify:

(1) The paper prints no p-values. The sig flags come from whether the 95% CI excludes 1 and from what the authors say in the text. Two CIs have a lower bound printed as 1.00: Table 2 Wave 1 mild SMA, Model 2, PR 1.35 (1.00-1.84), and Table 3 mild SMA, Model 3, RR 1.37 (1.00-1.87). The authors call both non-significant, so I set sig false.

(2) The p0 values are marginal BE prevalences I computed from reported counts: Wave 1 is 249/1940 = 0.128 and Wave 3 is 237/1940 = 0.122. The paper does not report the BE rate in the reference group. The mild SMA group (24.6%) and the increased trajectory class (23.5%) are each more than 10% of the sample, so the RR-to-OR step is approximate for those cells.

(3) M1 is cross-sectional and reports prevalence ratios. I coded it as native_metric "other:PR" with value fields. A PR converts to d the same way as an RR, so check whether the pipeline needs "RR" here instead.

(4) SMT is per 1 hour/day and the paper reports no SD for it, so the d for SMT is per hour, not standardized.

(5) The trajectory class sizes contradict each other. The text on p. 350 says decreased n=455 (7.4%) and increased n=143 (23.5%). Figure 2 gives decreased N=143 and increased N=455, and the percentages fit the Figure 2 counts. I used the Figure 2 assignment in the axis meta.

(6) The paper does not say whether SMT and SMA were entered in the same model or in separate models.

(7) M3's IV is a latent SMA trajectory across Waves 1-3, which includes Wave 3, the outcome wave. It is unclear which wave the BMI and behavioral covariates come from in M3.

(8) Supplementary Tables S3-S7 are not in the PDF: frequent BE among cases (the high-SMA RR of 1.57 is quoted in the text), sex and BMI interactions and stratified results, the reporter sensitivity analysis, and the larger sample without a social media account. These are listed in excluded_models. Add them if someone obtains the supplement.

(9) Including the paper is not in doubt. The SMA measure is a six-item scale adapted from the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, and SMT is time on social media.

d_transformation.notes: p0 values are marginal sample BE prevalences computed from reported counts, not unexposed-group rates (the paper does not report BE rates within the reference SMA group or trajectory class): Wave 1 BE = 249/1940 = 0.128 (Table 1, p. 349); Wave 3 BE = 237/1940 = 0.122 (text p. 351). Because the mild-SMA group (24.6% at Wave 1, 18.8% at Wave 3) and the increased-SMA trajectory class (23.5%) are well above 10% of the sample and these groups have elevated BE, the marginal rate overstates the reference-group rate, so the RR-to-OR conversion is approximate. For SMT, the derived d is a per-1-hour/day contrast rather than a standardized contrast; no SD of SMT is reported (Table 1 has no SMT descriptives; Figure 1 shows only group means), so a per-SD rescaling is not possible. No SDs are needed for the categorical SMA contrasts. p-values are not reported anywhere in the tables; significance flags are based on whether the 95% CI excludes 1 and on the authors' text (two CIs have a lower bound printed as 1.00 and are treated as non-significant, consistent with the text).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Treat PR as RR. OR = RR * (1 - p0) / (1 - RR * p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000). Apply the same conversion to each CI bound.
d_transformation.contrast_type: SMT: per 1 hour/day of average daily social media time. SMA (M1, M2): mild symptoms (score 7-23) or addiction (score >=24) vs. no symptoms (score 6). Trajectories (M3): decreased, increased or consistently high SMA class vs. consistently low SMA class.
d_transformation.native_metric: Prevalence ratio (M1, cross-sectional) and relative risk (M2, M3, prospective), both from modified Poisson regression with robust variance

d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: clinical vs non-significant baseline CBCL category; OR for being in the medium or high (vs 0 h) social screen time category one year later. d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound
d_transformation.notes: All extracted cells are ORs with 95% CIs from the Results text, so the Chinn conversion can be applied mechanically. Marked partial because (1) most of the paper's social screen time estimates are only plotted in Fig. 1 or in the unbundled Supplementary Tables 1-2, so only 16 of the social cells are numerically extractable; (2) the ORs come from an ordinal/categorical model whose exact parameterization (separate medium and high ORs) is unclear, so the logistic-latent-variable assumption behind Chinn is approximate; (3) both IV and DV are categorical, so the d reflects a group contrast (clinical vs non-significant, or exposure category vs 0 h), not a per-unit slope, and is not comparable to per-SD d's from continuous-IV papers. No SDs needed. Baseline prevalence for categories is in Table 1 p. 2282; follow-up CBCL prevalence is not reported. Very narrow CIs likely reflect weighting and should not be used for precision-weighting without checking.

primary_models.estimation: Cumulative logistic regression in R with the VGAM package, run separately for each CBCL scale x screen outcome combination. ABCD propensity weight approximating the American Community Survey sociodemographics of 9- and 10-year-olds applied. No random effects for site or family are described. No multiple-comparison correction reported. Alpha not stated; significance here is judged by whether the 95% CI excludes 1. No p-values printed. No sex or race interaction or stratified analyses reported. Separate ORs are reported for the medium and high outcome categories (Fig. 1), which is not what a single proportional-odds cumulative logit returns, so the exact parameterization (non-parallel cumulative logit or category-specific contrasts) is unclear. The very narrow CIs (e.g., 0.74-0.75) suggest the weights may have been treated as frequency weights.
primary_models.dv: Social screen time = sum of youth-reported hours texting, using social media, and video chatting (Youth Screen Time Survey; each item on a 7-point scale 0=none, 0.25=<30 min, 0.5=30 min, 1, 2, 3, 4=4+ hours), computed separately for a typical weekday and weekend day. Because of right skew, trichotomized by percentile rank (1-33, 34-66, 67-100) pooled across waves 1 and 2: 0 h (reference), 0.25-0.5 h (medium), 0.75-12 h (high), for both weekday and weekend social. Composite is built exclusively from phone/SM/digital-socializing items, so it qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2. Distribution at baseline: weekday social 0 h 47.8%, 0.25-0.5 h 33.5%, 0.75-12 h 18.7%; weekend social 50.1%/28.8%/21.2%. At follow-up: weekday social 36.8%/31.7%/31.5%; weekend social 37.2%/27.5%/35.3% (Table 1, p. 2282).

primary_models.design: Longitudinal, two waves. Baseline (wave 1) CBCL symptom category is the IV and social screen time category one year later (wave 2) is the DV, controlling for the baseline level of the same screen time measure (residualized change model). primary_models.iv: Parent-report CBCL (112 items, 0-2 scale) T-scores at baseline for total problems, internalizing (subscales: anxious-depressive, withdrawn-depressive, plus DSM depressive), attention, externalizing (subscales: aggressive, rule-breaking). Because of right skew each scale was trichotomized using recommended cut-scores into non-significant (reference), borderline, and clinical (typically borderline 65-69 and clinical 70+; for internalizing, externalizing and total problems borderline 60-63 and clinical 64+), and dummy-coded. Baseline clinical prevalence (Table 1): total problems 6.8%, attention 2.8%, internalizing 9.8%, depressive 3.1%, anxious-depressive 2.9%, withdrawn-depressive 2.4%, externalizing 5.7%, aggressive 2.2%, rule breaking 2.1% (194). Only the contrasts for which a social screen time OR is printed are extracted here: clinical vs non-significant for total problems, internalizing, withdrawn-depressive, externalizing and rule breaking.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0. Baseline Sept 2016-Aug 2018 (N=11,876), one-year follow-up 2017-2019 (10,001 followed up with non-zero weight). Mean age 119.3 months at baseline (range 107-132 months). 48.1% female (n=4,362), 51.9% male (n=4,704). Non-Hispanic White 55.2% (5,002), Non-Hispanic Black 13.8% (1,255), Hispanic/Latino 18.7% (1,693), Non-Hispanic other 12.3% (1,116). papers.title: Childhood internalizing, externalizing and attention symptoms predict changes in social and nonsocial screen time
papers.extraction_flags: The bundled PDF has no supplement. Fig. 1 plots the main results with no printed values, and the full ORs are in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2, which are not in the PDF. Only the 16 social-screen-time ORs printed in the Results text (pp. 2284-2285) were extracted: 12 for M1 (symptoms predicting social screen time) and 4 for M2 (social screen time predicting symptoms). No values were read off the figure. The remaining social cells are listed under excluded_models and should be added from the supplementary tables if those can be obtained. Social screen time is texting + social media + video chat, which qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2. The 0 / 0.25-0.5 / 0.75-12 h cut-points apply to social time; the nonsocial measure has its own cut-points. Ambiguities: (1) For total problems, the text does not say whether the weekday 1.02 and weekend 1.15 ORs are for the medium or high category. I assigned them to high based on where the points sit in Fig. 1; please verify. (2) In M2 the text says "higher" social screen time without naming medium or high vs 0 h. (3) The paper calls the method cumulative logistic regression in VGAM, yet it reports separate ORs for the medium and high categories. That does not fit a single proportional-odds model, so the parameterization is unclear and the Chinn conversion is only approximate. (4) No p-values are printed; sig is set from whether the 95% CI excludes 1. (5) The CIs are implausibly narrow (e.g., 0.74-0.75), which suggests the propensity weights were treated as frequency weights. Be careful using these CIs for precision weighting. (6) Follow-up CBCL prevalence is not reported, so p0 is null.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1). Apply to B, B_lo and B_hi.
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV from Table 1 (p. 1483), Year 1 typical hours/day, propensity-weighted: texting 0.7, video chat 0.6, social media 0.6. SD_DV = 2.5, Year 3 manic symptoms (7 Up) from Table 1 (p. 1483). Table 1 descriptives are weighted estimates, not unweighted analytic-sample SDs. The M2 indirect effect is a product term (a*b); converting it with the same beta_std formula is an approximation and the bootstrap CI is not symmetric. Converted d values will be small (e.g., social media M1: beta_std = 0.20*0.6/2.5 = 0.048). Not directly comparable to papers using high vs. low group contrasts.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 hour/day of the Year 1 screen subtype (native); per 1 SD of the IV after conversion

papers.title: Screen time and manic symptoms in early adolescents: prospective findings from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
papers.extraction_flags: 1) The PDF has no supplement. Supplemental Tables 1 (cross-sectional Y3) and 2 (logistic regression on the clinical cutoff) may contain per-subtype texting, video chat and social media estimates, and someone should check the online supplement. 2) SD_IV and SD_DV come from Table 1, which is propensity-weighted, so they are not unweighted analytic-sample SDs. The social media IV is heavily floored (M 0.2, SD 0.6). 3) For the M2 mediation, the covariates are only described as "adjusting for covariates". I assumed the M1 set and flagged that in the file. The paths are labeled beta in Fig. 1 but B in the text, and nothing says they are standardized. The p-value for the indirect effect is <0.001 only. Converting the indirect effect (a*b) to d is approximate. 4) The paper is inconsistent about the sleep mediation: the abstract and results text say video game screen time, while Fig. 3 and the Methods say total screen time. It is excluded either way. 5) The video chat lower CI bound is printed as -0.012 (three decimals) in Table 2. 6) Study site is listed as an adjustment variable, and it is unclear whether it was a fixed or random effect.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The M1 (full-sample RI-CLPM) point estimates come from the path labels in Fig. 1. Their SEs, CIs and exact p-values are in supplementary Tables S2/S3, which are not in the PDF, so M1 has no CIs and its significance is read from the asterisks. Fig. 1 was checked at high resolution, but each label's assignment to its path (for example, -0.009 is OSA T1->ADHD T2 and -0.006 is ADHD T1->OSA T2) should be confirmed against S2/S3. 2) Table 3 has printing problems in the male column. Two male ADHD->OSA CIs do not contain their own point estimates: -0.057 printed with [-0.029, -0.002], and -0.051 printed with [-0.040, -0.004]. Several other male CIs, such as -0.013 (SE 0.023) printed with [-0.253, 0.141], are much wider than 1.96*SE implies. They were copied as printed; do not convert those CIs without checking. 3) The between-person random-intercept correlation r = 0.068 is printed with '95% CI, 0.07-0.35', which does not contain 0.068, so the CI was left null. It is included in M1 as a beta_std cell. 4) The standardized coefficients are within-person (RI-CLPM), so the d's are not directly comparable to between-person d's. The Table 1 SDs are total SDs and were not used. 5) M2 (sex multigroup, Table 3) was extracted as a separate card because the authors interpret it. The paper does not say whether sex was dropped as a covariate in that model. 6) The content-type moderation (Tables S5-S7) and the non-imputed sensitivity analysis are supplement-only and were excluded for lack of numbers. 7) The SEM software is not named, and the OSA time units are implied hours/day but not stated explicitly. 8) OSA qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2 (texting + social networking sites + video chat only). In the ADHD->OSA paths, OSA is the DV.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1). Applied to CI endpoints where CIs are printed (M2 only).
d_transformation.notes: No SD_IV or SD_DV is needed because the paper reports standardized coefficients. For reference, Table 1 (p. 2198) gives OSA time SDs 1.15/1.57/2.15/2.63 and CBCL ADHD T-score SDs 6.17/5.98/5.58/5.62 at T1-T4, but these are total (between + within) SDs, and the coefficients are standardized on the within-person components. The resulting d's describe within-person lagged effects and are not directly comparable to between-person regression d's from other papers. M1 has no CIs in the PDF (they are in supplementary Tables S2/S3), so M1 d's have no CI. In M2, two male ADHD -> OSA CIs do not contain their point estimates and several male CIs are wider than SE implies; converting those CIs would give misleading d intervals.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 within-person SD of the predictor (deviation from the child's own mean) at wave t, predicting the within-person SD of the outcome at wave t+1, net of the autoregressive path and covariates. The between-person cell is a correlation of stable person-level means.

Within level for t = 1..3: w_OSA[i,t+1] = a_t*w_OSA[i,t] + c_t*w_ADHD[i,t] + u_OSA[i,t+1]; w_ADHD[i,t+1] = b_t*w_ADHD[i,t] + d_t*w_OSA[i,t] + u_ADHD[i,t+1]; cov(w_OSA[i,1], w_ADHD[i,1]) and cov(u_OSA[i,t], u_ADHD[i,t]) estimated. Time-invariant covariates (age, sex, race, ethnicity, marital status, parental education, income) and time-varying VCA time enter as predictors; exact placement of covariates in the model is not described. Focal effects: d_t (OSA -> ADHD) and c_t (ADHD -> OSA), reported as standardized coefficients.
primary_models.estimation: SEM software not named (covariate imputation in R v4.3.1, mice v3.16.0). Maximum likelihood robust (MLR) estimator; missing outcome data handled with FIML. Missing covariates (age 0.01%, race 1.43%, ethnicity 1.29%, marital status 0.81%, parental education 0.12%, income 8.57%) imputed by chained equations, 100 imputations combined into one dataset using modes (categorical) and medians (continuous); supplementary materials repeat analyses on the non-imputed data. No survey weights and no site or family clustering reported. Fit: CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.920, RMSEA = 0.040, SRMR = 0.044, chi-square(102) = 2028.860, p < 0.001. Significance flagged as *p <= 0.05, **p <= 0.01, ***p <= 0.001; no multiple-comparison correction. Moderation by sex and by OSA content type (video- vs image-based most-used platform) tested with multigroup models compared against cross-lag-constrained models via Satorra-Bentler chi-square tests (sex: see M2; content type: no moderation, Table S5-S7).
primary_models.name: Random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) of OSA time (texting + social networking + video chat) and CBCL ADHD problems across four annual waves, full sample, adjusted for demographics and video-centric screen time
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.0. 11,868 enrolled at baseline; 43 excluded for missing baseline OSA time and 8 for missing baseline ADHD problems, leaving N = 11,819 analyzed with FIML. Wave-specific available N (Table 2): OSA time 11,819 / 11,157 / 10,884 / 10,259 and ADHD 11,819 / 11,165 / 8,053 / 7,428 at T1-T4. Baseline mean age 9.92 (SD 0.62). 6,163 male (52.1%), 5,656 female (47.9%). Race: White 7,587 (64.2%), Black 1,865 (15.8%), Asian 273 (2.3%), Mixed/Other 2,094 (17.7%). Hispanic 2,392 (20.2%). Parents married or living with partner 73.5%; parental college education 72.7%. Family income <$25,000 18.0% through $200,000+ 10.6% (Table 1).
primary_models.design: Longitudinal, four annual ABCD waves: baseline T1 (2016-2018, ages 9-10), 1-year follow-up T2 (2017-2019), 2-year follow-up T3 (2018-2020), 3-year follow-up T4 (2019-2021). OSA time and ADHD problems are measured at every wave. The RI-CLPM separates stable between-person differences (random intercepts for OSA and ADHD, allowed to correlate) from within-person wave-to-wave deviations. The within-person part has autoregressive paths, lag-specific cross-lagged paths in both directions (OSA t -> ADHD t+1 and ADHD t -> OSA t+1, freely estimated per lag, not constrained equal), and within-wave residual correlations. OSA time is the IV in the OSA -> ADHD paths and the DV in the ADHD -> OSA paths. Pre-registered at OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/KXYZP).

primary_models.equation: Same within- and between-person structure as M1, estimated separately per group g in {female, male} with free cross-lags: w_ADHD[i,t+1] = b_t,g*w_ADHD[i,t] + d_t,g*w_OSA[i,t] + u; w_OSA[i,t+1] = a_t,g*w_OSA[i,t] + c_t,g*w_ADHD[i,t] + u. Focal effects d_t,g and c_t,g, reported as standardized coefficients.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2), applied to the coefficient and to each CI bound (guidelines §4a).
d_transformation.notes: All variables were standardized before modelling (Data Analysis, p. 910; Discussion p. 915 calls them 'standardized beta weights'), so no SD_IV/SD_DV is needed; sd_iv and sd_dv are left null. Table 1 (p. 911) SDs are recorded in iv_axis meta for reference but look implausible for minute-scale variables (e.g., weekday texting M = 11.99, SD = 0.51, range 0-240) and should not be used for rescaling. Because the outcome variables were also standardized, using the sample CBCL SDs (anxiety 5.939, depression 5.57) rather than the normative T-score SD of 10 is implicit in the coefficients. Effects are adjusted for covariates with partial-out of site/family random effects, so the beta-as-r approximation is approximate.

Parallel models additionally controlling for depression (anxiety DV) or anxiety (depression DV) are reported in Supplemental Tables 1-2, which are not in the PDF; Tables 4-5 only flag with footnote a which estimates stayed significant. papers.extraction_flags:
1. Anchoring model: the authors also read their findings off parallel models that control for depression or anxiety. Those coefficients are in Supplemental Tables 1-2, which are online only and not in the PDF. Only footnote 'a' flags in Tables 3-5 show which estimates stayed significant. I extracted the printed versions without that control (Tables 4/5 for the full sample, Table 3 sex-stratified) and listed the controlled versions under excluded models. If the supplement can be obtained, add those coefficients.

2. Separate or joint models: the paper does not say whether each media category was its own GLMM or all categories went into one model. I assumed one category per model.

3. Coefficients are treated as standardized betas because the paper says all variables were standardized. The SPSS link function / GLMM family is not stated; I assumed linear on continuous T-scores.

4. Table 1 SDs for the media categories look implausible (e.g., weekday texting mean 11.99 min, SD 0.51, range 0-240). They are recorded only as meta. sd_iv and sd_dv are left null because the betas are already standardized.

5. M2 (sex-stratified, weekend only) has no per-stratum N. The 2162 boys and 1977 girls are the full-sample sex counts.

6. ABCD release is inferred as 1.0 from reference 36 and the NDA DOI.

The article prints no number for any phone/SM edge. Texting, social media and video chat appear as nodes in a cross-sectional mixed graphical model with the six K-SADS-5 mood symptoms, but their edges are shown only as line width and colour in Fig. 1 (p. 1640). The per-edge values are in ESM Table S1, which is not in the bundled PDF and is not anywhere in the repo. So all 18 estimate cells (3 phone/SM nodes x 6 symptoms) are null, including value, p and sig, and each has a note saying so. A human should get ESM Table S1 (and S2) from the publisher to fill in the edge weights, bootstrap CIs and significance flags, including the female and male subsample values if they are given. The only qualitative statement is in the Results text: common screen types, which include social media, texting and video chat, "lacked a consistent pattern" with mood symptoms. Network edge weights cannot be converted to Cohen's d under guidelines §4a, so transformable is false. The exact analytic N after missing data is not reported, since one child per family was sampled per bootstrap from 9987 families. The edges are undirected, so calling phone/SM the IV is only a convention for this review. If ESM Table S1 turns out to print no phone/SM edge values either, Stage-2 FT-IC3/IC4 eligibility (a numeric result is required) should be rechecked. The 6 sd_iv/sd_dv/p0 values I spot-checked against Table 1 (p. 1639) matched, as did the two connectivity regression numbers in excluded_models.json

primary_models.equation: Pairwise mixed graphical model (exponential family): log P(x) proportional to sum_j theta_j*x_j + sum_{j<k} theta_jk*x_j*x_k, with nodes = 6 binary mood symptoms, 8 Poisson screen time nodes, 4 Gaussian BIS/BAS nodes, 1 Gaussian parental monitoring node. Focal parameters are the edge weights theta_jk between {texting, social media, video chat} and each mood symptom. Estimated with l1 (LASSO) penalty tuned by cross-validation; final edge = mean of 1000 bootstrap estimates.
primary_models.dv: Six binary youth-report K-SADS-5 (computerized) screening items, 0 = absent, 1 = present: irritability, depressive mood, anhedonia (depression); elevated mood, anger, decreased need for sleep (mania). Specified as binary nodes. Full-sample prevalence (Table 1): irritability 0.03, depressive mood 0.02, anhedonia 0.05, elevated mood 0.02, anger 0.02, decreased need for sleep 0.02.
primary_models.native_metric: other:network edge weight (MGM, LASSO-regularized, bootstrap mean)
primary_models.location_in_paper: Network Analysis methods p. 1638; Fig. 1 (full sample top panel; female and male subsample panels below), p. 1640; results text pp. 1640-1641; Discussion p. 1642. Per-edge numbers in ESM Table S1 (not in the bundled PDF).
primary_models.name: Mixed graphical model (LASSO-regularized, bootstrapped) of binary K-SADS-5 mood symptom nodes with screen time type nodes, partialling out other screen types, BIS/BAS and parental monitoring
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD baseline wave only (2016-2018). All nodes measured at the same visit. Undirected network, so no IV/DV direction is estimated; for this review the texting, social media and video chat nodes are treated as the phone/SM side and the six mood symptom nodes as the trait side. Networks estimated in the full sample and separately in female and male subsamples.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Curated Annual Release 2.0, baseline (N = 11,875 enrolled; M age = 9.91, SD = 0.62, from 9987 families). Because siblings were present, one child per family was randomly sampled in each bootstrap, so each network uses one child per family (Discussion cites 9987 families). Baseline ABCD composition reported as 48% female; 49% non-Hispanic White, 17% non-Hispanic Black, 23% Hispanic, 5% Asian, 5% other. Exact analytic N after missing data is not reported. Increased sexuality was dropped because no child endorsed it.
primary_models.iv: Three phone/SM screen time nodes from the ABCD youth screen time questionnaire: texting, visiting social media sites, video chatting. Typical weekday and weekend day each rated 0 = none, 0.25 = <30 min, 0.5 = 30 min, 1 = 1 h, 2 = 2 h, 3 = 3 h, 4 = 4+ h; average daily value = weekday x 5/7 + weekend x 2/7, rounded to the nearest integer (so effectively an ordinal 0-4 count). Specified as Poisson nodes in the MGM. Full-sample descriptives (Table 1): texting M = 0.14 (SD 0.55), social media M = 0.08 (SD 0.43), video chatting M = 0.12 (SD 0.50), all ranging 0-4. Females reported more texting (0.16 vs 0.12) and social media (0.1 vs 0.07) than males. The network also includes five non-phone screen nodes (TV/movie, video, video game, mature video game, R-rated movie).
primary_models.estimation: R package mgm (Haslbeck & Waldorp 2015), also qgraph and bootnet. Node distributions chosen from Q-Q plots. l1-regularization with cross-validation. One child per family randomly sampled per bootstrap; 1000 bootstraps with replacement (N_family - 1); final edge weights averaged over bootstraps. Edge significance tested against simulated random networks (Su et al. 2017); an edge was called stable if its bootstrap CI did not contain opposite signs. Edge stability (correlation of absolute/rank-order edge weights): 0.88/0.8 full, 0.79/0.71 female, 0.83/0.75 male. Sensitivity analysis on node selection reported in ESM S2 (little impact). Sex differences in screen-symptom edges tested with permutation tests (NetworkComparisonTest); no sex difference reported for common screen time types. No multiple-comparison correction stated beyond the simulation significance test.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: None. Guidelines §4a list network edge weights as non-convertible; native metric displayed alone with 'no common-scale d available'.
d_transformation.notes: Edge weights are LASSO-shrunk, averaged across 1000 bootstraps, and come from a mixed Poisson/binary/Gaussian graphical model, so they have no Cohen's d mapping. In addition, the article prints no numeric value for any texting, social media, or video chat edge: they appear only as line width/colour in Fig. 1 (p. 1640), with per-edge values deferred to ESM Table S1, which is not in the bundled PDF. SD_IV values in iv_axis are from Table 1 (p. 1639, full sample: texting 0.55, social media 0.43, video chat 0.50); symptom prevalences (p0) and SDs from the same table. Paper goes to later review level for non-d metrics.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Regularized conditional association (pairwise MGM interaction parameter) between a Poisson-coded screen time node (0-4) and a binary symptom node, conditional on all other 18 nodes; not a per-unit regression slope on a common scale.

primary_models.name: Survey-weighted logistic regression of year-2 eating disorder symptoms on baseline social media hours/day, adjusted for baseline parent-reported ED symptom, BMI percentile, anxiety and BAS reward responsiveness
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal. Social media use is measured at the ABCD baseline visit (2016-2018, ages 9-10); the five eating disorder symptoms are measured once, by youth-report KSADS-5, at the year-two follow-up (2018-2020). Each symptom is a single binary follow-up outcome (no repeated measures, no time interaction). Because youth were not asked the ED items at baseline, the parent-reported baseline KSADS-5 version of the same symptom is entered as a covariate. Social media and total screen time are reported in separate columns of Table 2; the paper does not state that social media models adjust for other screen modalities.
primary_models.iv: Baseline social media use in hours per day from the self-reported ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey (social media item, e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter), asked separately for typical weekday and weekend day and combined as ((weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)) / 7. Entered as a continuous variable; ORs are per additional hour/day. Table 1: social media 0.1 (SD 0.4) hours. (Total screen time, the headline exposure, is a six-modality sum including TV, videos and video games and is excluded below.)
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0, 21 U.S. sites. Analytic N = 10,246 after excluding participants missing screen time or eating disorder symptom data (N = 1,552, 13.1%; included vs excluded comparison in Additional file 1 Table S1, not bundled in the PDF). Missing baseline sociodemographic data were filled by Gaussian normal regression imputation in Stata. Baseline (Table 1, weighted): mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6); 48.6% female, 51.4% male; 54.4% White, 19.7% Latino/Hispanic, 16.0% Black, 5.4% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.4% Other; 45.0% household income < $75,000; 81.2% parent with college education or more. The N per Table 2 cell is not printed separately.
primary_models.estimation: Multiple logistic regression in Stata 18.0 using svyset/svy commands with ABCD propensity weights (American Community Survey raking to age, sex and race/ethnicity). Site entered as a covariate; no random effects or family clustering described. Significance at p < 0.05 (bold in table); no multiple-comparison correction reported. Interactions between sex and the exposures were tested, were not significant, and results were not stratified by sex (no numbers printed). Age is named as a confounder in the Methods text but is not listed in the Table 2 covariate footnote. No unadjusted model is printed. No sensitivity analyses reported.

primary_models.name: Survey-weighted logistic regression of year-2 eating disorder symptoms on concurrent problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic mobile phone use (MPIQ), adjusted for BMI percentile, anxiety and BAS reward responsiveness
primary_models.iv: (a) Problematic social media use: 6-item adolescent Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ), modeled after the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, items rated 1 (never) to 6 (very often); Table 1 score 1.9 (SD 0.9). (b) Problematic mobile phone use: 8-item Mobile Phone Involvement Questionnaire (MPIQ), items rated 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree); Table 1 score 3.1 (SD 1.1). The magnitudes in Table 1 suggest item-mean scoring, but the paper does not state the scoring or the unit of the OR (presumably per 1-point increase in the scale score). Entered continuously.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. SMAQ and MPIQ were first administered at the year-two follow-up (2018-2020), the same visit at which the youth-reported KSADS-5 eating disorder symptoms were measured. Each problematic-use scale and each symptom is modeled separately (2 IVs x 5 DVs). Baseline covariates are included, but unlike M1 the baseline parent-reported ED symptom is not in the Table 3 covariate list. Authors note they could not test prospective associations because problematic use was not measured at baseline.
primary_models.estimation: Same as M1: Stata 18.0 svy logistic regression with ABCD ACS-based propensity weights; site as covariate; no random effects; alpha 0.05 with no multiple-comparison correction; sex interactions tested and non-significant (not printed). Age named as a confounder in Methods text but absent from the Table 3 covariate footnote. SMAQ and MPIQ are entered in separate models (no mutual adjustment reported).
primary_models.sample: Subsamples of the N = 10,246 ABCD Release 4.0 analytic cohort: SMAQ models n = 5,587 (only youth reporting at least one social media account were asked the SMAQ); MPIQ models n = 7,280 (only youth reporting having a mobile phone were asked the MPIQ). Demographics are reported only for the full 10,246 (Table 1; see M1), not for these subsamples.
primary_models.dv: Same five binary year-two KSADS-5 youth-reported symptoms as M1 (fear of obesity, self-worth tied to weight, inappropriate compensatory behaviors, binge eating, distress with binge eating). Prevalence within the SMAQ and MPIQ subsamples is not reported; full-sample prevalence is 1.4%, 1.6%, 0.7%, 7.5%, 2.9%.

papers.extraction_flags: (1) The paper never states the scoring unit for SMAQ and MPIQ, so for M2 the contrast is assumed to be per 1 point on an item-mean score. That assumption comes from the Table 1 means (1.9 and 3.1) and the item ranges. (2) The Methods text names age as a confounder, but neither the Table 2 nor the Table 3 covariate footnote lists it. The extraction follows the footnotes and flags the gap. Smaller points: the p0 values are full-sample year-two prevalences from Table 1. Prevalences within the SMAQ (n=5,587) and MPIQ (n=7,280) subsamples are not reported, but Chinn's OR-to-d conversion does not need p0. Table 1 does not say outright that the 'Social media (hours)' SD of 0.4 is from baseline; it is read as baseline because it sits under the table's 'baseline' header. Per-cell N is not printed for Table 2. The Table 3 models leave out the baseline parent-reported eating disorder symptom covariate, so their specification differs from M1. The total-screen-time column is excluded as a mixed composite. The supplement (Tables S1 and S2) is not in the PDF. I checked all 15 ORs, CIs and p-values against the table text pulled from the PDF.
papers.title: Screen time, problematic screen use, and eating disorder symptoms among early adolescents: findings from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study
papers.journal: Eating and Weight Disorders - Studies on Anorexia, Bulimia and Obesity (2024) 29:57

d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: per 1 additional hour/day of baseline social media use. M2: per 1-unit increase in SMAQ or MPIQ score (unit not explicitly stated; item-mean scale assumed from Table 1 means).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.notes: Both models report adjusted ORs with 95% CIs, so the Chinn conversion applies directly and p0 is not needed. p0 values given in dv_axis are the full-sample (N = 10,246, weighted) year-two prevalences from Table 1 (p. 5); prevalences within the SMAQ (n = 5,587) and MPIQ (n = 7,280) subsamples are not reported. SD_IV values from Table 1 (p. 5): social media 0.4 hours/day (baseline), SMAQ 0.9, MPIQ 1.1; these are full-sample/subsample descriptives as printed and could be used to rescale ORs to a per-SD contrast (ln OR x SD_IV) if a per-SD comparison is wanted. Because social media hours have a very small SD (0.4 h), the per-hour OR of 1.55 corresponds to a much smaller per-SD effect; per-hour d values are not directly comparable to per-SD d values from other papers.

SD_IV from Table 1 (p. 751): baseline texting 0.53, video chat 0.47, social media 0.39 h/d (used for M1); year-1 texting 0.73, video chat 0.63, social media 0.60 h/d (used for M2). SD_DV = 2.45 from Table 1 'MIND diet sum score 8.00 (2.45)'. That row sits under the 'Sociodemographic Characteristics (Baseline)' heading, but the MIND score was only collected at year 1 (Results text: average at year 1 was 8 points out of 14), so it is taken as the year-1 outcome SD for the analytic sample. Table 1 values are propensity-weighted. Each B comes from a single-modality model, so it is not mutually adjusted for the other screen modalities.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1). CI endpoints converted the same way.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 SD of the IV (hours/day of the modality at the wave of measurement), derived from per-1-hour/day B
d_transformation.native_metric: B (unstandardized linear regression coefficient, MIND score points per hour/day)

papers.title: Associations of Contemporary Screen Time Modalities With Early Adolescent Nutrition
papers.extraction_flags:
The PDF at the listed path is the wrong paper...) is actually Nagata et al., "Neighborhood Quality and Screen Use", Acad Pediatr 2026;26:103164...), and the extraction comes from that file. The copy in docs/pdfs should be replaced; I did not change it. The same mismatch exists in the archive data/pdfs/ folder, so other papers' PDFs may have been swapped the same way.

On the extraction: the prospective model (year-0 IV) and the cross-sectional model (year-1 IV) are split into M1 and M2 because they have different designs. The authors interpret both, but stress the cross-sectional findings for texting and social media. Texting and social media are significant only cross-sectionally (M2). In the prospective model (M1) all phone/SM estimates are null.

Three things need human checks:
- SD_DV = 2.45 is the Table 1 "MIND diet sum score" row. It sits under the "Baseline" heading, but MIND was only measured at year 1, so the label is ambiguous.
- How study site was modeled (fixed or random) is not stated.
- Supplementary Appendix A (the exclusion flowchart) is not bundled in the PDF.

Each modality is its own single-IV regression, so the estimates are not mutually adjusted for other modalities. All 6 B values, CIs, p-values and all 6 SD_IV values were checked against Table 2 and Table 1.

primary_models.equation: MIND_Y1[i] = b0 + b1*phoneSM_Y0[i] + b2*race_eth[i] + b3*sex[i] + b4*age[i] + b5*income[i] + b6*parent_ed[i] + b7*CBCL_depression[i] + b8*parent_monitoring[i] + b9*site[i] + e[i], where phoneSM_Y0 is one of texting, video chat, or social media hours/day at year 0 (separate model per modality), with ABCD propensity weights.
primary_models.dv: MIND (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay) diet sum score at the 1-year follow-up, from the parent-completed ABCD Child Nutrition Assessment, a 14-item food frequency questionnaire modeled on the MIND diet questionnaire (wine item omitted, so the maximum is 14). Items cover intake of protective food groups (whole grains, vegetables, berries, nuts, poultry, beans, fish, olive oil) and neurodegenerative food groups (fried foods, pastries and sweets, butter, cheese) over a week. Higher score indicates better diet quality. Table 1 reports MIND diet sum score 8.00 (SD 2.45); Results text says the average at year 1 was 8 points out of 14.
primary_models.design: Prospective (longitudinal) analysis with two waves. The IV is screen time at the ABCD baseline visit (year 0, 2016-2018, ages 9-10) and the DV is the MIND diet score from the caregiver-reported Child Nutrition Assessment at the 1-year follow-up (year 1, 2017-2019, ages 10-11). The outcome is a single follow-up measurement, not repeated measures. There is no baseline nutrition score (the nutrition assessment was only collected at year 1), so the model does not adjust for prior diet; the authors list this as a limitation. Each screen modality was entered in its own regression (the paper reports 16 separate regression models in Table 2: 7 continuous IVs plus the categorical total-screen-time IV, at each of two waves), so each phone/SM estimate comes from a model containing only that one modality plus covariates.
primary_models.estimation: Multivariable linear regression in Stata 15.1, with ABCD propensity weights applied to match the ACS (US Census) on key sociodemographic variables. The paper does not state the variance estimator, clustering by family, or how site was modeled. Significance at P < .05 (bold in Table 2). No multiple-comparison correction reported. No interaction or stratified analyses reported. Covariates measured at year 0.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0, baseline and 1-year follow-up. Analytic N = 8267 after excluding 3695 participants missing Youth Screen Time Survey, Child Nutrition Assessment, or demographic data (flowchart in Supplementary Appendix A, not bundled in the PDF). Baseline age 9.94 (SD 0.63) years; 49.0% female, 50.1% male; 56.9% White, 19.2% Latino/Hispanic, 14.3% Black, 5.4% Asian, 3.0% Native American, 1.3% Other (43.1% non-White). Household income: 15.3% <$25,000, 18.1% $25,000-$49,999, 15.7% $50,000-$74,999, 14.8% $75,000-$99,999, 26.9% $100,000-$199,999, 9.4% >=$200,000. 89.7% had a parent with college education or more. Percentages in Table 1 are propensity-weighted.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, Prospective Analysis columns, rows Texting, Video chat, Social media (p. 752); Methods: Statistical Analysis (p. 751); Results p. 751; Discussion pp. 752-753

primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. Screen time and NIH Toolbox cognition taken from the same ABCD assessment (the paper calls the design cross-sectional in the Limitations, p. 5; mean age 119.00 months matches the baseline visit, although the wave is not named explicitly). One observation per child, no repeated measures, no time interactions. Each cognitive domain is a separate DV. The per-device analysis in Table S1 is a supplementary breakout of the headline total-screen-time model; the paper does not say whether each device was entered in its own model or all devices jointly, but the slightly different r2 values per device within a domain suggest separate models per device.
