primary_models.sample: ABCD COVID-19 Rapid Response Research Release, December 2020 survey. Analytic N = 4,106 adolescents aged 12-14 years (35% response rate among ABCD participants invited). 50.6% female, 49.4% male; 60.5% White, 16.7% Latino/Hispanic, 11.3% Black, 8.2% Asian, 2.1% Native American, 1.2% Other (39.5% racial/ethnic minorities). Household income <$75,000 47.7%, >=$75,000 52.3%. Parent highest education high school or less 12.8%, college or more 87.2%. Schooling in past week: online/school-at-home 65.2%, in person 15.9%, hybrid 13.3%, other 5.7%. Parent-reported child COVID-19 diagnosis 4.4%. Percentages in Table 1 are ABCD propensity-weighted. Included vs excluded participant characteristics are in the Supplemental Appendix (not bundled in this PDF); the authors note responders were more likely to be White, female and higher SES.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. Single wave: the December 2020 ABCD COVID-19 Rapid Response Research survey. IV (adolescent self-reported frequency of checking COVID-related information on social media in the past week) and DV (adolescent self-reported masking in the last week) were collected in the same survey. One observation per adolescent; no repeated measures. Sociodemographic confounders were taken from the baseline parent survey. All four information-source variables (social media, internet, television, parent counseling) enter the same adjusted model, so the social media ARR is adjusted for the other three.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The authors interpret both the combined-effect models and the within/between decomposition (both appear in the Abstract), so I extracted two cards: M1 with 36 combined estimates and M2 with 72 within- and between-person estimates. A reviewer should decide whether both cards belong in the meta-matrix or only one; they share the same data. 2) Native metric is set to the standardized beta printed in Table 3. Each estimate's note gives the unstandardized B per minute. No CIs or SEs are printed in Table 3. Fig. 1 plots 95% CIs for the M2 betas, but I did not read values off the figure, so beta_lo and beta_hi are null. 3) The paper does not say how beta_std was standardized. Recomputing it from B and the grand SDs in Table 2 matches the printed values only approximately (e.g., -0.136 vs. -0.128), so use the printed beta_std. 4) The covariate set "varied by model" per the Table 3 note. The 'school night' covariate is listed in that note but not in the Methods, and the paper does not say which models include which covariates. OS was included only in the keyboard models. 5) The analytic N per model (days and participants) is not reported, since each model uses pairwise-complete days. App-use IVs are Android-only (302 participants); keyboard IVs cover 791. 6) The sleep-onset and wake-time SDs were printed as '2 h, 14 m' and '2 h, 17 m' and converted to 134 and 137 minutes. 7) I counted significance at P<.05 with no multiple-comparison correction, across 108 tests. 8) The hourly-binned models (Supplementary Fig. S1) and all sensitivity analyses are supplementary and not printed in the PDF, so they are excluded; reviewers may want to check the online supplement.json

d_transformation.notes: The paper prints standardized betas directly in Table 3 (p. 6), so d can be derived without SDs. No CIs or SEs are printed in the table, so d CIs cannot be computed from the table; Fig. 1 (p. 7) plots 95% CIs for M2 betas but these were not read off the figure. sd_iv for M1 is the grand (all-observation) SD from Table 2 (p. 5); sd_iv for M2 between-person terms is the participant-mean SD from Table 2; the within-person deviation SD is not reported (null). sd_dv is the grand SD from Table 2: steps 4578.02, sedentary 333.41, exercise 47.52, total sleep 95.39; sleep onset SD printed as '2 h, 14 m' and wake time as '2 h, 17 m', converted to 134 and 137 min. The paper does not state exactly how beta_std was standardized (e.g., grand vs. within SDs); recomputing B*SD_IV/SD_DV with the grand SDs reproduces the printed beta_std only approximately (e.g., app 6AM-7:59PM on exercise: -0.046*140.26/47.52 = -0.136 vs. printed -0.128), so the printed beta_std should be used. Effects are per-day associations from intensive longitudinal data and are not directly comparable to between-person cross-sectional d's from questionnaire-based papers.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 SD of daily minutes of smartphone app or keyboard use in the given time window (combined effect, M1); per 1 SD of the within-person daily deviation (M2 within) or of the participant mean (M2 between)
d_transformation.native_metric: beta_std (standardized beta from linear mixed models; unstandardized B per minute also printed)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines section 4a). Alternative from raw B: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV, then the same formula.

primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, Year-4 follow-up visit (ages 13-14), participants in the ABCD EARS/Fitbit wearables substudy who concurrently provided up to three weeks of passively sensed smartphone, sleep and physical activity data (data collection ended after 21 days of data or 42 elapsed days). N = 791 participants overall (Table 1): mean age 14.12 (SD 0.69); 369 male (46.6%), 422 female (53.4%); Asian 17 (2.1%), Black 75 (9.5%), Hispanic 144 (18.2%), White 471 (59.5%), another race 84 (10.6%); highest parent education: no HS diploma 15 (1.8%), HS/GED 40 (5.1%), some college 241 (30.5%), bachelor's 225 (28.4%), graduate/professional 270 (34.1%); iOS 486 (61.4%), Android 305 (38.6%). Keyboard measures come from all 791 participants (11,797 day-observations for daytime and evening, 10,159 for late night); application-use measures come only from Android users (302 participants, 6340 days; 5993 for late night). Fitbit outcomes: steps 791 participants / 6228 days; sedentary and exercise 791 / 6748 days; total sleep and sleep onset 604 / 5634 nights; wake time 604 / 5375 nights (Table 2). The paper reports 6748 days of concurrent smartphone and physical activity data and 5634 nights of concurrent smartphone and sleep data. Each model uses all pairwise-complete day-observations for that IV-DV pair; the exact day-level and participant-level N per model is not reported. Attrition and inclusion detail is in Supplementary Figure S1 (not in this PDF). The authors note the sample is more female and more non-Hispanic White and less low-income than the US population of 10-14 year olds.
primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed-effects models fit with the nlme package in R 4.3.0, with individual-level random intercepts. A separate model was fit for every smartphone measure x outcome pair. Table 3 reports both the unstandardized beta (per additional minute of use) and the standardized beta; no CIs or SEs are printed in the table, though Fig. 1 plots 95% CIs for the within- and between-person standardized betas. Significance judged at P < .05 (Fig. 1 marks * P < .05); no multiple-comparison correction is reported across the 36 combined or 72 disaggregated tests. No interaction or stratified analyses by sex or other demographics. Sensitivity analyses reported only in the supplement (not in this PDF) and summarized narratively on p. 5: adding race and socioeconomic status (all significant effects retained), adding time recorded awake to the physical activity models (11/15 retained), redefining late night as 9:00PM-4:59AM or 11:00PM-6:59AM, winsorizing outcomes at +/-3 SD (30/31 retained), and inverse-propensity weighting by proportion of complete days (25/31 retained). Standardized effects in all sensitivity models were within 0.10 SD of the primary effects.

primary_models.design: Intensive longitudinal (daily diary-style) design within the ABCD Year-4 follow-up: up to three weeks of daily passive sensor data per participant. IV and DV are measured on the same day (activity outcomes), the same night (sleep onset, total sleep) or the next morning (wake time). Days are repeated measures nested within participants, handled by a participant random intercept. The combined effect uses raw daily minutes of use, so it does not separate within-person from between-person variation. No time trend or IV x time interaction.

primary_models.iv: Passively sensed smartphone use from the EARS app. Application use (Android only) is the minutes any application, third-party or native, was in the foreground each day, after removing system apps and apps meant to stay foregrounded during sleep (lock screens, alarm clocks). Keyboard use (Android and iOS) is the total minutes the keyboard was open and logging keystrokes (time between first and last keystroke of each session), with the same app exclusions; on Android it was recorded from the native keyboard, on iOS via an EARS keyboard overlay that participants were told to use exclusively. Each is split into three time windows: daytime/evening 6:00AM-7:59PM, 'night time' 8:00PM-9:59PM, and late night 10:00PM-5:59AM the next morning. Six IVs total, each entered in a separate model, in minutes. Table 2 descriptives: Smartphone application use, 6:00AM-7:59PM (min/day): grand M = 190.47 min, SD = 140.26; participant-mean M = 188.68, SD = 96.00; Smartphone application use, 8:00PM-9:59PM (min/day): grand M = 37.66 min, SD = 36.89; participant-mean M = 36.98, SD = 23.10; Smartphone application use, 10:00PM-5:59AM (min/night): grand M = 71.52 min, SD = 97.11; participant-mean M = 70.53, SD = 69.58; Keyboard use, 6:00AM-7:59PM (min/day): grand M = 11.68 min, SD = 21.28; participant-mean M = 9.89, SD = 14.62; Keyboard use, 8:00PM-9:59PM (min/day): grand M = 2.90 min, SD = 7.27; participant-mean M = 2.47, SD = 4.52; Keyboard use, 10:00PM-5:59AM (min/night): grand M = 4.04 min, SD = 12.25; participant-mean M = 3.33, SD = 7.68.

primary_models.dv: Six Fitbit Charge-derived daily outcomes, each modeled separately: total daily steps (grand M = 7553.73, SD = 4578.02); minutes of sedentary activity (METs < 1.5; M = 973.01, SD = 333.41); minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise (METs >= 3.0; M = 31.73, SD = 47.52); total minutes of sleep between 5:00PM and 4:59PM the next day (M = 449.98, SD = 95.39); sleep onset, first minute recorded asleep each night, modeled as minutes delayed (grand M = 11:48PM, SD = 2 h 14 m; labeled 'Bedtime' in Table 3); wake time, first minute awake followed by at least 30 consecutive minutes awake, modeled as minutes delayed (grand M = 8:02AM, SD = 2 h 17 m). Physical-activity outcomes are same-day; sleep onset and total sleep are same-night; wake time is next morning. Days with < 599 min of valid waking wear, > 20% of steps excluded in QC, or < 30 s of recorded sleep were excluded. Grand means/SDs from Table 2 (p. 5).
primary_models.equation: Outcome[i,t] = b0 + b1*PhoneUse_minutes[i,t] + b2*sex[i] + b3*age_c[i] + b4*weekend[t] + b5*school_night[t] + b6*summer[t] + b7*fitbit_wear[i,t] (+ b8*OS[i] in keyboard models) + u_i + e[i,t]; one model per PhoneUse measure (6) x Outcome (6). Covariate set 'varied by model' per the Table 3 note.

primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed-effects models fit with the nlme package in R 4.3.0, with individual-level random intercepts. A separate model was fit for every smartphone measure x outcome pair. Table 3 reports both the unstandardized beta (per additional minute of use) and the standardized beta; no CIs or SEs are printed in the table, though Fig. 1 plots 95% CIs for the within- and between-person standardized betas. Significance judged at P < .05 (Fig. 1 marks * P < .05); no multiple-comparison correction is reported across the 36 combined or 72 disaggregated tests. No interaction or stratified analyses by sex or other demographics. Sensitivity analyses reported only in the supplement (not in this PDF) and summarized narratively on p. 5: adding race and socioeconomic status (all significant effects retained), adding time recorded awake to the physical activity models (11/15 retained), redefining late night as 9:00PM-4:59AM or 11:00PM-6:59AM, winsorizing outcomes at +/-3 SD (30/31 retained), and inverse-propensity weighting by proportion of complete days (25/31 retained). Standardized effects in all sensitivity models were within 0.10 SD of the primary effects. Fig. 1 marks a reference line at standardized beta = 0.2 described as a 'clinically significant effect size'.
primary_models.dv: Same six Fitbit outcomes as M1.
primary_models.name: Linear mixed-effects regression of daily Fitbit sleep and physical activity outcomes on within-person (person-mean-centered) and between-person (person-mean) smartphone app or keyboard minutes, same covariates as M1

primary_models.iv: Same six smartphone measures as M1, each decomposed into two terms: between-person (participant mean minutes) and within-person (daily minutes minus participant mean). Participant-mean SDs from Table 2: app 6:00AM-7:59PM 96.00; app 8:00PM-9:59PM 23.10; app 10:00PM-5:59AM 69.58; keyboard 6:00AM-7:59PM 14.62; keyboard 8:00PM-9:59PM 4.52; keyboard 10:00PM-5:59AM 7.68. The SD of the within-person deviation is not reported.
primary_models.equation: Outcome[i,t] = b0 + b1*(PhoneUse[i,t] - mean_i(PhoneUse)) + b2*mean_i(PhoneUse) + b3*sex[i] + b4*age_c[i] + b5*weekend[t] + b6*school_night[t] + b7*summer[t] + b8*fitbit_wear[i,t] (+ b9*OS[i] in keyboard models) + u_i + e[i,t]; b1 = within-person effect, b2 = between-person effect; one model per PhoneUse measure x Outcome.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, Year-4 follow-up visit (ages 13-14), participants in the ABCD EARS/Fitbit wearables substudy who concurrently provided up to three weeks of passively sensed smartphone, sleep and physical activity data (data collection ended after 21 days of data or 42 elapsed days). N = 791 participants overall (Table 1): mean age 14.12 (SD 0.69); 369 male (46.6%), 422 female (53.4%); Asian 17 (2.1%), Black 75 (9.5%), Hispanic 144 (18.2%), White 471 (59.5%), another race 84 (10.6%); highest parent education: no HS diploma 15 (1.8%), HS/GED 40 (5.1%), some college 241 (30.5%), bachelor's 225 (28.4%), graduate/professional 270 (34.1%); iOS 486 (61.4%), Android 305 (38.6%). Keyboard measures come from all 791 participants (11,797 day-observations for daytime and evening, 10,159 for late night); application-use measures come only from Android users (302 participants, 6340 days; 5993 for late night). Fitbit outcomes: steps 791 participants / 6228 days; sedentary and exercise 791 / 6748 days; total sleep and sleep onset 604 / 5634 nights; wake time 604 / 5375 nights (Table 2). The paper reports 6748 days of concurrent smartphone and physical activity data and 5634 nights of concurrent smartphone and sleep data. Each model uses all pairwise-complete day-observations for that IV-DV pair; the exact day-level and participant-level N per model is not reported. Attrition and inclusion detail is in Supplementary Figure S1 (not in this PDF). The authors note the sample is more female and more non-Hispanic White and less low-income than the US population of 10-14 year olds.

primary_models.dv: Nine continuous sleep variables: sleep duration (hours, SDSC item), sleep onset latency (SDSC 5-pt), insomnia symptoms (7-item SDSC subscale, alpha=0.73), disordered breathing (3-item, alpha=0.37), arousal disturbances (3-item, alpha=0.56), sleep-wake transition disturbances (6-item, alpha=0.59), excessive sleepiness (5-item, alpha=0.72), sleep hyperhidrosis (2-item, alpha=0.81), total sleep-wake disturbance score (26 items, alpha=0.65).
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of a single ABCD timepoint (baseline, Release 2.0). Both IV and DVs measured at same visit. One observation per child. Pre-registered hypotheses H1-H7; IVs were pre-registered as continuous but data skew forced dichotomization at the AAP <2 vs >=2 hr threshold.
primary_models.estimation: OLS. Software not specified; analyses pre-registered on OSF. No survey weights. No random intercept for family despite siblings/twins in sample; sensitivity check with vs. without them yielded similar findings. alpha = 0.001 (paper's MC correction). Race and ethnicity interactions with IV all p > 0.001; no stratified per-modality estimates reported.
primary_models.iv: Six binary IVs (3 modalities x 2 day-types), each 0 (<2 hr) or 1 (>=2 hr). Instrument: 12-item ABCD screen-time questionnaire with continuous response options (none/<30m/30m/1h/2h/3h/4+h). Dichotomization at AAP <=2 hr recommendation; deviates from pre-reg (right-skew). beta_1 is a group difference, not per-hour slope. Cohen's d from adjusted group means and pooled SD.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: passthrough (native is already d). M2: OR = RR * (1-p0) / (1 - RR*p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000). p0 = 0.155 (insufficient sleep marginal base rate); 0.275 (disturbed sleep).

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The IV set goes beyond the Stage 2 pointer (talk/text). I also included bedtime social media, the phone-at-bedtime ringer categories (silent/vibrate, ringer on and outside the room, each vs turning the phone off), and being woken by phone calls, texts or emails (this item also covers emails). Please confirm the ringer and woken-by-phone items count as phone-specific under FT-IC2. 2) I excluded 'spend time in chat rooms' (ARR 1.27/1.08) and 'used phone or other device after waking' (mixed device and activities). A coder may want chat rooms back in. 3) Table 3 gives social media vs sleep disturbance as 1.06 (1.01, 1.11), but the Results text on p. 500 says 1.01-1.13. I used the table value. 4) The IV coding is unclear. Methods describe a 5-point Likert scale (1 never to 5 every night), Table 2 shows 4 categories (0, 1-2, 3-4, 5-7 nights), and the exposures were 'treated as continuous'. So the per-unit contrast is ambiguous, and no SD is reported for any IV. 5) The covariates are inconsistent. Age is listed among confounders in Methods but is missing from the Table 3 footnote and the abstract. 6) p0 values are marginal rates (15.5%, 28.0%), not rates in the unexposed group, and exposure prevalence is over 10%, so the RR-to-OR conversion is approximate. 7) Each exposure seems to be modeled separately, but the paper does not say so. 8) The ABCD data release is not stated. p-values printed as '<.001' are stored as p null with p_label.

d_transformation.native_metric: RR (adjusted risk ratio from modified Poisson regression)
d_transformation.notes: p0 values are marginal sample prevalences from Table 1 (15.5% and 28.0%), not unexposed-group rates; exposure prevalence here is well above 10% (e.g., about 34% any bedtime texting), so the marginal-rate approximation from guidelines section 4a is weaker than usual and the derived d values should be treated as approximate. primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of ABCD Year 2 follow-up (2018-2020), when participants were mostly 11-12 years old. primary_models.iv: Items from the 9-item ABCD Screen Usage Around Bedtime questionnaire (adapted from Lemola et al. 2014 and Arora et al. 2014) plus four sleep-and-phone items adapted from a National Sleep Foundation poll, youth self-report. Qualifying items: (1) 'Talk on the phone or text' and (2) 'Spend time online on social media (eg, Facebook)', both asked as how often in the past week the youth did the activity while already in bed before going to sleep. Methods describe a 5-point Likert scale from 1 (never) to 5 (every night), while Table 2 shows four response categories (0 nights, 1-2, 3-4, 5-7 nights); the authors state exposures were treated as continuous variables, so the ARR is per one-step increase on this frequency scale. Distribution (Table 2): talk/text 65.9% 0 nights, 19.6% 1-2, 7.9% 3-4, 6.6% 5-7; social media 69.4%, 16.5%, 7.5%, 6.6%. (3) 'What do you usually do with your phone when you are ready to go to sleep?' coded categorically with 'Turn the phone off' (54.9%) as referent versus 'Put the ringer on silent or vibrate' (18.3%), 'Leave the ringer on' (11.8%), and 'Put it outside of the room where I sleep' (14.9%). (4) 'In the past week, how often have you had phone calls, text messages or emails that wake you after trying to go to sleep?' (83.1% none/0, 11.0%, 3.6%, 2.3% across the four Table 2 columns), treated as continuous. No means or SDs are reported for any IV.
primary_models.dv: Two binary sleep outcomes. (1) Trouble falling or staying asleep, adolescent report: single KSADS DSM-5 item about problems falling or staying asleep in the past 2 weeks, rated 0 (not at all) to 4 (nearly every day), binarized into problem on at least several days vs rarely or never; 15.5% yes (Table 1). (2) Overall sleep disturbance, caregiver report: 26-item Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children total (items 1-5, past 6 months), dichotomized at the developers' cutoff of 39 (Table 1 footnote says score > 39); 28.0% yes.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The methods describe logistic regression for SDSC sleep disturbance, but the table footnotes say the output comes from "modified Poisson and linear regression" models. The columns are labeled OR, so I recorded the values as OR. 2) The paper does not say whether each bedtime item was fit in its own model or whether all items were entered together; "in addition to all variables listed" in the footnote is ambiguous. 3) No SDs are reported for the 1-5 Likert bedtime items or for MCTQ sleep duration, so the B models (M2, M3) cannot be converted to d. The ORs can be converted with the Chinn formula. 4) I included the item about being woken by "phone calls, text messages, or emails" as phone-qualifying even though emails could come from a non-phone device; please check that call. I excluded the night-waking "phone or other device ... play games/browse ..." item as a mixed composite (OR 1.25, B -0.25); coders may want to revisit it. 5) I extracted the sex-stratified Table 5 estimates as separate cards (M3 linear, M4 logistic) because the authors interpret the sex differences. If you prefer, strike them or treat them as interaction results. 6) The ABCD release is not stated, and the online Appendices A and B are not in the PDF. 7) The paper's description of the sleep-duration weights ("weekdays (7) and weekends (2)") is copied as written but looks like an error for 5/2. All 12 values were checked against the Table 4 and Table 5 text.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The analytic N conflicts inside the paper: the abstract and Results say 11,633, but the Table 1 title says 11,363. I used 11,633. 2) Age is listed as a confounder in Methods 2.4 but is missing from the Table 2 footnote, so it is unclear whether the final adjusted model includes age. 3) There is another inconsistency about baseline suicidal behaviors. Methods says participants missing baseline suicidal behaviors were excluded, the Table 2 footnote lists baseline suicidal behaviors as a covariate, and a sensitivity analysis that excluded baseline cases is described only as "unchanged", with no numbers printed. 4) The paper never says whether each modality was run as its own model or all were entered together. I assumed separate models, based on the one-row-per-modality layout next to a separate total-screen-time row. 5) The ORs are per 1 hour/day of each modality. The baseline SDs are 0.45-0.56 h/day, so one hour is about 2 SDs, and the derived d will not be on the per-SD scale used by some other papers. 6) Social networking was not significant in the adjusted model (OR 1.27, CI 0.97-1.66, p=0.076). It is extracted as a null estimate. 7) Table 1 has a copy-paste error in its title ("binge eating characteristics"). Values were checked against both the page images and pdftotext output: Table 2 adjusted ORs, CIs and p-values, and the Table 1 SDs.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.notes: OR converts directly via Chinn, so no SD or base rate is needed. The resulting d is per 1 hour/day, not per 1 SD. Baseline SDs from Table 1 (p. 10, propensity-weighted): texting 0.56, video chat 0.52, social networking 0.45 h/day; a 1 hour/day contrast is about 1.8-2.2 SDs of these right-skewed IVs, so a per-SD rescaling (ln(OR)*SD_IV) would give smaller values. Outcome base rate p0 = 0.0138 (1.38% at two-year follow-up, Table 1 and Results p. 4), so the outcome is rare and the OR approximates the RR. The Chinn conversion assumes an underlying logistic latent variable.

Prevalence at two-year follow-up 1.38% (Table 1; Results p. 4).

papers.extraction_flags: 1) Eligibility: in this paper, age of smartphone ownership is used only to split the sample into 5 groups (8 & under, 9 & 10, 11 & 12, 13 & 14, No Phone) for multi-group models (M1 Table 3/4, M2 latent growth). It never enters a model as a regressor with its own coefficient, so in practice it works as a moderator, and FT-IC2 clarification 7 says moderators do not qualify. The only direct phone-trait numbers are the unadjusted bivariate r values in Table 1 (M3: 'Cellphone age' with youth/parent internalizing Y1-Y4) and three Wald chi-square tests comparing adjacent groups' informant effects. A human should confirm whether Stage-2 inclusion holds. 2) M1 is the analysis the authors use to interpret their findings, but it is not convertible to d. Only M3 converts (r to d), and M3 is unadjusted. It also treats the coded group variable (No Phone presumably = 5) as continuous, and the coding is not printed explicitly. 3) Table 3 errors in the No Phone column: the informant row (.03/.02/.064) and the time row (.06/.07/.401) duplicate the screen-time and puberty rows. The text reports b = -.04, SE = .06, p = .694 and b = -.09, SE = .05, p = .068. I extracted the table values and flagged them in notes. 4) The text gives SE = .17 for the 11 & 12 informant effect; Table 3 gives .03. 5) Table 4, 13 & 14 column: every printed z equals b, and Y4 z = .40 vs b = -.40, which looks like a typesetting error. Y1 b = .22, p = .039 contradicts the text's claim that 13 & 14 was significant only at Y4. 6) Per the text, beta1/beta2 in Table 3 come from the model before the interaction was added and beta3 from the interaction model. 7) M2 (post-hoc latent growth curve) values come from the Results text p. 5, which matches Figure 1. Covariates for that model are not reported. 8) The full-sample interaction CI [-.29, -.23] does not contain b = -.21 (excluded, not phone-specific). 9) There is no supplement in the PDF; Supplemental Table 1 and Figure 1 are online only and were not reviewed.

papers.title: The role of smartphones in adolescent-parent discrepancy in reporting adolescents' internalizing problems

primary_models.estimation: Mplus 8.3, maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR), FIML for missing data (MAR). ABCD propensity weights (ACS-calibrated) applied in all models. Random vs fixed effects compared in the full sample with the Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square difference test (chi2_SB(2) = 8753.51, p < .001), so random effects retained. Group differences in the informant effect tested with post-hoc Wald tests for adjacent groups (9 & 10 vs 11 & 12, 11 & 12 vs 13 & 14, 13 & 14 vs No Phone; 8 & under vs 9 & 10 not reported as significant). Interaction probed by computing the informant effect at each year (Table 4, Figure 2). Alpha = .05; no multiple-comparison correction reported. No sex interaction tested. A full-sample (not grouped) version was also run (time b = 0.04, informant b = -0.47, time x informant b = -0.21).
primary_models.native_metric: other:within-group unstandardized MLM coefficient (b); Wald chi-square for group contrasts
primary_models.design: Longitudinal, four annual waves (Year 1 to Year 4 follow-ups, mean ages 10.9, 12.0, 12.9, 14.1). Internalizing problems from both reporters (youth BPM and parent CBCL) at each wave are stacked as repeated observations nested within dyads; informant (youth = 0, parent = 1) and time are level-1 predictors and the time x informant product tests whether the parent-youth discrepancy changes over time. Age of smartphone ownership (parent-reported, earliest reported age used) does not enter as a predictor; it defines five groups (8 & under, 9 & 10, 11 & 12, 13 & 14, No Phone) for a multi-group model in which all parameters are estimated separately by group. The phone variable therefore functions as a grouping/moderating variable: the phone 'effect' is the between-group difference in the informant effect and in its change over time, tested with post-hoc Wald tests for adjacent groups. Per the Results (p. 6), beta1 and beta2 in Table 3 come from the model before the time x informant term was added; beta3 comes from the final model with the product term. Table 4 probes the informant effect at each year from the interaction model.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, complete parent-adolescent dyads. Wave Ns: baseline 11,876 (mean age 9.9), Year 1 11,219 (10.9), Year 2 10,972 (12.0), Year 3 10,335 (12.9), Year 4 4,754 (14.1; about half of the sample per ABCD's release schedule). Abstract and Participants: 52.0% White, 20.3% Hispanic, 15.0% Black, 2.1% Asian, 10.5% Other; 47.8% female. Parent reporters 85.3% biological mothers, 10.0% biological fathers, 2.3% adoptive, 1.0% custodial, 1.4% other. Smartphone ownership groups (Table 2): 8 & under n = 677, 9 & 10 n = 2,641, 11 & 12 n = 5,037, 13 & 14 n = 744, No Phone n = 376 (sum 9,475). Attrition about 15% by Year 3 for internalizing and 17.9% missing for smartphone age; boys and youth of less-educated parents were more likely to drop out. Missing data handled with FIML under MAR.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3 (p. 7) for beta1, beta2, beta3 by group; Table 4 (p. 8) for probes of the informant effect at each year; Figure 2 (p. 7); Results pp. 6-8; interpreted in Discussion pp. 8-9.
primary_models.name: Multi-group two-level model of parent- and youth-reported internalizing problems on time, informant, and time x informant, grouped by age of smartphone ownership, adjusted for screen time, puberty, sex, and parent education

primary_models.iv: Age of first smartphone ownership. Parents were asked whether the child owns a smartphone and, annually, at what age the child first owned a cell phone; if answers changed, the earlier response was used. Youth whose parent answered 'No' to ownership at Year 4 were coded 5 (No Phone). Recoded into five groups: 8 & under, 9 & 10, 11 & 12, 13 & 14, No Phone. Columns of the estimate matrix are model parameters within each group: beta1 time, beta2 informant (parent minus youth difference averaged over waves), beta3 time x informant, and the probed informant effect at each year.
primary_models.equation: Level 1: IP[ijk] = beta0i + beta1i*Time[ij] + beta2i*Informant[k] + beta3i*(Time[ij] x Informant[k]) + b_PD*Puberty[ij] + b_ST*ScreenTime[ij] + e[ijk]. Level 2: beta0i = gamma0 + g1*Sex[i] + g2*ParentEd[i] + g3*PDmean[i] + g4*STmean[i] + u0i; beta1i = gamma1 + u1i; beta2i = gamma2 + u2i; beta3i = gamma3 + u3i. All parameters estimated separately in each of the five smartphone-ownership groups (multi-group). Probe: informant effect at year t = beta2 + beta3*t.

d_transformation.notes: M3 correlations are directly convertible; SD_IV (0.85) and SD_DV per wave/reporter are from Table 1 (p. 5) but are not needed for the r-to-d conversion. M3 is unadjusted and treats a five-category variable (with No Phone coded as the highest value) as continuous, so the derived d is a rough association, not the authors' focal estimate. M1 is the analysis the authors use to interpret the smartphone finding, but it is a multi-group model in which smartphone age only defines groups; the parameters are the informant (parent minus youth) effect and its change over time within each group, in raw internalizing-score units (0-12). A between-group phone contrast exists only as Wald chi-square tests (df = 1) with no effect size, so no Cohen's d for smartphone ownership can be derived from M1 or M2 without the raw between-group differences and their SEs, which are not reported. M2 slopes are within-group change over time, likewise not a phone effect.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M3: per unit of the coded ownership-age variable expressed as a correlation (higher code = later or no smartphone ownership); sign is negative for youth-report internalizing, so later ownership goes with fewer youth-reported problems. M1/M2: smartphone age is a grouping variable; estimates are within-group parameters (parent vs youth difference, change per year), not effects of phone ownership.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: M3 only: d = 2r / sqrt(1 - r^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009). M1 and M2: no conversion.

primary_models.estimation: Mplus 8.3, full information maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR). Model selection by Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square difference tests across M1 (all constrained over time) to M4 (all free), then gender multigroup models M5-M8; for social EMU, M8 (all parameters free over time and across gender) was selected (Supplemental Table 4). Fit: CFI = .99, TLI = .97, RMSEA = .04, SRMR = .02, chi2(20) = 195.91, p < .001 (Figure 3/4 notes print CFI = .991, TLI = .966, RMSEA = .038, SRMR = .015). Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction applied (p-adj reported). Gender differences tested via multigroup comparison and reported as separate boys/girls estimates. Sensitivity analysis adding youth internalizing/externalizing problems and parents' screen-use behavior as covariates on the random intercepts is described narratively as similar (p. 1033); its path estimates are not printed. Paper reports both unstandardized b (with SE and 95% CI) and standardized beta (no CI).
primary_models.name: Multigroup (boys vs girls) random-intercept cross-lagged panel model of within-person social EMU (social media + texting) and family conflict across four annual waves, adjusted for family income
primary_models.equation: Within-person part, per group g (boys, girls): FC_w[t+1] = a_F[t,g]*FC_w[t] + c_EF[t,g]*SEMU_w[t] + e_F[t+1]; SEMU_w[t+1] = a_E[t,g]*SEMU_w[t] + c_FE[t,g]*FC_w[t] + e_E[t+1], for t = T1,T2,T3, with cov(e_F[t], e_E[t]) free. Observed: FC[i,t] = mu_F[t] + RI_FC[i] + FC_w[i,t]; SEMU[i,t] = mu_E[t] + RI_SEMU[i] + SEMU_w[i,t]; cov(RI_FC, RI_SEMU) free; RI_FC and RI_SEMU regressed on income. Focal effects: c_EF (social EMU -> later family conflict) and c_FE (family conflict -> later social EMU); cov(RI_FC, RI_SEMU) is the between-person association.

primary_models.iv: Social electronic media use (social EMU), youth self-report on the ABCD Youth Screen Time Questionnaire at T1-T4. Composite of two items: 'Text on a phone, tablet, or computer (e.g., GChat, Whatsapp, etc.)' and 'Visit social networking sites like Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, etc.', each asked separately for a typical weekday and weekend day in hours and minutes; weekday and weekend totals were combined as a weighted mean per type and the social composite summed social media + texting (hours per day). Winsorized at +/- 3 SD. Table 1 (p. 1031), full sample: T1 M = 0.34, SD = 0.82; T2 M = 0.61, SD = 1.16; T3 M = 1.16, SD = 1.66; T4 M = 1.89, SD = 2.07. In the RI-CLPM the focal predictor is the within-person deviation of social EMU at wave t. For the reverse-direction paths the IV is within-person family conflict at wave t.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study youth (release not stated). Wave Ns: T1 N = 11,876 (M age 9.9), T2 N = 11,219 (M age 10.9), T3 N = 10,972 (printed as '100,972'; M age 12.0), T4 N = 10,335 (M age 12.9); abstract gives T1 N = 11,787. Table 1 Ns for social EMU: T1 11,847, T2 11,204, T3 10,367, T4 10,298. Full information maximum likelihood used so the analytic sample is all available cases; group-specific (boys/girls) Ns not reported. Sample described as White 52.0%, Hispanic 20.3%, Black 15.0%, Asian 2.1%, Other 10.5%; female 47.8%; 31.2% income < $50,000, 40.8% >= $100,000; 73.5% married two-parent households. Missingness increased over time (T2 5.6-5.7%, T3 7.8-7.9%, T4 13.2%); attrition higher for boys, lower-income families, and families with greater baseline conflict.
primary_models.dv: Family conflict: youth report on the 9-item Conflict subscale of the Family Environment Scale (True/False, summed, range 0-9) at T1-T4; alpha = .68, .67, .64, .68. Table 1 full-sample: T1 M = 2.04, SD = 1.95; T2 M = 1.91, SD = 1.88; T3 M = 1.92, SD = 1.83; T4 M = 2.10, SD = 1.94. Outcome is within-person family conflict at wave t+1. For the reverse-direction paths the DV is within-person social EMU at wave t+1 (descriptives as above).
primary_models.design: Longitudinal four-wave panel: ABCD baseline (T1, age ~9.9), 1-year (T2), 2-year (T3), and 3-year (T4) follow-ups. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (Hamaker et al., 2015) separating stable between-person components (random intercepts for social EMU and family conflict, allowed to correlate) from within-person deviations at each wave. Within-person part has autoregressive paths, same-wave residual covariances, and lag-1 cross-lagged paths in both directions (social EMU at t -> family conflict at t+1, and family conflict at t -> social EMU at t+1) for T1-T2, T2-T3, and T3-T4. The selected model (M8) frees all autoregressive and cross-lagged parameters across time and across gender (boys and girls estimated as separate groups), so each lag and each sex has its own estimate. Social media/texting is the IV for the EMU -> conflict paths and the DV for the conflict -> EMU paths.

papers.title: Youth electronic media use and family conflict: Bidirectional associations across early adolescence
papers.authors: Carvalho C, Ravindran N, Koss KJ
papers.extraction_flags:
There is one model card (M1): the gender-multigroup RI-CLPM M8 for social EMU (social media + texting) and family conflict, adjusted for income. It has 12 cross-lagged estimates (both directions x 3 lags x boys/girls) and 2 between-person random-intercept associations. All values come from the Results text (pp. 1030-1032). I checked each one against Figures 3 and 4. I recorded native beta_std and also kept b with its 95% CI in B/B_lo/B_hi, because the paper prints no CI for beta.

Printed values a human should check:
(1) Girls social EMU T1->FC T2: b = -0.59 with SE = .02 and CI [-0.94, -0.25]. The SE does not fit the CI.
(2) Boys FC T3->social EMU T4: b = -0.04, but beta = .03 and the CI [-0.00, 0.07] is positive. The figure shows .03, so the sign on b is probably a typo.
(3) Girls FC T1->social EMU T2: the text says beta = -.07, the figure says -.06.
(4) The girls random-intercept sentence says 'total EMU' even though it is in the social EMU paragraph. Its beta is .24 in the text and .22 in Figure 4.
(5) The girls T2->T3 b CI is asymmetric.

Other issues:
- sd_dv values are full-sample observed SDs from Table 1. They are not within-person or sex-specific SDs.
- Group-specific Ns are not reported. T3 N is printed as '100,972'.
- The ABCD release is not stated.
- Supplemental Tables 1-5 are not in the PDF.
- Texting is defined as 'on a phone, tablet, or computer'. I counted it as qualifying under the activity-defined clarification 5.
- I excluded the sensitivity-model coefficients for parents' screen behavior -> youth social media intercept (girls beta = -.05, p = .049; boys beta = -.12, p < .001), because they are covariate effects the authors do not interpret further. A coder may disagree.

1. The PDF does not include Supplementary Tables S1-S9. The full LMM/GLMM coefficients (Tables S2-S5) are only in the web supplement. Because of that, the extraction relies on the in-text likelihood ratio chi-squares and simple slopes. Someone should get the supplement and check for social media coefficients, SEs and SDs of the sleep outcomes.

2. The seven simple slopes for social media and time in bed (p. 7: -0.24, -0.08, -0.07, 0.05, -0.15, -0.13, -0.12) are the same numbers as the age and time-in-bed slopes printed just above them. The only difference is the sign of the August value, which is printed as -0.05 for age and +0.05 for social media. This looks like a copy error in the paper. The August +0.05 also contradicts the text saying social media was linked to shorter time in bed. The bedtime slopes for social media and age are different from each other, so they look fine. A human should verify against Table S2 / Figure S4.

3. d is marked not transformable. The slopes are in raw sleep units (hours or minutes) per 1 SD of social media time, since predictors were standardized. The paper gives no SD for any sleep outcome and no CI or SE for any slope. Sleep onset latency and awakenings have only likelihood ratio chi-squares, with no coefficient. If the supplement gives SDs for the outcomes, the M1 slopes could be converted, so the status might change to partial.

4. The design is concurrent: social media and sleep are measured at the same assessment across 7 timepoints. It is not a prospective design. The model names were built from the methods text, because the full term list is only in the supplement. Results on p. 8 also mention an age x video game interaction that the methods do not list.

5. p-values printed as 'p < .01' are entered as p = null with p_label '<.01'. Page numbers in locations use the manuscript's printed page numbers. Texting and video chat were collected but dropped from all models because of multicollinearity, so no estimates for them can be extracted.

primary_models.dv: Three continuous sleep outcomes from items of the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (youth version), harmonized across timepoints: (1) time in bed (TIB), hours, computed from reported bedtime and wake-up time; (2) bedtime, clock time from the item 'I go to bed at...' (responses 7 PM to 6 AM), modeled in hours; (3) sleep onset latency, minutes, from 'I need __ minutes to fall asleep' (0 minutes to 4 hours, pseudo-continuous). All sleep variables winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Means and SDs are not printed in the main text; Figure 1A-C plots means by sex and assessment.

It counts as a phone/SM-only composite under FT-IC2 Step 2, but the texting item says 'cell phone, tablet, or computer'. 2. M1 (the latent change score SEM) is the anchor model. A coder should decide whether to keep M2 (the Table 1 correlations, which are descriptive and Holm-corrected but have no exact p-values or N), M3 (the post hoc sibling mixed models, where the paper prints 'r' for the baseline result and 'beta' for the change result and does not state the scaling) and M4 (the mediation indirect effect, which is not convertible). 3. A Socializing-only model is in the online Supplementary Information, which is not in this PDF. 7. Figure 1 draws the baseline-intelligence/change link as a double-headed arrow, but the gender section calls it an 'effect'. The M1 equation treats it as a covariance.json

primary_models.design: Longitudinal two-wave design. Screen time (Watching, Socializing, Gaming), cogPGS and SES are exogenous variables measured at baseline (ages 9-10). Intelligence is a latent factor measured at baseline and at the 2-year follow-up (ages 11-12) from the same five cognitive tasks with loadings and intercepts constrained equal across waves (strong invariance). The model estimates two outcomes simultaneously: the baseline latent intelligence (a cross-sectional association with baseline Socializing) and the latent change in intelligence from baseline to 2-year follow-up (a prospective association, with baseline intelligence also predicting change). Screen time is measured only at baseline; no repeated measurement of the IV and no time x IV interaction.

Response scale none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, >4 h. Units are hours, but the variable entered the SEM as a standardized residual after regression on age, site and 20 genetic PCs, so coefficients are in SD units. primary_models.dv: Latent general intelligence factor from five cognitive tasks (NIH Toolbox Picture Vocabulary, Flanker, Oral Reading Recognition; Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test; Little Man Task), each residualized for age, site and 20 genetic PCs. Two latent DVs: baseline intelligence (ages 9-10) and latent change in intelligence from baseline to 2-year follow-up (ages 11-12). Standardized loadings at baseline: Vocab 0.63, Flanker 0.28, Reading 0.70, RAVLT 0.41, LMT 0.36 (Fig. 1). Latent intelligence increased by beta = 0.24 (p < 0.001; 3.64 IQ points) over two years. Also reported in Figure 1: the covariance of Socializing with cogPGS (a genetic, individual-trait variable).
primary_models.estimation: R 4.0.3, lavaan 0.6-9 (also semTools). Full-information maximum likelihood with robust ML (Yuan-Bentler scaled test statistic). Fit: RMSEA = 0.023, CFI = 0.975. Covariates handled by prior residualization (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell argument) rather than in the SEM. No random effects; one child per family. No survey weights. No multiple-comparison correction stated for SEM paths; alpha 0.05 implied. Standardized betas reported, no CIs or SEs. Gender moderation tested by multigroup SEM (free vs constrained, chi-square difference = 1093, p < 0.001) with planned contrasts: Socializing -> baseline intelligence not different by gender (chi-square difference = 0.84, p = 0.357); Socializing -> change not different (chi-square difference = 0.94, p = 0.331); gender-specific Socializing betas not reported. Post hoc sensitivity analyses (SES replaced by parental education; Watching split into TV vs online video) did not report Socializing estimates. Separate Socializing-only models are said to be in the Supplementary Information (not in this PDF).

papers.title: The impact of digital media on children's intelligence while controlling for genetic differences in cognition and socioeconomic background

papers.authors: Nivins S, Sauce B, Liebherr M, Judd N, Klingberg T
papers.extraction_flags: 1) Standardization: the paper labels coefficients only as "beta" and never says whether variables were standardized. Raw volumes of about 150x10^3 mm^3 don't fit coefficients of 0.01-0.12, so the outcomes look standardized, but this is an assumption. I coded native_metric as beta_std. 2) The focal M1 estimates are social media x Poly(Time,2) interaction slopes (orthogonal polynomial). They don't convert cleanly to a between-person d; only the main effect and the M2 betas are roughly convertible. SD_DV is not reported anywhere. SD_IV = 0.95 for average social media use (Table 1); T0 SD = 1.06. 3) Composite: the social media IV is texting (cell phone/tablet/computer) + social networking sites + video chat. That qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2 and clarification 5. 4) The supplement (eTables 1-8) is not bundled in the PDF. M2 estimates (beta -0.01, p 0.10, eTable 5; beta -0.03, p 0.16, eTable 6) are from the text only, with no SE or CI, and their analytic N is unknown. The abstract anchors on the beta -0.03. Please check the online supplement. 5) The SNS-only sensitivity estimate (beta -0.02, p 0.002, text p. 6) does not name which model term it is. I inferred it is the Time^2 term for cerebellum and flagged this in its note. 6) The significance threshold is Bonferroni p<0.0027 (Table 2 caption), while the text says p<0.003. CSA x Time^2 has p = 0.004, so I coded it sig=false. 7) Coders may want to decide whether M2 (the abstract-cited accumulated-effect estimate) should be the primary anchor rather than the M1 interactions.

primary_models.equation: Y_ij = b0 + b1*cogPGS_i + b2*Poly(Time,2)_ij + b3*Sex_i + b4*AgeAtBaseline_i + b5*SMUsage_i + b6*SES_i + b7*Ancestry(20 PCs)_i + b8*SMUsage_i*Poly(Time,2)_ij + b9*SMUsage_i*Poly(Time,2)_ij*SES_i + b10*SMUsage_i*Poly(Time,2)_ij*cogPGS_i + (1|site) + u0_i + u1_i*Poly(Time,2)_ij + e_ij. Focal terms: b5 (main effect), b8 split into SMUsage x Time and SMUsage x Time^2.
primary_models.estimation: lme4::lmer in R, restricted maximum likelihood. Random intercept for site; per-child random intercept and random slope on time. No weights. Quadratic over linear age model chosen by AIC/BIC (eTable 1) and likelihood ratio test. Bonferroni correction across 3 DM types x 3 brain regions x (overall + sex) = 18 tests, significance p < 0.05/18 = 0.0027 (Table 2 caption; text says p < 0.003); p values in Table 2 are uncorrected. Separate models fit for each DM type (social media, video games, TV/videos); social media not mutually adjusted for the other DM types. Sex x DM x time three-way interactions tested (Eq. 2; eTable 4), all non-significant, so no sex-stratified estimates. Three-way DM x time x SES interactions non-significant (no numbers in main text). Sensitivity analyses: excluding preterm (<37 weeks), birth weight <2500 g or ADHD (n = 3979; eTable 7) and restricting to children with MRI at all three visits (n = 1462; eTable 8) reported narratively as remaining significant; and excluding texting/video chat from the social media composite (beta = -0.02, p = 0.002, text p. 6). primary_models.design: Longitudinal, three MRI waves: baseline (T0, age ~9.9), 2-year follow-up (T2) and 4-year follow-up (T4). The outcome enters as repeated measures (not averaged) with random intercepts and random slopes on time per child. The IV is time-invariant: average self-reported social media hours/day across all annual visits (T0-T4). The focal estimates are the interactions of average social media usage with the linear and quadratic (orthogonal polynomial) time terms, i.e. whether brain developmental trajectories differ by social media use; the social media main effect is also reported.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study release 5.0, data collected September 2016 to January 2022. Of 11,875 children, 6469 met inclusion criteria at T0 (age mean 9.9, SD 0.6; boys n = 3369, 52.1%; girls 3100), 4610 at T2 (age 12.0, SD 0.7; boys 2487, 53.9%) and 1697 at T4 (age 13.4, SD 0.6; boys 949, 55.9%); 1462 had usable MRI at all three time points. Exclusions: born <28 weeks or birth weight <1200 g, not proficient in English, neurological problems, seizure history, MRI contraindication, missing SES, genetic, DM usage or neuroimaging data, failed MRI QC or incidental findings; one child randomly selected per family. Race/ethnicity breakdown not reported.

d_transformation.contrast_type: M1 main effect and M2: per 1 unit (h/day) of social media use, or per 1 SD if the IV was standardized (not stated). M1 interaction terms: difference in the linear or quadratic orthogonal-polynomial time slope per unit of average social media use.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Treat beta as approximate r: d = 2*beta / sqrt(1 - beta^2). If beta proves to be unstandardized, beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV first (SD_DV not reported).
d_transformation.notes: The paper never says whether variables were standardized. Raw brain volumes (cerebellum ~150 x 10^3 mm^3, Fig. 1) are incompatible with time coefficients of 0.04-0.12 and SEs of 0.001-0.02, which suggests the outcomes were standardized; SES and cogPGS are explicitly z-scored, but social media hours apparently entered in hours/day. SD_IV for the average social media variable is 0.95 h/day (Table 1, p. 3, 'Average estimated time spent over four years on Using social media'); SD at T0 is 1.06 (Table 1). SD_DV is not reported anywhere in the PDF. The M1 main-effect beta and the M2 betas can be converted to an approximate d under the beta_std assumption. The M1 interaction coefficients with Poly(Time,2) (orthogonal polynomial terms) are slope-difference parameters and do not map onto a between-person Cohen's d; they should be displayed in native metric only. No CIs are reported (SEs only for M1; neither SE nor CI for M2 in the PDF), so d CIs cannot be produced.

primary_models.dv: Six outcomes, each modelled separately: CBCL internalizing and externalizing problems (parent report; internalizing = withdrawn/depressed, anxious/depressed, somatic complaints; externalizing = rule-breaking and aggressive behavior; the paper does not say whether raw or T-scores were used); NIH Toolbox picture vocabulary and picture sequencing memory (Year-4 cognition, higher = better); Fitbit average sleep duration and sleep duration variability (Fitbit measures are not described in Methods). All estimates are standardized.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. All measures come from the ABCD Year-4 follow-up visit. EARS passive sensing ran for 3 weeks around that visit; the self-report measures are the Year-4 ABCD Screen Time Questionnaire (typical day over the past 12 months) and a post-sensing survey covering the 3-week sensing period. CBCL, NIH Toolbox and Fitbit outcomes are from the same follow-up. One observation per youth; no repeated measures and no time interactions. Each SMA measure (EARS, SR 3-week, SR 12-month) and each category (total, social media, gaming) was entered in a separate model against each outcome.
primary_models.name: Linear mixed model (family random effect, standardized betas) of CBCL, NIH Toolbox cognition and Fitbit sleep outcomes on EARS-logged and self-reported social media / smartphone app time
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, Year-4 follow-up. Of 4,754 youth at Year 4, 1,483 agreed to install EARS, and EARS-logged app data were available only for 495 Android users (Apple blocked app scraping). Analytic sample N = 495; CBCL available for n = 492; NIH Toolbox cognition missing for at most 20; paired EARS vs self-report comparisons used n = 395 for social media and gaming and n = 376 for total time (Table 2). N for the Fitbit sleep outcomes is not reported. Seven participants with family income still missing after LOCF imputation were excluded from relevant analyses. Sample (Table 1): age 14.01 (SD 0.70) years; 288 male (58.18%), 207 female (41.82%); White 281 (56.77%), Black 54 (10.91%), Hispanic 97 (19.60%), Other 63 (12.73%); family income >=$100k 202 (40.81%), $50-100k 154 (31.11%), <$50k 132 (26.67%), missing 7 (1.41%); parents married 338 (68.28%). Compared with excluded Year-4 participants, the EARS sample had more boys, was slightly younger, and had lower parental education and income.
primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed models in R using lme4, with family as a random effect. Standardized estimates reported. Two-sided tests, alpha = 0.05. No multiple-comparison correction reported despite many SMA-measure x outcome tests. Missing family income, parental education and marital status imputed by last observation carried forward from earlier waves; no imputation for cognition or self-reported SMA. Fig. 3 prints only associations with p < 0.05; non-significant combinations are not printed. No interaction or stratified analyses for these models. A pubertal-stage sensitivity analysis is reported only for the reporting-bias models.

The covariates in the LMMs are unclear. Methods say only that the Table 1 demographics "were considered as potential covariates", plus a family random effect. 3. Total-EARS (all smartphone app time) and Game-EARS (smartphone gaming apps) are included as passively sensed phone or app time, and as mobile gaming for Game-EARS. Please confirm these count under FT-IC2. Self-reported total and gaming rows are excluded. 4. The Methods never describe the Fitbit sleep outcomes and give no N for them. 5. The SM-time vs SMAQ/VGAQ betas (text p. 3, e.g. SR 12-mos SMAQ beta = 0.15) are excluded under FT-IC2 clarification 1, which treats them as SM-to-SM associations. The reporting-bias multinomial logistic models (Table 3, picture vocabulary OR = 0.96) are excluded as measurement-concordance analyses. Please check both decisions. 6. It is not stated whether the CBCL scores are raw or T-scores. sd_dv is null, which does not matter here because the betas are already standardized. 7. The supplementary tables (4-7) are not bundled with the PDF. Values were read from the high-resolution Fig. 3 image and cross-checked against the Results text and Abstract where these report them.

primary_models.iv: Each of 41 digital and social media exposure variables, one per model, drawn from the ABCD Cyber Bullying Questionnaire and the Youth and Parent Screen Time Surveys (youth and parent report). Of 52 candidate variables, 7 were dropped for <1% endorsement and 4 for collinearity (|r| > 0.9); extreme values on continuous variables (e.g., number of followers) were removed. Exposures span five domains: screentime (minutes/hours per day by weekend/weekday), parental monitoring of social media (e.g., parent suspects secret accounts), apps used (yes/no per platform, platform-specific screentime, most-used app), overuse/addictive patterns of use (e.g., 'I use social media apps so much that it has had a bad effect on my schoolwork or job'), and peer interaction (e.g., connectedness via phone). Exact coding and units per variable are in Supplementary Table S1 and the Supplement, not the main text. Of the 35 FDR-significant exposures, 31 are phone/SM-specific and are extracted here; cyberbullying and three video-game screentime items are not. No descriptive statistics for the exposures are given in the main text, apart from 48% reporting a public account and 16% reporting TikTok as most-used app.

primary_models.estimation: R, lme4::lmer linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts for family nested within study site. Missing exposure data imputed with missForest (random forest) within each subsample. Collinear exposures (Pearson r > 0.9) removed with caret::findCorrelation. FDR correction across the 41 comparisons; exposures with FDR-corrected p < 0.05 and coefficient > 0 treated as risk factors, < 0 as protective; 35 of 41 survived. Sensitivity: ExWAS rerun with list-wise deletion instead of imputation yielded 31 significant variables (Table S1, not in PDF); per-variable sensitivity estimates not in main text. No interaction tests at the ExWAS level. No survey weights reported.

d_transformation.native_metric: B (unstandardized LME coefficient, BPM T-score points per unit of exposure)
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per one unit of each exposure as coded in Table S1: yes vs no for binary items (e.g., public vs private account), per unit of time or count for continuous items. Units are not given in the main text.
d_transformation.notes: SD_DV = 10 by construction for BPM T-scores (normed), but BPM T-scores are floor-truncated in community samples so the observed SD may differ; the paper reports no BPM descriptives. SD_IV is not reported for any exposure in the main text, and exposure units/coding are only in the Supplement. Only one qualifying coefficient is printed as a number in the main text (public social media account, B = 2.13, Discussion p. 6, no CI); this is binary, so d is computable with SD_DV = 10. All other 30 qualifying coefficients and all CIs are in Fig. 2B (graphic only) and Supplementary Table S1, which is not in the PDF. With Table S1, the binary items become convertible; continuous items still need SD_IV.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Binary exposures: d = B / SD_DV (adjusted mean difference over SD 10). Continuous exposures: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1).

2. Sample label conflict. The Methods and Results headings say the ExWAS ran in the training subsample (n = 5082). The Fig. 2 caption says "testing subsample". I followed the Methods; please check.

3. Units and coding of exposures are not given in the main text. SD_IV and per-model N are not reported. SD_DV is set to 10 because BPM scores are normed T-scores, but BPM T-scores are floor-truncated, so the observed SD may differ.

4. Six non-significant exposures (Table S1 numbers 10, 17, 23, 24, 25, 26) are not named in the main text. Some are probably phone/SM null results and should be added once Table S1 is available.

5. Eligibility calls a coder should check:
- Included: "Night chatroom use" (platform not specified), "Connectedness via phone", "Parent suspects secret account" (parent report) and "Follower/Following count".
- Excluded as gaming: "Screentime Video Games [20]", although Fig. 2A puts it in the App-type domain, so it may be app-based.
- Excluded: cyberbullying, per FT-IC2 clarification 3.
- Excluded: the headline exposomic risk score (Table 2, and the suicide-attempt ORs in Table S3). It is a weighted composite that includes cyberbullying and video-game items, so it fails FT-IC2 Step 2.

6. Spot-checked against the page images: Table 1 training demographics, Table 2 Model-4 (1.78, 1.58-1.98, t = 17.41, n = 4004), the text values 2.13 and 3.57, and the suicide ORs 1.76 [1.39-2.23] and 2.76 [1.88-4.05].

papers.extraction_flags:
1) How I grouped the models. M1 puts two separate regressions on one card, Table 2 Model 1 (social media time) and Model 2 (problematic social media use), because they use the same covariates. M2 is Table 2 Model 3, with both variables entered together. M3 is the GSEM mediation in Table 3. A coder may prefer to split Model 1 and Model 2 into separate cards, or to drop M2 and M3 as mediation scaffolding. The abstract's headline estimate is Model 1, RR 1.31.

2) The paper labels problematic social media use (SMAQ) as the "mediator variable". In Table 2 Model 2 it is the main predictor of sipping, so I kept it. Confirm this is acceptable under FT-IC2, which says a variable does not qualify if it appears only as a mediator.

3) The SMAQ score comes only from youth with at least one social media account. The paper does not say how youth without an account were scored. Table 1 gives M 5.9, SD 6.6, which looks like a summed score, though the text says item averages were used.

4) Converting RR to d uses p0 = 0.087, the overall Year 3 sipping rate for the whole sample (Table 1). It is not an unexposed-group rate, because both social media variables are continuous. The contrast is per 1 hour/day or per 1 SMAQ point, not per SD.

5) The Model 2 row is printed as 1.03 (1.03, 1.05), so the point estimate equals the lower bound, likely from rounding.

6) In the GSEM mediation (M3), the scale of B is not reported: no link function is given, and B = 0.03 does not match ln(1.21). So it is not convertible to d. The abstract gives the proportion-mediated p as 0.002, but Table 3 prints 0.001.

7) The authors call the outcome "new-onset" sipping, but participants who sipped at Year 1 were adjusted for, not excluded. The Results text also says "sipping alcohol (Year 2, Model 1)", which looks like a typo for Year 3.

8) Study site is listed as an adjustment variable, but the paper does not say whether it was entered as a fixed effect or a clustering term.

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 hour/day of social media time (Year 1); per 1 point on the SMAQ problematic social media use score (Year 2). Not per SD; per-SD rescaling would require RR^SD_IV (SD 0.59 h/day and 6.6 points from Table 1).
d_transformation.notes: p0 = 0.087 is the marginal Year 3 sipping prevalence for the full analytic sample (Table 1, p. 972), not the rate in an unexposed group; the IVs are continuous so no unexposed group rate exists, and with an 8.7% outcome the approximation is reasonable. SD_IV values from Table 1 (propensity-weighted, N = 7,514): social media time 0.59 h/day, SMAQ 6.6. M1 and M2 RRs are convertible. M3 (GSEM mediation, Table 3) is not convertible: the B coefficients are on an unreported scale (link function not stated) and indirect effects/proportion mediated have no Cohen's d analogue; flagged for later review level.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: OR = RR * (1 - p0) / (1 - RR * p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000). Applied to point estimate and each CI bound.

papers.extraction_flags:
Things a human should verify:

(1) Outcome scale. The S6/S7 footnotes and Supplementary S2/S3 say the DV is BMI percentile and WC percentile, with baseline percentiles as covariates. The main text and Table 1 describe raw BMI (kg/m2) and WC. I treated the DV as percentile and dropped the earlier draft's raw-unit SD_DV of 4.9. In its place I entered the baseline percentile SDs for the included sample from Supplementary Table 1 (BMI 30.3, WC 29.0), as proxies for the overall columns only. The sex-specific SD_DVs are null.

(2) SD_IV. No mean or SD for socializing time is reported anywhere, so d cannot be computed and transformable is false.

(3) IV coding. That socializing is in hours/day is my inference, not stated by the authors.

(4) Model contents. The paper does not say whether socializing was modeled alone or together with TV/movies and video games. The S6/S7 footnote also lists the sleep variables as IVs, which may be copied boilerplate.

(5) Supplement error. The Video games row of S7 is identical to the one in S6, which looks like a copy-paste error. It does not affect the socializing rows.

(6) Sample size. N is 7,445 in the main text but 7,455 in Supplementary Table 1.

(7) Interpretation. The authors never interpret socializing directly. They say subtype results were "consistent with the main findings" and highlight TV/movies and video games. The male BMI cell is the only significant one (B = 0.77, p = 0.001).

primary_models.equation: Y2_pct[i] = b0 + b1*socializing_hours[i] + b2*baseline_pct[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race_ethnicity + b10..b14*income + b15*parent_ed + b16*physical_activity + b17..*study_site + b..*pubertal_status + e[i], where Y2_pct is year-2 BMI percentile or year-2 WC percentile (separate models) and b1 is the focal estimate. Sex term omitted in the female and male models. The supplement does not say whether TV/movies and video games (or the sleep variables, which the S6/S7 footnote mentions) enter the same model as socializing.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study (data release not stated). N = 7,445 participants with complete baseline screen time, sleep disturbance and sleep duration and year-2 BMI and WC (Methods p. 3; Table 1 p. 17); Supplementary Table 1 gives the included group as N = 7,455 and the excluded group as N = 4,516. COVID-19 reduced year-2 anthropometric collection. Implausible anthropometrics excluded (BMI z <= -4 or >= 8 SD; WC z < -4 or > 4 SD). Missing covariates imputed (puberty 16.3%, income 7.6%, baseline BMI percentile 0.4%, parent education 0.2%, physical activity 0.1%; Supplementary S4). 3,511 females (47.3%) and 3,934 males; mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6). Weighted race/ethnicity: 5.9% Asian, 16.6% Black, 16.2% Latino/Hispanic, 3.5% Native American, 56.5% White, 1.3% Other; 57.0% household income < $75,000; 85.3% parent with college education or more (Table 1, p. 17). The sex-stratified columns use the female (n = 3,511) and male (n = 3,934) subsamples.

Subtype analysis described in Statistical Analysis (p. 4); referred to in Results (p. 6) as 'consistent with the main findings'. The Discussion (p. 6) singles out TV/movies and video games as 'particularly associated' and does not discuss socializing.
primary_models.estimation: Weighted multivariable linear regression in Stata 18, using American Community Survey-based propensity weights and study sites as clusters in the survey procedures (Supplementary S1, S5). Missing covariate data handled by multiple imputation by chained equations, 10 imputed datasets pooled (Supplementary S4). Regression assumptions reported as tested and met. alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. Sex-stratified estimates reported alongside the overall model; no formal sex x socializing interaction test reported. Complete-case sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Tables 8-13) cover total screen time and the joint categories only, not the subtypes.
primary_models.name: Weighted multivariable linear regression of year-2 BMI percentile and WC percentile on baseline socializing screen time (texting + video chat + social media), adjusted for baseline BMI/WC percentile, puberty and sociodemographics, overall and stratified by sex
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort. Socializing screen time is measured once at ABCD baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10). The outcome is a single follow-up value at the year-2 visit (BMI percentile in one model, WC percentile in the other), with the baseline percentile of the same measure entered as a covariate, so the coefficient is the association with year-2 adiposity net of baseline adiposity. No repeated measures. Screen time x sleep interaction terms were tested for the main total-screen-time models and reported as nonsignificant (p. 4); no interaction tests are reported for the subtype models. The subtype models are reported for the whole sample and separately for females and males.
primary_models.dv: Two continuous year-2 outcomes, modeled separately: (1) BMI percentile, computed from the mean of three measured weights and heights against CDC age- and sex-specific references; (2) waist circumference percentile, the mean of two WC measurements (inches, nearest 0.1) converted to percentiles using NHANES III reference data via the R package childsds (Supplementary S2). The footnotes of Supplementary Tables 6 and 7 state that the dependent variable is BMI percentile and WC percentile, and Supplementary S3 says baseline BMI and WC percentiles were the adjustment covariates. The main text and Table 1 instead describe BMI (kg/m^2; year-2 mean 20.6, SD 4.9) and WC (year-2 mean 28.8, SD 4.9), but those raw-unit descriptives do not appear to be the modeled scale. Year-2 percentile SDs are not reported; baseline percentile SDs for the included sample are BMI percentile 61.8 (SD 30.3) and WC percentile 61.1 (SD 29.0) (Supplementary Table 1).

papers.extraction_flags:
The paper is 7 pages and the supporting appendices are not in the PDF.

1. The M1 direct effects (0.138 and 0.153) are unstandardized log-odds from a binomial-logit gsem outcome equation. They are not linear B. I coded them as other:logit_B, the same way as sibling paper 107 (same authors and design, with a cannabis outcome). They should be converted with d = B*sqrt(3)/pi, per 1 hour/day.
2. The two direct effects come from the positive-expectancy and negative-expectancy mediation models. The authors interpret both, and neither is clearly the anchor. No total effect is printed.
3. The M2 a-path values (0.07* and 0.003) are read off the Figure 1 labels. There is no CI, SE or exact p, and the link function for the mediator equation is not stated.
4. p0 = 0.054 is the weighted whole-sample prevalence at Year 4, not the rate among non-users.
5. Study site is entered as a covariate, not a random effect, as far as the text says.
6. The ABCD release is not stated.
7. Including the a-path (social media time to smoking expectancies) as a qualifying analysis assumes expectancies count as an individual-trait construct (substance-related cognition). The coder should confirm this.

primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal mediation design across three ABCD follow-up waves. Social media time is measured at Year 2 (2018-2020), smoking expectancies (mediators) at Year 3 (2019-2021), and nicotine experimentation at Year 4 (2020-2022). The outcome is a single Year 4 binary measure, not repeated measures. Two separate mediation models were fit, one with positive expectancies as the mediator and one with negative expectancies; the direct effect of social media time on Year 4 nicotine experimentation is reported from each model. Year 2 nicotine experimentation and Year 2 smoking expectancies are included as covariates to address prior experimentation and beliefs. No time-by-IV interaction applies.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study, Years 2-4 (release not stated in the paper). N = 8292 after excluding participants with missing data on social media use, nicotine variables, or sociodemographic factors (exclusion flowchart in Appendix A, not bundled in the PDF). Mean age 12.0 years (SD 0.7) at Year 2; 48.7% female, 51.3% male; 56.7% White, 19.0% Latino/Hispanic, 14.4% Black, 5.3% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.3% Other (43.3% racial/ethnic minorities). Parent education: 10.5% high school or less, 89.5% college or more. Weighted descriptives (Table 1, p. 4).
primary_models.iv: Year 2 youth-reported social media time in hours per day. Adolescents reported usual daily time on social media separately for weekdays and weekends; the daily average is ([weekday x 5] + [weekend x 2]) / 7. Continuous, per 1 hour/day. Weighted M = 0.7, SD = 1.5 h/day (Table 1).
primary_models.estimation: Stata 18, generalized structural equation modeling (gsem); outcome equation binomial with logit link. Indirect effects and SEs by the delta method; proportion mediated = indirect / (indirect + direct). Sampling weights calibrated to the American Community Survey applied. Study site entered as a covariate; no random effects or family clustering described. Two-sided alpha = .05. No multiple-comparison correction. No interaction or stratified analyses reported. No sensitivity analyses reported. Coefficients are unstandardized log-odds (B); ORs are not printed.

The abstract quotes Model 1 numbers (basic adjustments), and the text says nothing changed after adding family conflict (Model 2). I extracted both as M1 and M2. Since the pooled within-group SD is not reported, d = B/66.14 is an approximation, and the outcome is highly skewed. 6) The paper does not say clearly whether the 'social media' category includes texting and video chat or only social networking sites. 7) The logistic model for any vs no social media use gives only a p-value range, with no ORs. primary_models.sample: ABCD baseline data released in 2019 (NDA DOI 10.15154/1524631), N = 11,875 enrolled; 10,650 participants with complete data on study variables. 5112 girls and 5538 boys, mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6). Child-identified ethnicity: Black n = 1480, Asian n = 215, White n = 5843, Hispanic n = 1746, Multiracial n = 1366. Main caregiver was the mother for 85% and father/other for 15%. 16.7% of children had a psychological problem (CBCL). Parental problem prevalence (Table 1): externalising 935 (8.8%), internalising 1425 (13.4%), total problems 446 (4.2%).
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD baseline visit (2016-2018). Parent-reported psychopathology (IV) and child-reported screen time (DV) measured at the same visit. One observation per child. Phone/SM is the DV here: the predictor is a binary indicator of clinically significant parental psychological problems and the outcome is the child's daily minutes of social media. Each parental problem scale (externalising, internalising, total) is entered as the predictor in a separate model, with the reference group being children whose parent does not have that problem.
primary_models.dv: Child-reported daily minutes of social media use from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey. The social media item covers visiting social networking sites such as Twitter or Instagram; the paper's methods list texting and video chat as separate questionnaire activities, and the paper does not state explicitly whether they were folded into the 'social media' category. Responses on a 7-point scale (none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, >=4 h) for a typical weekday and weekend day; daily minutes computed as (weekday minutes x 5 + weekend minutes x 2)/7. Mean 30.8 (SD 66.14) min/day in the full sample; girls 35.7 (69.9), boys 26.2 (62.1) (Table 1, p. 828). 43% of children reported no social media use.

primary_models.iv: Presence of a clinically significant parental psychological problem from the Adult Self-Report (ASR, 123 items, 0/1/2 response), completed by the main caregiver. Three broadband scales are used: externalising, internalising and total problems. Raw scores were converted to gender-normed T-scores and dichotomised at T >= 65 (clinically significant problem = 1) vs T < 65 (= 0). Prevalence: externalising 8.8%, internalising 13.4%, total 4.2% (Table 1, p. 828).
primary_models.equation: SM_minutes[i,site] = b0 + b1*ParentProblem[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*ethnicity + b5*family_income + b6*main_caregiver + b7*child_psych_problem + u_site + e[i], fitted separately with ParentProblem = externalising, internalising, or total problems (each coded 1 = T >= 65 vs 0 = T < 65). b1 is the adjusted difference in daily social media minutes between children of parents with vs without the problem.
primary_models.estimation: Multilevel general linear model with a random intercept for study site; coefficients are raw (unstandardised) minutes/day. Analyses conducted in RStudio 1.1.463. No survey weights reported. No multiple-comparison correction; significance flagged at p < 0.05 and p < 0.01. Table 3 column headers for the non-TV activities are printed as 'OR', but the table title and footnotes identify these as multilevel general linear model coefficients in minutes per day (the same as the TV 'Coeff.' column). Gender interaction terms (parental problem x child gender) were tested; results reported in Table S2 (not bundled in the PDF). A second step (Model 2) additionally adjusted for family conflict (extracted as M2). An additional logistic regression on any vs no social media use found no association (p-values 0.201 to 0.786; ORs not printed).

d_transformation.notes: SD_DV = 66.14 min/day from Table 1 (p. 828, 'All (n = 10650)' column; printed with two decimals while other rows use one). The pooled within-group SD is not reported, so the total-sample SD is used; with exposure prevalence of 4-13% the difference should be small. SD_IV is not needed for this contrast. The authors themselves report Cohen's d of 0.09-0.10 for Table 2 total screen time results, not for social media. The DV is right-skewed (43% report zero social media), so d based on SD of a skewed outcome should be read with caution. This d (group difference / SD) is not directly comparable to per-1-SD-of-IV d values from continuous-IV papers.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Parent with clinically significant problem (ASR T >= 65) vs parent without the problem
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Dichotomous IV -> continuous DV: d = (adjusted M1 - M0) / SD_pooled = B / SD_DV, using the full-sample SD of social media minutes/day (66.14) as an approximation of the pooled within-group SD. CI endpoints converted the same way (B_lo / SD_DV, B_hi / SD_DV).

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 hour/day of weekday activity (implied by STQ coding; slope not reported). The F-based d is a test-statistic conversion and does not depend on the IV unit.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Not one of the §4a conversions. A point d can be approximated from a 1-df F test as t = sqrt(F), d = 2*t/sqrt(df_error) (equivalently r = sqrt(F/(F+df_error)), d = 2r/sqrt(1-r^2)), with the sign taken from the authors' prose description (negative for social media and video chat with FCF; negative for social media and texting with sleep; positive for video chat with sleep; unknown for texting with FCF).
d_transformation.notes: No regression coefficients, SEs, or CIs are reported, so the §4a B-to-d route cannot be used even though SD_IV (Table 1, pp. 2040-2041: social network sites 0.42, texting 0.56, video chat 0.50) and SD_FCF (17.48, Results p. 2043) are available. Only F(1, df) and p are printed (p. 2044). A point d is recoverable from F and the error df, but no CI on d is possible, the sign depends on narrative wording, and the error df come from mixed models with site and family random effects (approximate df). Sleep length is an ordinal five-category item with no SD reported. The models carry no fixed-effect covariates, so these are essentially unadjusted associations apart from site/family clustering.

(2) Sleep length: parent-reported Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children item 'How many hours of sleep does your child get on most nights?', five ordered categories (< 5, 5-7, 7-8, 8-9, 9-11 hr; Table 1 p. 2040 gives counts only, no mean or SD). How this ordinal item was coded in the LME is not stated.
