primary_models.sample: ABCD Data Release 2.0.1, complete baseline sample N = 11,877. Excluded participants without the FCF composite, then randomly selected one child per family where multiple siblings were assessed, leaving N = 9,718 (mean age 9.89, SD 0.62, range 9.00 to 10.92). Male 5,125 (52.8%), female 4,590 (47.2%). White 4,937 (50.9%), Black or African American 1,459 (15.0%), Hispanic 2,066 (21.3%), Asian 225 (2.3%), Other/mixed 1,019 (10.5%). Twins 856 (8.8%). Income < $50,000 30.4%, $50,000-$100,000 41.3%, > $100,000 28.3% (Table 1, pp. 2039-2041). Model-specific N not printed; error df range from 9,662 to 9,670, implying roughly 9,660-9,690 children per model depending on random-effect df.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional, ABCD baseline visit only. Screen media time and both outcomes (age-corrected NIH Toolbox fluid cognition composite; parent-reported sleep amount) measured at the same baseline assessment. One observation per child (one child randomly kept per family). These LMEs are post hoc follow-ups to a stacked machine-learning ensemble in which the weekday Screen Time Questionnaire total was among the 15 most important predictors of FCF; the follow-up decomposes weekday screen time by activity type. The text says activity type was 'entered as fixed effects'; the error df differ by activity type (e.g., 9,664 for social media vs 9,670 for video chat in the FCF models), which suggests each activity was tested in its own model with its own listwise N, but this is not stated explicitly. Direction of the screen-sleep relation is not stated as causal; screen activity is treated as the fixed-effect predictor in both sets of models.
primary_models.estimation: R 3.5.1 (RStudio), package lme4 (Bates et al., 2014). Linear mixed-effects models with ABCD site and family ID as random effects. Only F(1, df) and p are reported; no coefficients, standard errors, or confidence intervals. Spearman correlations among screen types (Figure S6) were also computed. No multiple-comparison correction is described for the follow-up LMEs (FDR was applied only to the Table 2 univariate Spearman correlations). The authors state that, given the large sample, the analysis focused on effect sizes rather than significance, but no effect sizes are printed. No sex or other interaction tests and no stratified results. The parent machine-learning model (stacked elastic net, SVR, conditional inference forest, kNN with repeated nested cross-validation) is described separately and does not include per-modality phone/SM predictors.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Method, Follow-Up Analyses (p. 2042); Results, Follow-Up Analyses (p. 2044, in-text F statistics; also plotted in Figure S5, not included in the PDF). FCF findings interpreted in Discussion p. 2046 and p. 2047.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The stage2_reason gives the wrong pairings. F(1,9662)=6.79 is not in the paper. Social media→FCF is F(1,9,664)=6.79, p<.01. Texting→FCF is F(1,9,669)=0.10, p=.75, which is not significant. Video chat→FCF is F(1,9,670)=27.18, p<.001. The texting F(1,9,666)=7.99 and video chat F(1,9,666)=6.81 figures are for sleep length, not FCF. I extracted both outcomes (FCF and parent-reported sleep length), since sleep is also an individual-trait outcome. 2) The paper reports only F statistics and p values: no coefficients, SEs or CIs, and no signs. Direction comes from the authors' wording ('small negative', and 'small positive' for video chat→sleep). The sign for texting→FCF is unknown. 3) The §4a rules have no F-to-d conversion. A point d is possible via d=2*sqrt(F)/sqrt(df) using approximate mixed-model df, but no CI is possible, so I marked it partial. 4) The models have no covariates beyond site and family random effects, so they are essentially unadjusted. The family random effect is odd because only one child per family was kept. 5) It is unclear whether each activity type was tested in a separate model or all were entered together. The differing error df suggest separate models. 6) Sleep length is a 5-category ordinal SDSC item with no SD reported, and its coding in the LME is not stated. 7) Figures S5/S6 and Table S1 are in an online supplement that is not in the PDF, so they were not checked. 8) The headline ML/VI and Table 2 analyses use mixed STQ totals that include TV and gaming, so they are excluded.

The PDF is the 5-page short communication only. Appendices A and B are online supporting information that was not available, so the per-modality sensitivity estimates for BMI and BMI z-score were not extracted. Site is listed as a covariate, but the paper does not say whether it is a fixed effect or a random effect. Age is not among the covariates; this is presumably because BMI percentile is already age- and sex-specific. SD_DV is the raw SD of follow-up BMI percentile (30.5), but the model adjusts for baseline BMI percentile, so the derived d values will be very small and are not comparable to cross-sectional d values. The SDs in Table 1 are propensity-weighted. The social networking estimate was not significant (p=0.075). Texting and video chat were significant.

primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 3.0, baseline and 1-year follow-up. Of 11,875 children recruited at 21 U.S. sites, participants missing baseline screen time (N = 63) or 1-year follow-up BMI (N = 752) were excluded, leaving N = 11,066. Missing covariate data (N = 1016) were singly imputed by Gaussian normal regression. Baseline age mean 9.9 (SD 0.6); 48.8% female, 51.2% male; 52.2% White, 20.0% Latino/Hispanic, 17.3% Black, 5.5% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.9% Other. Household income: 18.7% <$25,000; 20.4% $25,000-49,999; 17.5% $50,000-74,999; 13.4% $75,000-99,999; 22.6% $100,000-199,999; 7.4% >=$200,000. 79.7% had a parent with college education or more. Major depressive disorder 0.2%; binge-eating disorder 0.7%. Baseline BMI category: 3.9% underweight, 62.5% normal, 15.9% overweight, 17.8% obese (Table 1, propensity-weighted).
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort with two waves. Screen time exposures measured at ABCD baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10); the outcome, BMI percentile, measured once at the 1-year follow-up (2017-2019, ages 10-11). Baseline BMI percentile is entered as a covariate, so the coefficient is the association with follow-up BMI percentile net of baseline BMI percentile. Single follow-up outcome, not repeated measures; no time interaction. Each screen modality was examined in a separate regression model (Table 2 note: 14 regression models in total across the 7 exposures x 2 adjustment levels).
primary_models.estimation: Multiple linear regression in Stata 15.1 (analysis performed in 2020). ABCD pre-constructed propensity weights based on the American Community Survey were applied. Single imputation by Gaussian normal regression for missing covariates. Site entered as a covariate; no family clustering, but a sensitivity analysis including only one sibling per family gave similar findings (numbers not printed). Significance at p < 0.05 (bold in Table 2); no multiple-comparison correction reported. Effect modification of screen time by sex was tested and was not present (p for interaction > 0.05); no stratified estimates reported. Appendices A and B (online supporting information, not in this PDF) repeat the analyses with BMI and BMI z-score as outcomes.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1)
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV from Table 1 (p. 3), baseline screen time hours per day for the analytic N = 11,066: texting 0.56, video chat 0.52, social networking 0.45. SD_DV = 30.5, the SD of BMI percentile at 1-year follow-up in Table 1 (p. 3). Table 1 values are propensity-weighted. Because baseline BMI percentile is a covariate, B reflects association with follow-up BMI percentile net of baseline; standardizing by the raw follow-up SD (not a residual/change SD) yields a very small d and is not directly comparable to cross-sectional estimates. primary_models.estimation: Stata 15.1. Modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors (Zou 2004) to estimate prevalence ratios. Propensity weights applied to yield nationally representative estimates based on the American Community Survey. Missing exposure, outcome, and covariate data imputed with Gaussian normal regression imputation. Alpha 0.05 (bold in tables indicates p<0.05); no multiple-comparison correction reported. Effect modification by sex tested; sex did not modify any screen time association with either disorder (all p>0.05), and no sex-stratified estimates are printed. Sensitivity analyses using logistic regression and using complete cases yielded similar findings (logistic slightly stronger), data not shown. Statistical assumption checks are in supplementary Table S1 (not included in this PDF).
primary_models.iv: Baseline child-reported hours per day of three phone/SM modalities, each in its own model: texting, video chatting (e.g. Skype, Facetime), and social media (e.g. Facebook, Instagram, Twitter; labeled 'Social networking' in Tables 2-3). Instrument: ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, typical weekday and weekend hours, combined as a weighted average [(weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)]/7 and entered as a continuous variable. Prevalence ratios are per 1 hour/day. Table 1 baseline means (SD): texting 0.2 (0.6), video chat 0.2 (0.5), social media 0.1 (0.4) hours/day. The Discussion notes that 80% of the sample reported zero social media use at baseline.
primary_models.dv: Two binary outcomes at one-year follow-up, modeled separately: conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder, each derived from the parent/caregiver-completed KSADS-5 computerized interview scored to DSM-5 criteria. Prevalence at follow-up (Table 1): conduct disorder 1.9%, oppositional defiant disorder 6.3%.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study release 3.0, baseline and one-year follow-up, 21 U.S. sites. Analytic N = 11,875 (full baseline cohort). Missing data were imputed with Gaussian normal regression imputation rather than excluded: baseline screen time missing n=63, outcome missing n=793, covariate data missing N=1,016. Table 1 (propensity-weighted): mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6); 48.8% female, 51.2% male; 52.2% White, 20.0% Latino/Hispanic, 17.3% Black, 5.5% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.9% Other; 79.7% of parents with college education or more; 66.7% married/partnered. At one-year follow-up 1.9% met criteria for conduct disorder (1.1% of girls, 2.8% of boys) and 6.3% for oppositional defiant disorder (4.7% of girls, 7.9% of boys).
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort with a single follow-up outcome. Each screen time modality is measured at baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10) and the binary disorder outcome is measured once at the one-year follow-up (2017-2019, ages 10-11). One observation per child; no repeated measures and no time interaction. Each modality was entered in its own model (one modality per model; Tables 2 and 3 each summarize fourteen models across unadjusted and adjusted versions), so the phone/SM estimates are not mutually adjusted for the other screen modalities. Baseline symptoms of the respective disorder are entered as a covariate; the outcome itself was not restricted to children free of the disorder at baseline, although the Discussion describes the finding as 'new-onset' disorder.
primary_models.equation: log(Pr(Disorder_1yr[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*PhoneSM_hours_baseline[i] + b2..b6*race_ethnicity + b7*sex + b8..b12*income + b13*parent_education + b14*marital_status + b_site*site[i] + b15*baseline_disorder_symptoms + b16*baseline_MDD + b17*family_history_psychopathology (+ age per Methods); Poisson working likelihood with robust (sandwich) SEs. PR = exp(b1) per 1 hour/day. Disorder is conduct disorder or oppositional defiant disorder; PhoneSM is texting, video chat, or social media, one per model.

d_transformation.native_metric: RR (adjusted prevalence ratio from modified Poisson regression)
d_transformation.notes: p0 values are the marginal sample prevalences at one-year follow-up from Table 1 (manuscript p. 19: conduct disorder 1.9%, ODD 6.3%), not the rate in an unexposed group; with a continuous IV there is no unexposed group, and because both outcomes are rare the PR/OR distinction is small. SD_IV values are from Table 1 (manuscript p. 18; propensity-weighted, full N=11,875): texting 0.6, video chat 0.5, social media 0.4 hours/day. The IVs are heavily right-skewed with floor effects (80% report zero social media), so per-hour and per-SD contrasts may both be unrepresentative. Binary DVs, so sd_dv is null. Not directly comparable to per-1-SD d values from linear models or to group-contrast d values (e.g. paper 156).
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 hour/day of the baseline modality (continuous IV); optionally rescaled to per 1 SD using Table 1 SDs
d_transformation.conversion_formula: OR = PR * (1 - p0) / (1 - PR * p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the point estimate and each CI bound. p0 = 0.019 for conduct disorder and 0.063 for oppositional defiant disorder (marginal one-year follow-up prevalence). To express per 1 SD of the IV rather than per 1 hour/day, ln(PR) could first be multiplied by SD_IV (ln(PR_SD) = SD_IV * ln(PR)) before the PR -> OR step.

It is coded as "RR". 2) The stage2_reason gives p<.001 for video chat and texting predicting ODD. Table 3 actually prints p=0.003 for video chat and p=0.002 for texting, and the file uses the table values. 3) Age is listed as a confounder in the Methods (p. 5) but is missing from the confounder footnotes of Tables 2 and 3, so it is unclear whether age is in the final models. Site appears as an adjustment variable, not a random effect. 4) p0 uses the marginal one-year prevalences from Table 1 (CD 1.9%, ODD 6.3%), not an unexposed-group rate, because the IV is continuous. SD_IV comes from the propensity-weighted Table 1: texting 0.6, video chat 0.5, social media 0.4. These SDs differ from paper 394's ABCD descriptives. 5) Each modality was modeled separately, so the estimates are not mutually adjusted for the other modalities. The analysis uses all N=11,875 after imputation (outcome imputed for n=793). Baseline cases were not excluded even though the Discussion calls the outcome "new-onset". 6) Supplementary Tables S1 to S3 are not in the PDF. They hold assumption checks, the share of each modality with zero use, and confounder estimates, and were not reviewed. 7) The two "<0.001" p-values are stored as p=null with p_label "<0.001". papers.extraction_flags:
Each gives 4 social media paths: the slope-slope covariance, i_sm -> s_cog, i_cog -> s_sm and the intercept-intercept covariance. That makes 12 estimates.

Things to check:
(1) The native metric is the standardized beta column. The 95% CI in Table 3 is on the unstandardized Est. scale, so beta CIs are null. I kept Est., SE and CI in each estimate's note. This means the d values will have no CIs.
(2) The covariance rows are latent correlations between growth factors, not directional effects. Please decide whether to convert them to d with the r -> d formula, or to keep only the directional paths.
(3) Table 3 is inconsistent with itself in two places. For i_sm -> s_cryst, SE = 0.12 is printed next to CI [-0.15, -0.07] and p < .001. For i_cryst <-> i_sm, the CI [-0.33, 0.01] includes 0 but p = .024.
(4) For i_flanker <-> i_sm, beta = +.06, but the zero-order correlation is negative and the Discussion says the two were negatively linked at baseline.
(5) The analytic N per model is not printed (FIML). Y2 N is printed as '100,972', which is probably a typo for about 10,972. The listwise sensitivity N is 4289 and is reported only as narrative.
(6) Race appears as a covariate in the Table 3 note but not in the Covariates section.
(7) Social media hours were log-transformed. It is unclear whether the SMU M/SD in Table 1 are raw or log values; this does not matter for converting the standardized betas.

primary_models.equation: For each domain cog in {cryst, flanker, pattern}: SM[i,t] = i_sm[i] + s_sm[i]*time_t + e_sm[i,t]; COG[i,t] = i_cog[i] + s_cog[i]*time_t + e_cog[i,t], time_t = 0, 2, 4 years. i_sm = a1 + g1*X + u1; i_cog = a2 + g2*X + u2; s_sm = a3 + b1*i_cog + g3*X + u3; s_cog = a4 + b2*i_sm + g4*X + u4; Cov(u1,u2) = intercept-intercept covariance; Cov(u3,u4) = slope-slope covariance. X = sex, race, parent education, Y0 TV hours, Y0 streaming hours, Y0 video game hours. Focal terms: Cov(u3,u4) (s_cog <-> s_sm), b2 (i_sm -> s_cog), b1 (i_cog -> s_sm), Cov(u1,u2) (i_cog <-> i_sm).
primary_models.estimation: Mplus 8.3. Full-information maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR) for non-normality of social media hours; data assumed MAR with race and parent education included as auxiliary covariates. Fit benchmarks RMSEA < .06, SRMR < .08, CFI > .95, TLI > .95; reported fit CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.97-0.98, SRMR = 0.01-0.02, RMSEA = 0.03-0.04. No random effect or clustering for site or family reported, and no survey weights. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR applied to cross-construct associations (p-adjusted column in Table 3). Alpha .05. No sex or other interaction tests. Sensitivity analysis re-estimated each model with listwise deletion (N = 4289); described narratively (slope-slope findings similar; crystallized i-i association and pattern intercept-slope associations no longer significant) with no numbers printed. Mplus syntax at https://osf.io/5d9s8/.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study Release 5.1, 21 U.S. sites. Baseline N = 11,876 (mean age 9.9); Y2 printed as N = 100,972 (apparently a typo for about 10,972; mean age 12.0); Y4 N = 4754 (mean age 14.1), reduced because of the ABCD staggered data release. Missing data handled by FIML, so the analytic sample is the full baseline cohort; exact analytic N per model is not printed. Listwise-deletion sensitivity N = 4289. Baseline composition reported as White 52.0%, Hispanic 20.3%, Black 15.0%, Asian 2.1%, Other 10.5%; female 47.8%; about 41% from families with income of $100,000 or higher and 73% from married two-parent households. Missingness at Y2 and Y4 was higher for Black and Hispanic youth (OR range 1.30-1.69) and lower at Y2 for higher parent education (OR 0.87-0.89).
primary_models.design: Longitudinal, three ABCD waves: baseline (Y0, mean age 9.9), 2-year follow-up (Y2, mean age 12.0) and 4-year follow-up (Y4, mean age 14.1). Social media hours and cognitive performance are both measured at all three waves. For each cognitive domain a separate bivariate parallel-process latent growth curve model estimates an intercept and a linear slope for social media hours and for the cognitive score (slope loadings rescaled to assessment timing, 0/2/4 years). Intercept-intercept and slope-slope covariances are freely estimated, and each slope is regressed on the other construct's intercept (i_sm -> s_cog and i_cog -> s_sm), so social media appears both as predictor and as outcome within the same model. Three separate models were run (crystallized, Flanker, Pattern Comparison) with identical specification.

Table 1 reports SMU Y0 M = .12, SD = .42; Y2 M = .68, SD = 1.32; Y4 M = 1.71, SD = 2.05 (the table does not state whether these are raw or log-transformed values). In the growth model the focal social media terms are the latent intercept (i_sm, baseline level) and latent linear slope (s_sm, rate of change per year). Social media is the predictor in the i_sm -> s_cog path, the outcome in the i_cog -> s_sm path, and a correlate in the covariance paths.

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 SD of the latent predictor (for i_sm -> s_cog and i_cog -> s_sm); for the covariance rows the standardized value is a latent correlation between growth factors (slope-slope or intercept-intercept).
d_transformation.native_metric: beta_std (standardized path coefficients / standardized covariances from parallel-process LGCM)
d_transformation.notes: Standardized coefficients taken from the beta column of Table 3 (p. 8); the conversion needs no SD_IV or SD_DV, so sd_iv and sd_dv are left null. No CI is printed on the standardized scale (the 95% CI column is on the unstandardized Est. scale), so d CIs cannot be derived; unstandardized Est., SE and CI are kept in each estimate's note. The d values describe associations between latent growth factors (levels and rates of change), not per-hour associations between observed social media time and cognitive score, so they are not directly comparable to per-SD observed-variable d's from regression papers. Social media hours were log-transformed. Table 3 contains internal inconsistencies (i_sm -> s_cryst SE 0.12 with CI [-0.15, -0.07] and p < .001; i_cryst <-> i_sm CI [-0.33, 0.01] with p = .024).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines section 4a, SEM path coefficients, standardized).

d_transformation.notes: The paper reports only chi-squared statistics with FDR-corrected p-values in the main text; no B, beta, SE, CI or df. SDs for Year 2/Year 4 SM use and sleep duration are not reported (Table 1 gives demographics only; Year 4 categories are given as percentages on pp. 4-5). Coefficients may be in Supplementary Tables S1-S2, which are not in the PDF. M2 is additionally a zero-inflated model on log(x + 1) SM, which complicates any d conversion. If the supplement provides standardized coefficients, M1 (continuous standardized IV and continuous DV) could become transformable.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: None applied. Guidelines §4a give no conversion for chi-squared Wald/ANOVA test statistics from mixed models; a chi-squared(1) could in principle be converted via r = sqrt(chi2 / N) and d = 2r / sqrt(1 - r^2), but df are not reported and the statistics come from multi-predictor mixed models (partial effects), so this would not be valid without further information.

papers.extraction_flags:
The main text reports only chi-squared statistics with FDR-corrected p-values. It gives no coefficients, SEs, CIs, df, or SDs for social media use or sleep, so none of the estimates can be converted to d. Supplementary Tables S1–S3 should hold the full model output, but they are not in the PDF; someone needs to get them. If they report standardized betas, M1 might become transformable, and the SM -> brain activation model (Set 2, Table S3), which is currently excluded for having no printed numbers, could be added.

1) The main effects of SM on sleep (χ²=7.76) and of sleep on SM (χ²=6.72) are each reported once. The paper fits 12 models per set, one per brain region, and does not say which of these models the numbers come from.

2) I included the SM × ROI interaction chi-squares as phone/SM estimates in M1. In M2 I included the effects of insula and middle frontal gyrus activation on SM, with SM as the DV. Please check that both choices meet the eligibility criteria.

3) The abstract says the sleep -> SM effect was moderated by insula and middle frontal gyrus activation. The results text instead reports these as main effects of brain activation on SM and gives no interaction statistics.

4) The methods say the log(x+1) transform and the zero-inflated glmmTMB model were used for the "first set" of models, but SM is the outcome only in the third set. It is also not stated whether the chi-squares come from the conditional component or the zero-inflation component.

5) The propensity weights are mentioned, but the paper does not say how they were applied in the models.

primary_models.estimation: R; psychometrics package panelgvar function; unweighted least squares estimator (because irritability and co-occurring symptoms were treated as ordinal). Variables with significant trends detrended to facilitate stationarity. Saturated model fit: CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.98, RMSEA = 0.092. Pruned with the 'stepup' estimator at alpha = .05. 1000 bootstrap iterations; only edges with at least a 50% chance of replication in the bootstrapped model were retained (Table S1). No survey weights; no site or family clustering reported; no multiple-comparison correction beyond stepup pruning. Visualized with qgraph. Sex differences tested in a supplementary analysis (Figure S4; see M2). Unadjusted version (no ADHD/depression/anxiety nodes) in Figure S8. Edge CIs and p-values are not printed in the main text.
primary_models.equation: Panel GVAR (psychometrics::panelgvar): for person i and wave t, y[i,t] = mu_i + B*(y[i,t-1] - mu_i) + zeta[i,t], where y = {irritability, TV, video, videogame, social media, online chat, ADHD, depression, anxiety} (detrended where trends were significant). Focal temporal edges are elements of B, reported as partial correlations: B[irr <- SNS], B[irr <- chat], B[chat <- irr], B[SNS <- irr]. mu_i are person-level random means (between-person network); zeta covariance gives the contemporaneous network.
primary_models.dv: Irritability: mean of five parent-rated CBCL items (e.g., mood swings, temper tantrums) per the validated irritability measure of Cordova et al. (2022), each 0-2; Cronbach's alpha 0.806-0.810 across the three waves; treated as ordinal in the network analysis. Table 2 M (SD): baseline 0.30 (0.39), Year 1 0.29 (0.38), Year 2 0.28 (0.37). For the irritability-to-screen edges, the DV is next-wave online chat or social media hours/day (as described in the IV field).
primary_models.design: Longitudinal three-wave panel (baseline, Year 1, Year 2). All variables measured at every wave. The temporal network gives lagged within-person associations from one wave to the next (t to t+1), averaged over the two lag intervals, controlling for all variables at the previous wave, estimated as partial correlations. Bidirectional by construction: each screen node predicts later irritability and irritability predicts later screen nodes in the same model. The panel GVAR also estimates contemporaneous and between-person networks, but the authors interpret only the temporal edges. No wave-specific lagged estimates.

primary_models.iv: Youth self-report ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, typical hours per day on weekdays and weekends, 7-point scale recoded to hours: none (0), <30 min (0.25), 30 min (0.5), 1 h (1), 2 h (2), 3 h (3), 4+ h (4). Weighted daily average = [(weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)]/7; Year 2 items were rephrased slightly and recoded for consistency. Continuous. Social media (SNS) is a single modality item (e.g., Instagram). Online chat is a composite the authors formed because of low engagement: texting + video chatting (e.g., FaceTime), so it is built exclusively from phone/SM items (FT-IC2 Step 2 met). Table 2 M (SD), hours/day: SNS baseline 0.09 (0.34), Year 1 0.18 (0.50), Year 2 0.41 (0.78); Chat baseline 0.31 (0.58), Year 1 0.49 (0.77), Year 2 0.60 (0.90). Variables showing significant trends (video, videogame, online chat, social media, irritability, co-occurring symptoms) were detrended before GVAR estimation. Because the model is bidirectional, social media and online chat are both predictors (wave t) and outcomes (wave t+1); the irritability-to-chat edge treats chat as the DV.

Figures 1-3 and Tables S1-S2 (the exact edge weights and bootstrap CIs) are missing, so every edge value comes from the Results text on pp. 9-10. No CIs or p-values exist for M1 edges; sig=true is inferred from retention after stepup pruning (alpha=.05) plus at least 50% bootstrap inclusion. 2) I added an irritability-to-social-media cell with value null and sig=false, inferred because the text never reports that edge and the Discussion calls social media "unidirectional." Please verify against Table S2/Figure 3. 3) M2 (sex comparison, Figure S4) gives online chat to irritability as 0.37 in males and 0.14 in females. Both are positive and much larger than the pooled adjusted -0.03, which may be an error in the paper or a different model (unadjusted?). The p=.047 tests the sex difference, not the edge vs. zero. Decide whether M2 should be kept as a primary model. 4) Online chat is a texting + video chat composite. It qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2, but texting and video chat are never broken out separately. 5) The journal name is not printed in the PDF. I filled in Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychopharmacology from the DOI/ISSN prefix 1044-5463, so confirm it. 6) The cross-sectional GGM phone/SM edges are implied to be zero but not printed (excluded). The internalizing/externalizing temporal network (Figure S6) gives only a 0.02-0.04 range (excluded). 7) Edge weights cannot be converted to Cohen's d, so this paper goes to the later review level.json

primary_models.estimation: Generalized linear mixed model with logistic link, R package glmmTMB, parameters estimated by restricted maximum likelihood. Random intercepts for research site and siblings nested within site. No weighting reported. No multiple-comparison correction reported; significance appears to be judged at p < .05. Base vs full model compared with ANOVA F-test and BIC (full model R^2 = 0.35 vs base R^2 = 0.34, BIC = 5146.9, deltaBIC = 52.8, LRT = 84.2; the full model did not significantly improve on the base model). No interaction or stratified tests. Unadjusted group comparisons (ANOVA/chi-square, tableone) reported separately in Suppl. Table 1. Same GLMM structure repeated for five specific activities (soccer, music, swimming, baseball, art).
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD baseline visit (data collected 2016-2017). IV and DV measured at the same visit, one observation per child. Two-stage approach: first, Group Factor Analysis (GFA) on four variable groups (12 SMA items, psychopathology, cognition, social environment) yields 15 robust latent group factors (GFs); second, the averaged GF scores enter a logistic GLMM as simultaneous predictors of recreational activity involvement. A base model (sociodemographics only) was compared with the full model (sociodemographics plus all 15 GFs). No interaction terms.
primary_models.dv: Any recreational activity involvement (binary yes/no), parent report on the Sports and Activities Involvement Questionnaire, 29 activities (sports, music, art, hobbies). Dichotomized because data were positively skewed with little gradation. 89.8% of parents endorsed at least one activity (8,308 of 9,254).
primary_models.sample: ABCD Data Release 2.0.1, baseline, 21 U.S. sites. Of 11,875 enrolled, N=9,254 with complete data on all relevant measures (listwise). Ages 9-10. 8,308 youth endorsed at least one recreational activity and 946 did not. Table 1 reports demographics by group only (no-activity vs activity): age M 9.8 (SD 0.6) vs 9.9 (0.6); male 50.4% vs 52.1%; White 29.7% vs 59.3%, Black 31.3% vs 10.7%, Hispanic 26.2% vs 17.6%, Asian 1.4% vs 2.2%, Other 11.4% vs 10.3%; household income <$50K 64.6% vs 22.9%, $50-100K 25.7% vs 29.0%, >$100K 9.7% vs 48.2%; married/living together 59.3% vs 79.5%; parent age M 37.2 (7.1) vs 40.5 (6.6). Whole-sample demographics not reported.
primary_models.name: Logistic generalized linear mixed model of any recreational activity endorsement on GFA-derived texting and weekday social SMA group factor scores, adjusted for the other 13 group factors and sociodemographics
primary_models.iv: Latent group factor scores from GFA (R package 'GFA'). The SMA group comprised 12 youth-report items: hours per day (none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 4 h) on weekdays and weekends for TV shows/movies, videos, video games, messaging on a cell phone/tablet/computer, social networking sites, and video chat. GFA was repeated 10 times with different seeds; GFs whose posterior component means correlated >=0.7 across chains and that appeared in >=70% of replicates were retained, and their scores averaged across replicates. Two of the six SMA-related GFs carry phone/SM-specific labels in Fig. 5: 'Texting' and 'Weekday social SMA'. Their item loadings are shown only in supplementary figures not in this PDF, so the extent to which they load on non-phone items cannot be verified here. ORs are per 1 SD increase in the GF score (Results p. 6). Descriptive statistics for GF scores not reported.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) Phone/SM eligibility is borderline. The IVs are latent group factor scores from a GFA run on all 12 SMA items. Only the 'Texting' and 'Weekday social SMA' factors have phone/SM labels, and their loadings sit in supplementary figures that are not in this PDF, so I could not confirm they are free of non-phone items. Check Suppl. Figs. 4-15. 2) Both estimates come from Fig. 5 (p. 8), where they are printed as 'OR ± 95% CI' half-widths: 1.05 ± 0.09 and 0.96 ± 0.09. I left the CI bounds null rather than rebuilding them. Where the text gives CIs for other factors, they don't quite match a symmetric ± (games vs SM: 0.83 ± 0.07 in the figure, 0.76-0.89 in the text). No p-values are printed. Non-significance comes from the text, which says only 2 of 6 SMA factors were significant. 3) I excluded the authors' headline significant SMA finding: the 'games vs social media' bipolar factor, OR 0.83 (0.76-0.89). It contrasts games/movies/videos against social media, so the SM part is not isolated. Coders may disagree. 4) The five activity-specific GLMMs (soccer, swimming, baseball, music, art) report texting and weekday-social factor estimates only in Suppl. Figs. 16-20, which are not available. A second model card could be added if the supplement is obtained. 5) The OR is per 1 SD of a latent factor score, not per hour, so the derived d is not comparable with per-hour designs. p0 = 0.898 is the marginal endorsement rate, recorded for context only.

d_transformation.notes: All SDs from Table 1 (p. 6), weighted descriptives. SD_IV: social media time 1.62 h/day (computed on N = 9,008); SMAQ 0.90 (computed on the n = 5,642 subset with a social media account). SD_DV: positive expectancies 0.61, negative expectancies 0.78, both computed on N = 9,008, whereas Model 3 is presumably fit on the n = 5,642 subset; SDs in that subset are not reported, so the sample-level SDs are an approximation. Social media time is heavily right-skewed (M 0.71, SD 1.62).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1); CI endpoints converted the same way.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1-SD change in the IV (B itself is per 1 hour/day of social media time, or per 1 point of SMAQ mean score)

d_transformation.notes: SD_DV = 10 is the CBCL t-score norming SD; the paper does not report the sample SD of the year-3 anxiety or depression t-scores (Tables 1-2 give no outcome descriptives). Because ABCD CBCL DSM-5 t-scores are floored at 50 and right-skewed, the actual sample SD is likely below 10, so d computed with SD = 10 may understate the standardized difference. SD_IV is not applicable (categorical group contrast), so sd_iv is null; d is a group-difference d, not a per-1-SD or per-hour slope, and is not directly comparable with per-SD d's from continuous-IV papers. Group main effects are conditional on the no-substance-use stratum because the model includes group x substance use interactions; since 98% of the sample is in that stratum the difference from a marginal effect is expected to be small. Table 4 footnote labels the coefficients as 'standardized regression coefficient', but the Results text describes the interaction estimates as t-score points (e.g., '9.84-point higher depression t-score') and the magnitudes match t-score units, so they were coded as unstandardized B.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Dichotomous contrast (group k vs reference group) on a continuous DV: d = (adjusted M_k - M_1) / SD_pooled = B / SD_DV, with SD_DV = 10 (CBCL t-score norm). CI endpoints converted the same way.
d_transformation.native_metric: B (unstandardized adjusted mean difference in t-score points, group k vs Group 1)
d_transformation.contrast_type: Membership in social media trajectory group k (2, 3, 4, or 5) versus the Persistent Low Use group (Group 1), among participants with no alcohol/e-cigarette use (reference level of the moderator)

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The Table 4 footnote calls the coefficients a "standardized regression coefficient". But the Results text describes them as t-score points, and their size fits t-score units, so I coded them as unstandardized B. A human should confirm this. 2) The IV is social media trajectory group membership from GBTM, compared against the Persistent Low Use group. That makes d a group-difference d (B/10) using the CBCL norm SD of 10. The paper reports no sample SD for the year-3 t-scores. Those scores are floored at 50 and right-skewed, so the real SD is probably below 10 and d may be understated. 3) The model includes group x substance-use interactions, so the group main effects apply only to the no-substance-use stratum, which is 98% of the sample. 4) The trajectory window runs from baseline to Y3 and overlaps the Y3 outcome, and baseline CBCL is not adjusted for. 5) The authors call the social media analysis exploratory, and the coding of the social media item changed between Y1 and Y2. 6) Group 4 n is 266 in the Results text but 226 in Table 2. 226 sums to N = 9,474, so I used 226. 7) Two p-values print as '< 0.001', and I stored 0.001 as the bound. 8) Supplementary Table 1 (GBTM fit indices) is not included in the PDF. The total screen time trajectory model (Table 3) is excluded because it bundles TV and gaming.json

primary_models.estimation: Two-stage. GBTM in Stata 17; regression in R 4.3.3. Ordinary multiple linear regression with complex survey weights applied to adjust for sampling design and attrition. No random effects for site or family are reported. alpha = 0.05 implied by bolded p-values. No multiple-comparison correction reported. Effect modification by alcohol/e-cigarette use tested through the interaction terms (for anxiety only 3*Unknown reached p < .05, p = 0.049, printed unbolded; for depression only 3*Unknown, p = 0.013; the authors conclude no moderation). Sex interactions were not tested (listed as future work). No sensitivity analyses reported. GBTM fit indices for 2-6 class solutions are in Supplementary Table 1, which is not bundled in the PDF. primary_models.iv: Social media trajectory group membership from GBTM (5 groups; Group 1 Persistent Low Use is the reference). Social media use was self-reported by the youth in hours per weekday and weekend day, standardized across follow-ups to make it comparable with the screen time variable, and aggregated to hours/week. GBTM fit 2-6 group solutions and chose the 5-group solution by BIC, polynomial order, entropy (> 0.8), posterior probability (> 0.7), and group size (> 2.5%). Group descriptions (Results p. 4, Fig. 1b): Group 1 Persistent Low Use (42.6%), less than 1 h/week, order 2; Group 2 Gradual Increase to Moderate Use (43.9%), reaching about 7 h/week, order 3; Group 3 Sharp Increase to High Use (7.2%), peaking at 25 h/week, order 3; Group 4 Moderate Increase to High Use (2.4%), peaking at 19 h/week, order 2; Group 5 Fluctuating High Use (3.9%), reaching 20 h/week, order 3. The authors note the social media item coding changed between the Y1 and Y2 follow-ups. Each coefficient is the adjusted difference in t-score between a group and Group 1.

primary_models.name: Survey-weighted multiple linear regression of year-3 CBCL anxiety and depression t-scores on social media trajectory group (GBTM), adjusted for demographics with a trajectory group x alcohol/e-cigarette use interaction
primary_models.design: Longitudinal two-stage design. Stage 1: group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) of self-reported social media hours/week across four ABCD waves (baseline, Y1, Y2, Y3; ages 9-10 to 12-13) assigns each participant to one of five latent trajectory groups. Stage 2: the trajectory group enters as a categorical IV in a linear regression predicting CBCL anxiety and depression t-scores measured once, at the year-3 follow-up. The DV is a single follow-up outcome, not repeated measures. Because the trajectory spans baseline through Y3, the IV window overlaps the wave at which the DV is measured. No baseline CBCL score is adjusted for. Two separate regressions are run, one per DV (anxiety, depression), with the same specification.
primary_models.dv: Two continuous parent-reported outcomes at the year-3 follow-up: CBCL DSM-5-oriented anxiety t-score and CBCL DSM-5-oriented depression t-score (ABCD-provided t-scores, range 50-97, higher = more symptoms). Sample means and SDs of the t-scores are not reported. The authors note the t-scores were right-skewed.

papers.authors: Parker MA, Harton MR, Mattey-Mora PP, Streck JM

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per one unit of the social media variable, which the authors describe as one hour/day; the Methods also state ST was categorized into four groups (<1 h, 1-1.99 h, 2-2.99 h, >=3 h), so one unit may be one category step.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: IRR treated as OR at first approximation, d = ln(IRR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), with ln(IRR) = B; CI on d from the printed B CI endpoints, d_lo/hi = B_lo/hi * sqrt(3)/pi. M2: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV, d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2). M3: not converted.
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV = 1.15 h/day for social media and SD_DV = 1.11 h for sleep duration and CBCL raw-score SDs are from Table 1 (p. 4), full baseline sample (n = 11,769 for social media, 11,869 for sleep, 11,864 for CBCL). CBCL scales are raw scores, not T-scores, so SD_DV is not 10. The M2 conversion assumes the IV is in hours/day; if the model used the 4-category coding, SD_IV in hours is the wrong scale. The aggressive behavior CI (.029, .053) printed in Table 2 excludes its own point estimate (.06), so its d CI should be treated with caution. papers.extraction_flags:
It has three cards, all from one Mplus negative binomial SEM:
- M1: 8 direct effects of social media on the 8 CBCL raw scales. The metric is IRR, and B with its CI is stored alongside.
- M2: the social media -> sleep duration path. The metric is B.
- M3: 8 indirect effects of social media through sleep, none significant.

Please check:
(1) The IV units are unclear. The Methods say screen-time behaviors were binned into 4 groups (<1, 1-1.99, 2-2.99, >=3 h), but the Results read coefficients as per one hour. The SD_IV of 1.15 h/day comes from Table 1 and may be on the wrong scale for converting M2.
(2) Table 2 prints the CIs on the B (log) scale only. No IRR CI is printed, so IRR_lo and IRR_hi are null.
(3) In Table 2, the CI for social media -> aggressive behavior is printed as (.029, .053), which excludes its own B of .06. This looks like a typo in the paper. I copied it as printed.
(4) The paper does not state the distribution of the sleep-duration path. I assumed it is linear, yet Table 2 still prints an 'IRR' of .968 for it.
(5) Social media is a composite of texting, social networking sites, and video chat. All three are phone/SM items, so it qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2. There are no per-item estimates.
(6) The CBCL outcomes are raw counts, not T-scores. SD_DV values come from Table 1, which uses the full baseline sample. Converting IRR to d via Chinn is only a rough approximation for negative binomial outcomes.
(7) The ABCD release number is not stated, and the TYPE=COMPLEX cluster variable is not named.
(8) Supplement Additional file 1 was not bundled in the PDF.

I checked every social media number against the PDF text layer (Tables 2 and 3) and all of them match.

primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0 (September 2021); baseline 2017-2018 and one-year follow-up 2018-2019, both pre-COVID. Of 11,876 enrolled, 156 were dropped for missing baseline exposure or covariate data (85 BMI z-score, 39 socializing, 7 gaming, 9 streaming, 10 physical activity, 4 internalizing, 2 race/ethnicity), 777 for missing follow-up BMI z-score, 78 for BMI z-score < -3 at baseline or follow-up, and 321 for > 13 h/day screen time (reports summing to > 24 h/day), giving an isotemporal substitution analytic N = 10,544 (Fig. 1). Analyses stratified by caregiver-reported sex assigned at birth: females n = 5,058 (48.9% weighted), males n = 5,486. Weighted mean (SE) baseline age 9.9 (0.03) in females and 10.0 (0.03) in males. Race/ethnicity, females / males, n (weighted %): Asian 120 (4.0%) / 107 (3.3%); Black 693 (12.3%) / 679 (11.0%); Hispanic 996 (23.0%) / 1,095 (23.5%); Other/Multiracial 534 (6.9%) / 565 (6.7%); White 2,715 (53.8%) / 3,040 (55.5%). Overall 45.4% non-White. Income-to-needs ratio range 0.1-15.4; 972 'not reported'.
primary_models.iv: Baseline socializing screen time, defined as the sum of youth-reported texting, video chatting, and using social networking sites from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey (weekday and weekend items; response options none, <30 min coded 0.5 h, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 4+ h coded 4.8 h). Usual daily hours = weekday*0.71 + weekend*0.29, converted to minutes/day, then divided by 30 so one unit = 30 min/day. Weighted mean (SE) socializing: females 31.5 (2.0) min/day, males 22.3 (1.9) min/day (Table 1); overall 26.8 (1.9) min/day; 4,623 participants reported 0 min/day. Each estimate is a 30-min substitution: either 30 more min of socializing replacing 30 min of streaming, gaming, physical activity, or sleep, or 30 more min of one of those behaviors replacing 30 min of socializing. Other behaviors: streaming (TV shows/movies + videos e.g. YouTube), gaming (video games), physical activity (YRBSS days active >=60 min x 60 / 7), sleep (caregiver SDSC single item, category midpoints in minutes). SD of socializing not reported (only SE of mean).
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2 (p. 7); methods p. 4 (Isotemporal substitution analysis); results p. 5; interpreted in Abstract and Discussion pp. 8-9.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal, two waves. All behaviors (including socializing) and covariates measured at ABCD baseline (2017-2018); outcome is BMI z-score at the one-year follow-up (2018-2019), a single follow-up value per child, with baseline BMI z-score as a covariate. Not repeated measures. Isotemporal substitution: for each sex, five linear regressions are fit, each dropping one behavior while keeping the other four plus total time, so each coefficient is the association of adding 30 min of the row behavior while removing 30 min of the dropped (column) behavior. Socializing is the qualifying phone/SM variable and appears both as the behavior added (row) and the behavior displaced (column). Phone/SM is the IV.
primary_models.equation: For sex s and dropped (displaced) behavior R: BMIz_FU[i] = b0 + sum over k != R of b_k*(time_k[i]/30) + b_T*(total_time[i]/30) + b_age*age + b_race*race/ethnicity dummies + b_SES*income-to-needs dummies + b_int*internalizing + b_bmi*BMIz_baseline + e[i], where k ranges over {socializing, streaming, gaming, physical activity, sleep}. b_k is the association with adding 30 min/day of behavior k while removing 30 min/day of behavior R. Focal cells: k = socializing (R = each other behavior) and R = socializing (k = each other behavior).
primary_models.estimation: Linear regression with complex survey design in SAS v9.4 SURVEY procedures; study site specified as the cluster variable and ABCD sample weights applied to approximate the American Community Survey. Model formulation informed by a DAG (Supplemental Fig. 1, not bundled in this PDF). All analyses stratified by sex; no formal sex interaction test reported. Significance flagged *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001; exact p-values not printed. No multiple-comparison correction reported. Sensitivity analysis including participants whose reported time summed to > 24 h/day said to give qualitatively similar results (data not shown).

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The qualifying IV is the 'socializing' composite (texting + video chat + social networking sites). Under §5 it counts as phone/SM-only, so it was extracted as the IV. 2) M1 is an isotemporal substitution model. For each sex I extracted all 8 cells that involve socializing in Table 2: the 4 cells in the ↑Socializing row, where socializing is added, and the 4 in the ↓Socializing column, where socializing is displaced. Each cell comes from a different drop-one regression. The authors anchor their claims on the column cells (PA replaces socializing in females; gaming and sleep replace socializing in males). Coders should decide whether to keep both directions. 3) For both models, Table 1 gives only weighted mean (SE), not SD, so sd_iv and sd_dv are null and d_transformable is false. BMI z has a reference SD of 1, but the sample SD is not reported. 4) No exact p-values are printed. M1 uses asterisks, which I recorded in p_label. M2 counts as significant when the CI excludes 0. 5) In Table 2, the females ↑Streaming/↓Socializing estimate is printed as '.003'; I recorded it as 0.003. 6) In the M2 equation, the sqrt(5/6) ILR scaling is my standard-SBP reconstruction; the paper does not print it. 7) Supplemental Table 1 and Supplemental Fig. 1 (the CoDA sensitivity analysis and the DAG) are not in the bundled PDF. 8) M2 drops the 4,623 participants with zero socializing, so it is a selected subsample (N = 5,164).

Would require beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein 2009 eq 7.1), but no SDs are reported and the M1 contrast is a fixed-total-time substitution rather than a one-unit change in a single IV. BMI z-score has reference-population SD 1 by construction, but the sample SD is not reported and the IV SD is still missing. Isotemporal substitution coefficients are conditional on total time and on the displaced behavior, so even with SDs a per-SD d would have no single-IV interpretation. CoDA ILR coefficients are not convertible without the SD of the ILR coordinate. Exact p-values are not printed for either model (M1 uses asterisks; M2 uses CI excluding 0).

Of those enrolled, 3,305 were missing depression symptom data, 51 missing dating app data and 162 missing sociodemographic data, giving 8,444 complete cases (Appendix A). papers.extraction_flags: 1) The paper calls its coefficients "standardized beta" but never says which variables were standardized. A fully standardized beta of 0.42 is implausible for a binary IV with 0.9% prevalence, so the value is probably standardized on Y only (d-like) or in raw score points. The r-to-d rule in guidelines 4a gives d of about 0.93, while passing the value through gives d of about 0.42. A human needs to choose before converting. 2) The PDF has only the 6 main-text pages. Appendices A-E are online-only, so the M2 values (youth-reported internalizing, Appendix E: 0.66, 0.34-0.99, p<0.001) and the Appendix D sensitivity values (0.44, 0.03-0.85, p=0.035) come from the Results text and could not be checked against the appendix tables. M2's covariates and N are assumed to match M1. 3) The 'don't know what a dating app is' vs never-used estimate (0.04, -0.33 to 0.41, p=0.817) is included in M1 with a note. It is not a use contrast, so coders may want to strike it. 4) N=11,530 is after multiple imputation of the exposure and the outcome; there are 8,444 complete cases. 5) SD_IV is not reported (binary exposure). SD_DV is 2.9 (Table 1).json

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Coefficients are treated as Y-standardized mean differences for a binary IV (ever used vs never used dating apps), i.e. already on the Cohen's d scale: d = beta. Not passed through r -> d.
d_transformation.notes: Paper labels them 'standardized betas' without saying which variables were standardized. With a binary IV at 0.9% prevalence a fully standardized beta of 0.42-0.66 is impossible, so they are read as Y-standardized group differences (SD units of the outcome) and used directly as d. Coders should confirm against Appendix E. The paper labels coefficients as standardized betas from linear regression but does not say whether X, Y, or both were standardized. With a binary IV at 0.9% prevalence, a fully standardized beta of 0.42 would be implausibly large, so the value most likely reflects Y-standardized units (i.e., a mean difference of about 0.42 SD of the depression score, d-like) or possibly raw score points. SD_DV for CBCL depression sum score = 2.9 (Table 1, p. 3). SD_IV not reported (binary indicator, 0.9% used, Table 1). Applying r-to-d to 0.42 gives a very different d than passthrough, so the human coder should decide which interpretation applies before conversion. M2 SD_DV not available (Appendix E not in PDF).

papers.extraction_flags:
The qualifying estimates are missing from the PDF. All of the texting, social media and video chat coefficients are in Supplementary Tables S6-S31: S6-S18 cover weekday use and S19-S31 cover weekend use, with one table per outcome, each split by sex. PLOS ONE publishes these as separate DOCX files, and they are not bundled in the 23-page PDF. Pages 18-21 list only their titles. I did not download them, because downloading a file needs explicit permission.

I set up two model cards. M1 covers weekday use (N=11,727) and M2 covers weekend use (N=11,672). Each card has the full specification, 6 IV slots (3 modalities x 2 sexes) and 13 DV slots, but the estimates are empty (n_estimates = 0). A human needs to get S6-S31, for example from journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0256591, and fill in about 156 cells (2 day types x 2 sexes x 3 modalities x 13 outcomes).

Things to check against the supplement:
(1) Whether each screen type was its own regression or all types were entered together in one regression per outcome. The PDF does not say.
(2) Whether the supplement tables report standardized beta, t, p, SE and partial r, like Tables 3 and 5. I assumed beta_std is the native metric.
(3) Race/ethnicity (coded 1-5) and SES (coded 1-10) look like they were entered as single numeric predictors, because Tables 2 and 4 show one coefficient each. The paper does not confirm this.
(4) These per-type analyses are labelled secondary and tested at alpha .05 with no correction.

SD_IV for each modality, day type and sex comes from Table 1 (p. 8). I spot-checked all 12 against the table. SD_DV for the CBCL outcomes is set to 10 by construction, but the in-sample SDs are about 5-11. That does not matter for conversion, because beta_std converts directly once the values are in. d_transformable is false only because no values are available yet. It becomes true once the supplement is entered.

The ABCD release number is not stated; the paper cites only NDA DOI 10.15154/1519271. The headline total-screen-time models in Tables 2-5 were excluded because total screen time includes TV, videos and gaming.

d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: smartphone owner vs non-owner at age 12. M2: per 1 year earlier age of first smartphone acquisition (inverted OR, positive d = earlier acquisition associated with higher odds of the adverse outcome). M3: acquired a smartphone in the past year vs did not, net of the prior-year outcome.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.notes: All estimates are adjusted odds ratios printed in the Results text (pp. 5-6) and matching Figures 2-3; no values were read off a figure. Chinn conversion needs no SDs. p0 for M1 is the outcome prevalence in non-owners from Table 1 (p. 17): depression 4.52%, obesity 11.80%, insufficient sleep 31.02%. p0 for M2 is the outcome prevalence among owners from Table 1 (there is no unexposed group for a continuous IV). p0 for M3 is not reported: Table 2 gives only 2-year (pre-exposure) prevalences, not 3-year outcome rates. SD of age at acquisition is not reported (median 11, IQR 10-11), so M2 cannot be put on a per-1-SD basis; its d is per one year earlier. M2 d values are not directly comparable to the group-contrast d values of M1 and M3.

papers.title: Smartphone Ownership, Age of Smartphone Acquisition, and Health Outcomes in Early Adolescence
Digital Media, Genetics, and Risk for ADHD Symptoms in Children: A Longitudinal Study
papers.extraction_flags:
1. The supplement is not bundled in the 10-page PDF. As a result, the M2 cumulative-change covariates, the CLPM (M3) covariates, missing-data handling and estimator, the full M4 reverse-direction spec, Supplemental Tables 1-8 (moderation and sensitivity analyses) and analytic Ns other than 8,324 could not be checked.
2. The 'social media use' IV is a composite of texting, social networking sites and video chat (YSTS items 4+5+6). All three items are phone/SM, so it qualifies under Step 2. Texting is asked as cell phone/tablet/computer, which is activity-defined and qualifies under clarification 5.
3. The exposure is averaged over T0-T4, the same waves as the outcome, so the IV and DV are not temporally ordered in M1 and M2.
4. In M1 the authors anchor on the SM x time interaction, which gives a difference in yearly slope. A d derived from it is a per-year rate. I included the three-way SM x time x PGS-ADHD terms as estimates and flagged them as not convertible; a coder may prefer to strike them.

primary_models.design: Longitudinal cohort, ABCD baseline (T0, ages 9-10) and four annual follow-ups (T1-T4). The outcome enters as repeated measures at T0-T4 (not averaged), with random intercepts and slopes. The exposure is a single time-invariant value per child: average daily social media hours across all available visits (T0-T4), chosen by the authors to absorb the COVID-19-era increase in use. The focal longitudinal term is the two-way social media use x time interaction (described by the authors as the between-person longitudinal effect, i.e. difference in yearly symptom slope); the social media main effect is the association with symptom level at time = 0. A three-way social media use x time x PGS-ADHD term tests genetic moderation of the slope. Because the exposure is averaged over the same waves as the outcome, IV and DV are not strictly temporally ordered.

papers.extraction_flags:
1. The supplement is not bundled in the 10-page PDF. As a result, the M2 cumulative-change covariates, the CLPM (M3) covariates, missing-data handling and estimator, the full M4 reverse-direction spec, Supplemental Tables 1-8 (moderation and sensitivity analyses) and analytic Ns other than 8,324 could not be checked.
2. The 'social media use' IV is a composite of texting, social networking sites and video chat (YSTS items 4+5+6). All three items are phone/SM, so it qualifies under Step 2. Texting is asked as cell phone/tablet/computer, which is activity-defined and qualifies under clarification 5.
3. The exposure is averaged over T0-T4, the same waves as the outcome, so the IV and DV are not temporally ordered in M1 and M2.
4. In M1 the authors anchor on the SM x time interaction, which gives a difference in yearly slope. A d derived from it is a per-year rate. I included the three-way SM x time x PGS-ADHD terms as estimates and flagged them as not convertible; a coder may prefer to strike them.
5. Table 2 prints only beta (SE) with Bonferroni footnote markers. Cells without a marker are coded sig=false with p null. CIs are null throughout and the SEs are in the notes.
6. In M3 the CLPM cross-lagged values look constrained equal across lags; this is inferred from the figure.
7. The M4 total effect (-0.01) has no SE or p. sig=false is set only because no test is reported.
8. The Figure 2 caption quartile cutoffs (0.61/1.22/1.97) disagree with the Figure 2B panel legend (0.54/1.36/1.86).
9. The year is recorded as 2025 per items.json, but the journal issue is Vol 2, Issue 1, 2026.
10. Spot-checked all 9 Table 2 social media cells plus the in-text values 0.15, 0.03/p=.004, -0.002/p=.64 and -0.01/SE 0.001 against the PDF text layer; all match.

primary_models.design: Longitudinal cohort, ABCD baseline (T0, ages 9-10) and four annual follow-ups (T1-T4). The outcome enters as repeated measures at T0-T4 (not averaged), with random intercepts and slopes. The exposure is a single time-invariant value per child: average daily social media hours across all available visits (T0-T4), chosen by the authors to absorb the COVID-19-era increase in use. The focal longitudinal term is the two-way social media use x time interaction (described by the authors as the between-person longitudinal effect, i.e. difference in yearly symptom slope); the social media main effect is the association with symptom level at time = 0. A three-way social media use x time x PGS-ADHD term tests genetic moderation of the slope. Because the exposure is averaged over the same waves as the outcome, IV and DV are not strictly temporally ordered.

Total CLPN sample N = 3,954 (abstract and Table 1); this female network N = 1,863 (47.12% of the CLPN sample). Females: age at T2 143.21 months (SD 7.77), age at T4 168.53 months (SD 7.88). primary_models.design: Longitudinal two-wave cross-lagged panel network (CLPN). Predictors are the 20 nodes measured at the ABCD 2-year follow-up (T2, ages 11-12, 2018-2020); outcomes are the same 20 nodes at the 4-year follow-up (T4, ages 13-14, 2020-2022). Each T4 node is regressed on all 20 T2 nodes, including its own T2 value (autoregressive path), so each cross-lagged coefficient is the prediction of a T4 node by a T2 node adjusted for all other T2 nodes. The 20 nodes are 3 problematic-use nodes (A1 problematic video game, A2 problematic social media, A3 problematic mobile phone), 8 CBCL syndrome scales (C1-C8), 3 behavioral-tendency nodes (UPPS, BIS, BAS) and 6 environmental nodes (E1-E6). Screen-time and phone-checking nodes from the cross-sectional networks were not carried into the CLPN. 20 x 19 = 380 possible cross-lagged edges per network. Single follow-up, no repeated measures beyond the two waves. Networks estimated separately by sex.
primary_models.native_metric: other:CLPN cross-lagged edge (LASSO-penalized regression coefficient B on standardized residuals)
primary_models.estimation: R (glmnet for LASSO; qgraph for plotting; bootnet; NetworkComparisonTest). LASSO-penalized maximum-likelihood regression with 10-fold cross-validation to select the tuning parameter. No random effects or weights; one child randomly selected per family to ensure independence. Missing data: minimum-value imputation for structurally missing problematic-use items, predictive mean matching for remaining missingness (MCAR per Little's test, eFigs 2-4). No p-values, confidence intervals or multiple-comparison correction are reported for individual cross-lagged edges; edges reported in text are non-zero LASSO coefficients and the authors describe them as significant associations. Mean autoregressive B: female 0.406, male 0.391; mean cross-lagged B: female 0.012, male 0.013. Stability via CS coefficients (eFig. 12); female/male network structure correlation r = 0.47, t = 10.382, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.39, 0.55]. Sensitivity analyses with pairwise deletion and categorical problematic-use indicators reported only in supplementary eFigs 18 and 21 (narrative: results stable). Sex differences handled by stratification; no formal sex x edge test for the CLPN.

primary_models.estimation: R (glmnet for LASSO; qgraph for plotting; bootnet; NetworkComparisonTest). LASSO-penalized maximum-likelihood regression with 10-fold cross-validation to select the tuning parameter. No random effects or weights; one child randomly selected per family to ensure independence. Missing data: minimum-value imputation for structurally missing problematic-use items, predictive mean matching for remaining missingness (MCAR per Little's test, eFigs 2-4). No p-values, confidence intervals or multiple-comparison correction are reported for individual cross-lagged edges; edges reported in text are non-zero LASSO coefficients and the authors describe them as significant associations. Mean autoregressive B: female 0.406, male 0.391; mean cross-lagged B: female 0.012, male 0.013. Stability via CS coefficients (eFig. 12); female/male network structure correlation r = 0.47, t = 10.382, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.39, 0.55]. Sensitivity analyses with pairwise deletion and categorical problematic-use indicators reported only in supplementary eFigs 18 and 21 (narrative: results stable). Sex differences handled by stratification; no formal sex x edge test for the CLPN.
primary_models.dv: T4 nodes on the other side of the cross-lagged edge. CBCL syndrome scales, caregiver-report (C1 anxious/depressed, C2 withdrawn/depressed, C3 somatic complaints, C4 social problems, C5 thought problems, C6 attention problems, C7 rule-breaking, C8 aggressive); impulsivity from the brief UPPS-P (UPPS); Behavioral Inhibition (BIS) and Behavioral Activation (BAS) from the BIS/BAS scale; environmental factors E1 family conflict (FES conflict subscale), E2 prosocial peer involvement (Peer Behavior Profile, reverse scored), E3 delinquent peer involvement / peer rule-break (Peer Behavior Profile), E4 perceived school environment (SRPF, reverse scored, so higher = more adverse), E5 positive school involvement (SRPF, reverse scored, so higher = less involvement), E6 school disengagement (SRPF). Whether CBCL raw or T-scores were used is not stated. All entered as standardized residuals after covariate adjustment.

papers.extraction_flags:
1. Where the numbers come from: every estimate is a B copied from the Results text on pp. 730-731. The paper has no results table, and the full edge matrix is in supplementary eTable 10, which is not in the PDF. Fig. 4B hides edges with |B| < 0.05. So only the edges the authors chose to report in the text are extracted. There may be other A2/A3 edges that are non-zero but not reported.

2. pdftotext drops minus signs. I checked the page image: A2→C5 in the female network is B = −0.251. The positive signs on the other A2/A3 edges match the narrative text.

3. No SE, CI or p-value is reported for any edge. I set sig=true on every estimate on the basis that the edge is non-zero after LASSO and the authors describe these as significant associations. A coder should decide whether that is acceptable.

4. The male A2→C1 edge is printed with the symbol β instead of B (0.113). I assume it is the same metric as the other edges.

5. On d_transformable=false: the paper says covariate-residualized standardized residuals were used, so the coefficients may in effect be in SD units. However, they are LASSO-shrunk and conditional on 19 other T2 nodes, including the autoregressive term. Following the rule that network edges are non-convertible, I marked the paper not transformable. A coder could choose to treat them as approximate beta_std instead.

6. E4 (perceived school environment) and E5 (positive school involvement) are reverse-scored. A positive B therefore means a more adverse school environment and lower school involvement. Whether perceived school environment counts as an individual-trait or a contextual variable should be checked.

7. Cross-sectional GGM edges involving social media time (B2), checking (B3), A2 and A3 with CBCL/UPPS/BIS/BAS appear only in figures (Fig. 2A, Fig. 3) and in supplementary eTables 8-9. I excluded them rather than read values off the figures. A coder may want to pull eTable 8 from the online supplement.

8. Whether CBCL raw scores or T-scores were used is not stated. The PDF reports no SDs for SMAQ, MPIQ or the outcomes.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) M1 (Table 2) treats phone/SM minutes as the DV and parent-reported autism status as the IV. Autism counts as a clinical-diagnosis trait, so it qualifies, but please confirm. The native metric is a Poisson-GEE ratio of means. No SDs are reported for minutes/day, so d can only be approximated by the rough rate-ratio-as-OR route, which makes M1 effectively non-convertible. 2) "Social and video chat" combines social networking sites with video chat. That composite is entirely phone/SM, so it is extracted as a qualifying IV/DV. 3) The overall p-value for texting and obesity conflicts within the paper: the abstract says 0.02, while Table 3 and the Results text say 0.04. Separately, the pairwise texting 30+ min PR is 1.42 (1.00-2.01) with printed p = 0.05, which I coded sig=false. Please check that call. 4) The paper does not say whether Table 3's all-children PRs come from a model that includes the autism factor or are marginal. Tables 3 and 5 are in one card (M2), with obesity columns for all children, autism and TD. p0 varies by panel, so I put it on each estimate (reference-row prevalence) and left it null on dv_axis. Please confirm the pipeline reads p0 per estimate. 5) The printed prevalences do not equal raw n/N (for example 5/20 is shown as 23.9%), which suggests they are model-based. 6) The ABCD data release is not stated. There are no covariates beyond propensity matching on age, gender, race/ethnicity and SEP, and no multiple-comparison correction.

primary_models.estimation: SAS 9.4. Generalized linear models estimated with generalized estimating equations; Poisson distribution with log link chosen because screen time was count-like and positively skewed; compound-symmetry working correlation for within-site clustering. Effect reported as ratio of means (autism / TD) with 95% CI. Alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. No sample or propensity weights beyond 1:5 matching. No sensitivity analyses reported.

d_transformation.notes: p0 for M2 comes from the reference-row prevalences in Table 3 (14.8% social/video chat, 15.2% texting) and Table 5 (autism 17.6% / TD 14.2% social/video chat; autism 16.6% / TD 14.8% texting), p. 5-6. Exposure prevalence is not small (e.g., 30+ min texting 12.5% of sample) but p0 is the unexposed-group rate, so the RR-to-OR conversion is exact under the guideline formula. M1 has no SD for any DV (only group means in Table 2), so its d is only the Poisson-rate-ratio approximation, which is weak for skewed continuous minutes; treat M1 d's with caution. Neither contrast is a per-SD contrast, so these d's are not directly comparable to per-SD d's from papers like 394.
d_transformation.native_metric: M1: ratio of means (Poisson GEE, log link); M2: prevalence ratio (log-binomial GEE)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M2: OR = RR * (1 - p0) / (1 - RR * p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), with p0 = printed obesity prevalence in the 0-min reference category of the same panel. M1: if treated as a Poisson rate ratio per guidelines §4a, d ~ ln(ratio) * sqrt(3)/pi as a first approximation; an exact d = (M_autism - M_TD)/SD_pooled is not possible because SDs of minutes/day are not reported.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: autism vs typically developing (within boys, within girls), on phone/SM minutes per day. M2: duration category (1-44 or 45+ min social/video chat; 1-29 or 30+ min texting) vs 0 min, on obesity.
